**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 13, Verse 5:**

There are two opinions regarding the verse:

The first: "If you are amazed at their saying, ﴿When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾"

Then their saying is amazing! How can they deny this when they were created from dust and were nothing?

The second: "If you are amazed at their associating others with Allah, and their failure to submit to His Tawhid and to worship Him alone, without partner, then their denial of the Resurrection and their saying, ﴿When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5] is even more amazing."

According to both interpretations, denying the return (al-ma'ad) is an amazing thing on the part of a human being. It is pure denial of the Lord, disbelief in Him, and rejection of His divinity, His power, His wisdom, His justice, and His authority.

**(Benefit)**

Amazement (al-ta'ajjub) indicates Allah's love for an action, as in: "Your Lord is amazed at a young man who has no inclination toward sinful pleasures," and "Your Lord is amazed at a man who rises from his bed and his warm covering to pray," and similar expressions.

It may also indicate the act itself to some degree, as in His saying: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾, and His saying: ﴿Rather, you are amazed, while they mock﴾, and: ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah, while you are recited to by the verses of Allah?﴾

It may also indicate the impossibility of a ruling and its unsuitability, as in: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists?﴾ And it may indicate the wrongness of prohibiting something and that such an act does not befit Him, as in: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?﴾ ...

[Section: Those who relied on the pardon of God and neglected His command and prohibition]

Many of the ignorant have relied upon the mercy, pardon and generosity of God, and have neglected His command and His prohibition, forgetting that He is severe in punishment, and that His might is not turned away from the wrongdoing people. Whoever relies on pardon while persisting in sin is like one who is obstinate.

Ma'ruf said: Your hope for the mercy of One whom you do not obey is [a sign of] humiliation and foolishness.

Some scholars said: One who cuts off a limb of yours in this world for stealing three dirhams—you cannot be sure that his punishment in the Hereafter will not be of this same kind.

It was said to al-Hasan: "We see you weeping much." He said: "I fear that He will cast me into the Fire and not care."

He used to say: Some people have been distracted by the wishful thinking of forgiveness until they left this world without repentance. One of them says: "Because I think well of my Lord"—and he lies. Had he truly thought well of Him, he would have done good deeds.

A man asked al-Hasan: "O Abu Sa'id, how should we act regarding sitting with people who frighten us until our hearts nearly fly away?" He said: "By God, to keep company with people who frighten you until you attain security is better for you than to keep company with people who give you security until the terrors overtake you."

It is established in the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Usama ibn Zayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and cast into the Fire, and his entrails will spill out, and he will go round in the Fire as a donkey goes round its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what has befallen you? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good and not do it myself, and forbid you from evil and do it myself.'"

Imam Ahmad related from the hadith of Abu Rafi', who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by al-Baqi' and said: 'Uff to you!' I thought he meant me. He said: 'No, but this is the grave of so-and-so. I sent him as a collector to the family of so-and-so, and he embezzled a cloak, and now he is clothed with a similar one of Fire.'"

In his Musnad also, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I passed by a people whose lips were being clipped with scissors of fire. I said: 'Who are these?' They said: 'Preachers from your community from among the people of the world, who used to command people to righteousness and forget themselves.'"

Also in it, from the same narrator, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When I was taken up (to heaven), I passed by a people who had nails of copper with which they were scratching their faces and chests. I said: 'Who are these, O Jibril?' He said: 'These are those who eat the flesh of people and slander their honour.'"

Also from him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would often say: "O Turner of hearts and sights, make my heart firm upon Your religion." We said: "O Messenger of God, we have believed in you and in what you brought. Do you fear for us?" He said: "Yes, indeed the hearts are between two of the fingers of God; He turns them however He wills."

Also from him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is it with me that I have never seen Mika'il laughing?" He said: "He has not laughed since the Fire was created."

In Sahih Muslim, from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The one who was most blessed in the world among the people of the Fire will be brought, and he will be dipped once in the Fire. Then it will be said to him: 'O son of Adam, have you ever seen any good? Has any blessing ever passed you by?' He will say: 'No, by God, O Lord.' And the one who was most afflicted in the world among the people of Paradise will be brought, and he will be dipped once in Paradise. Then it will be said to him: 'O son of Adam, have you ever seen any hardship? Has any distress ever passed you by?' He will say: 'No, by God, O Lord; no hardship has ever passed me by, and I have never seen any distress.'"

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever has a wrong against his brother concerning property or honour, let him come to him and seek his forgiveness for it before it is taken from him, when he has no dinar or dirham. If he has good deeds, some of his good deeds will be taken and given to that man; and if not, some of that man's evil deeds will be taken and placed upon him, and then he will be cast into the Fire."

In the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever takes a span of land unjustly will be sunk with it to the seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."

In the Two Sahihs, from him, who said: The Messenger of God said: "This fire of yours which the children of Adam kindle is one part of seventy parts of the Fire of Jahannam." They said: "By God, it would be sufficient." He said: "It has been made superior to it by sixty-nine parts, each of which is like its heat."

In the Musnad, from Mu'adh, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) enjoined me, saying: "Do not associate anything with God, even if you are killed or burned; do not disobey your parents, even if they order you to leave your family and property; do not deliberately abandon an obligatory prayer, for whoever deliberately abandons an obligatory prayer, the protection of God is withdrawn from him; do not drink wine, for it is the source of every immorality; and beware of disobedience, for disobedience brings down the wrath of God."

The hadiths on this subject are many times more than what we have mentioned, so it is not fitting for one who gives sincere advice to himself to turn a blind eye to them, to let himself loose in sins, and to cling to good hope and good opinion.

Abu al-Wafa' ibn 'Aqil said: Beware of him and do not be deceived by him, for he cut off the hand over three dirhams, and flogged the prescribed punishment for an amount the size of a needle's head of wine. A woman entered the Fire because of a cat, and a cloak set on fire for the one who misappropriated it, though he had been killed as a martyr.

(Section)

The Qur'an is the speech of God, and God has manifested Himself in it to His servants through His attributes. At times He manifests Himself in the garb of awe, majesty and grandeur, so necks bow, souls are broken, voices become humble, and pride melts as salt melts in water. At other times He manifests Himself in the attributes of beauty and perfection, which are the perfection of the Names and the beauty of the Attributes and the beauty of the Acts, indicating the perfection of the Essence; so the servant's heart is drained of all the strength of love by love for what he has come to know of His attributes of beauty and descriptions of perfection, and the heart of His servant becomes empty except of His love. When the jealous one wishes to hang that love on something other than Him, the heart and its inner parts refuse it entirely, as it has been said:

"Forgetting you is what the heart is asked for, but natures refuse the one who transfers them."

So love for Him remains as a natural disposition, not a forced one. When He manifests Himself through attributes of mercy, kindness, gentleness and benevolence, the power of hope is roused in the servant, his expectation expands, his longing grows strong, and he journeys toward his Lord, with hope driving the caravan of his journey. The more hope grows, the more earnest he becomes in action, just as the sower, the more his expectation of harvest grows, the more he fills his land with seed; and when his hope weakens, he falls short in sowing. When He manifests Himself through attributes of justice, retribution, anger, wrath and punishment, the commanding soul is subdued, its powers of desire, anger, frivolity, play and greed for what is forbidden are suppressed or weakened, and the reins of its recklessness are drawn in, so the mount brings its share of fear, dread and caution. When He manifests Himself through attributes of command, prohibition, covenant and charge, the sending of messengers, the sending down of books and the legislating of laws, there arises in the servant the power of compliance and implementation of His commands, of conveying them, enjoining them, mentioning and remembering them, affirming the report, complying with the demand and avoiding the prohibition. When He manifests Himself through the attributes of hearing, seeing and knowledge, there arises in the servant the power of modesty, so he is shy before his Lord that He should see him in what He dislikes, or hear from him what He dislikes, or that he should conceal in his inner self what He abhors; thus his movements, words and thoughts remain weighed by the scale of the Shari'ah, neither neglected nor left free under the rule of nature and desire. When He manifests Himself through attributes of sufficiency, sufficing, taking charge of the interests of His servants, driving their provisions to them, repelling calamities from them, supporting His friends, protecting them and granting them His special companionship, there arises in the servant the power of trust in Him, entrusting himself to Him and contentment with Him, and in all that He does to His servant and establishes for him that pleases Him, He is glorified. Trust is a meaning formed from the servant's knowledge of God's sufficiency, His good choice for His servant, his confidence in Him, and his contentment with what He does and chooses for him. When He manifests Himself through attributes of might and greatness, the soul at peace gives what it has attained of humility before His majesty, brokenness before His might, submission to His greatness, and the heart and limbs' humility before Him; so tranquility and dignity come upon his heart, tongue, limbs and bearing, and his frivolity, strength and haste depart.

The sum of this is that He, glorified is He, makes Himself known to the servant through His attributes of divinity at times and through His attributes of lordship at other times. The attributes of divinity cause in him special love, longing for His meeting, intimacy and joy with Him, delight in serving Him, eagerness for nearness to Him, drawing close to Him through obedience, constant remembrance of Him, and fleeing from creation to Him, so that He alone becomes his concern, to the exclusion of all else. The attributes of lordship cause in him trust in Him, need for Him, seeking help from Him, and humility, submission and brokenness before Him. The perfection of this is that he witnesses His lordship in His divinity and His divinity in His lordship, His praise in His kingdom, His might in His pardon, His wisdom in His decree and destiny, His blessing in His trial, His giving in His withholding, His goodness, gentleness and kindness, His mercy in His self-subsistence, His justice in His retribution, His generosity and bounty in His forgiveness, concealment and passing over; and he witnesses His wisdom and blessing in His command and prohibition, His might in His good pleasure and anger, His forbearance in His delay, His generosity in His turning toward, and His self-sufficiency in His turning away.

When you reflect upon the Qur'an, and keep it free from distortion and from judging it by the opinions of the theologians and the notions of the over-elaborators, it will show you a King, Self-Subsisting, above His heavens, upon His Throne, managing the affairs of His servants: He commands and forbids, sends messengers and sends down books, is pleased and angered, rewards and punishes, gives and withholds, exalts and humbles, lowers and raises. He sees from above seven heavens, hears, and knows the secret and the open; He does what He wills, is described with every perfection, and is exempt from every defect. Not an atom's weight moves except by His permission, nor does a leaf fall except by His knowledge, nor can intercession with Him avail except by His permission. His servants have no protector and no intercessor besides Him.

Al-Hadi: He is the guide (dalil) who guides by means of them on the path to God and the Last Abode. This does not contradict His saying ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56] nor His saying ﴿For indeed, God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8].

God, glorified is He, has spoken of both. His messengers are the guides with the guidance of direction (hidayat al-dalala) and clarification (al-bayan), while He is al-Hadi with the guidance of divine success (hidayat al-tawfiq) and inspiration (al-ilham). The messengers are truly the guides (adillah), while God, glorified is He, is the One who grants success (al-Muwaffiq) and inspires (al-Mulhim), the Creator of guidance in the hearts.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 13, verse 8:

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: ﴿And that which the wombs diminish﴾ means what they lose of nine months, ﴿and that which they increase﴾ means what they exceed them by.

His companions agreed with him on this, such as Mujahid and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Mujahid also said: When a woman menstruates while pregnant, that is a diminution of the child. ﴿And that which they increase﴾: he said, if it exceeds nine months, that is a completion of what the child lost.

He also said: (al-ghayd, diminution) is what a pregnant woman sees of blood during her pregnancy, and that is a diminution of the child; (al-ziyadah, increase) is what exceeds nine months, and that is the completion of the diminution.

Al-Hasan said: ﴿That which the wombs diminish﴾ is what is a miscarriage, ﴿and that which they increase﴾ is a woman giving birth after ten months.

ʿIkrimah said: ﴿The wombs diminish﴾ is menstruation after conception. Every day she saw blood while pregnant, the pregnancy was reduced by that day in terms of clean days, and whenever she menstruated for a day, the pregnancy increased by a day.

Qatadah said: al-ghayd is miscarriage, and ﴿and that which they increase﴾ is beyond nine months.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: When a woman sees blood during pregnancy, that is the ghayd for the child, and it is a diminution in the child's nourishment and an increase in the pregnancy.

(Taghid and tazdad) are two transitive verbs whose object is omitted, and it is the pronoun referring back to (ma), the relative pronoun. Al-ghayd means diminution, and from it comes ﴿and the water subsided﴾.

Its opposite is increase (al-ziyadah).

The verified meaning of the verse is that He knows the duration of the pregnancy and what occurs in it of increase and decrease. He is the One who knows that, not you, just as He is the One who knows what every female carries, whether it is male or female.

This is one of the kinds of the unseen that none knows except Allah, as in the authentic report from him (ﷺ):

"The keys of the unseen are five, none knows them except Allah: none knows when the Hour will come except Allah; none knows what is in tomorrow except Allah; none knows when the rain will come except Allah; none knows what is in the wombs except Allah; and no soul knows in what land it will die except Allah."

So He, glorified is He, alone knows what is in the womb, and the knowledge of the time it remains therein, and what increases of its body and what decreases.

Whatever other than this statement is a consequence and necessary result of it, such as miscarriage and full-term birth, and seeing blood and its cessation.

The intended purpose is to mention the duration of the pregnancy in the belly and what is connected to it of increase and decrease.

(Fasl)

God, glorified is He, did not give this enemy, the sins, power over His servant the believer, who is the most beloved of His creatures to Him, except because jihad is the most beloved thing to Him, and its people are the highest of creation in rank before Him and the nearest of them to Him in means. So He, glorified is He, raised the banner of this war for the essence of His creation, which is the heart, the place of His knowledge and love, of worship of Him and sincerity toward Him, of trust in Him and turning back to Him. He entrusted to it the command of this war and supported it with a host of angels who never leave it: ﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11].

They follow one another; whenever one departs, another replaces him. They strengthen him, command him to good, and urge him toward it. They promise him the honor of Allah and encourage him to be patient, saying: "It is only an hour of patience, and you will rest a rest that lasts forever."

Then He, glorified is He, reinforced it with another host from His revelation and His speech. He sent to it His Messenger (ﷺ) and sent down to it His Book, so its strength increased upon its strength, its support upon its support, and its equipment upon its equipment. Along with that, He supported it with intellect as its minister and manager, with knowledge as its advisor giving it counsel, with faith as its steadfast, confirming and victorious helper, and with certainty as one who reveals to it the reality of the matter, until it is as though it sees what Allah, the Exalted, has promised His allies and party in fighting its enemies. So intellect manages the affairs of its army, knowledge arranges for it the matters of war, its causes, and the places fitting for them, faith makes it firm, strengthens it and gives it patience, and certainty makes it advance and carry out true charges.

Then, glorified is He, He supported the one who carries out this war with outward and inward faculties: He made the eye its vanguard, the ear the bearer of its news, the tongue its interpreter, and the two hands and two feet its helpers. He also set up His angels and the bearers of His Throne to ask forgiveness for it, praying that He protect it from evil deeds and admit it into the Gardens. Glorified is He took upon Himself the repelling and defense of it Himself, and said: "These are My party, and the party of Allah are the successful ones," as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22].

And "These are My soldiers": ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers are they who will be victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173].

He taught His servants the manner of this war and jihad, gathering it for them in four words, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed and fear Allah that you may be successful﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 200].

The matter of this jihad is not complete except by these four matters. Patience is not complete except through *musabara* (outlasting the enemy), which is confronting and grappling with him. When he outlasts his enemy, he needs another matter, which is *murabata* (garrisoning, ribat, i.e., holding the frontier posts), namely, staying at the frontier of the heart and guarding it lest the enemy enter through it, and staying at the frontiers of the eye, ear, tongue, belly, hand and foot. These frontiers are where the enemy enters, roaming through the lands and corrupting whatever he can reach. So *murabata* is remaining at these frontiers, and one must not leave their place, lest the enemy find the frontier empty and enter through it.

These are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the best of creation after the prophets and messengers, and the greatest in protection and guarding against Satan. Yet they vacated the place they were commanded to hold on the day of Uhud, so the enemy entered through it, and what happened, happened.

The sum of these three and their pillar upon which they stand is the fear of Allah, the Exalted. Patience, outlasting, and garrisoning benefit only with taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of Allah), and taqwa is not established except upon the leg of patience.

Ibn al-Qayyim's Commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 13, Verse 14:

The author of "al-Manazil" said:

Tabattul (exclusive devotion) is turning wholly toward Allah with complete singleness. And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14], that is, pure tajrid (single-minded detachment).

By pure tajrid he means tabattul that is detached from considering compensations, such that the one who devotes himself is not like the hired laborer who serves only for the sake of his wage. When he takes it, he turns away from the door of the employer. This is unlike the slave, who serves by the requirement of his servitude, not for the wage. He does not turn away from the door of his master except if he is a runaway.

The runaway has left the honor of servitude, and he has not attained the freedom of being released. Thus he becomes debased in the eyes of his master and in the eyes of his fellow slaves.

The highest honor of the soul is its entry under the bondage of servitude willingly, by choice, and out of love, not unwillingly and by compulsion, as it has been said:

﻿A poet's verse: The honor of souls is their entry into their bondage, * and the slave gains pride through being owned.

What makes his citing of the saying ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾ appropriate in this place is the intention of this meaning: that He, exalted is He, is the rightful possessor of the call of truth by His essence and attributes, even if He does not make a reward obligatory for the one who calls upon Him with it. For He deserves it by His essence. He is worthy to be worshipped alone, called upon alone, aimed at, thanked and praised, loved, hoped in and feared, relied upon, sought help from, sought protection with, taken refuge in, and turned to in need. Thus the divine call of truth belongs to Him alone.

Whoever has this established in his heart, through knowledge, experience, and state, his station of tabattul and pure tajrid is sound.

The early scholars (al-salaf) interpreted the call of truth as tawhid, sincerity in it, and truthfulness. This is what they meant.

So ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The call of truth is tawhid."

And Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah."

It was also said: "The supplication with sincerity. Sincere supplication is directed only to Allah."

And the call of truth is the call to divinity, its rights, its singling out, and its sincerity.

Allah has mentioned the two parables, the water and the fire, in Surah al-Ra'd, but concerning the believers. He said, may He be exalted: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from what they heat in the fire seeking an ornament or goods, there is similar foam. Thus Allah strikes forth truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum; but that which benefits people remains on the earth. Thus Allah sets forth parables.﴾

He likened the revelation that He sent down for the life of hearts, hearing and sight to the water that He sent down for the life of the earth through plants. He likened hearts to valleys. A great heart holds great knowledge, like a great valley holds much water, and a small heart holds only what it can hold, like a small valley. ﴿Valleys flow according to their measure﴾, and hearts take in guidance and action according to their measure. Just as the torrent, when it mixes with the earth and passes over it, carries along debris and foam, so guidance and knowledge, when they mix with hearts, stir up what is in them of desires (shahawat) and doubts (shubuhat) in order to uproot and remove them, as medicine when drunk stirs up the humours of the body, so that the one who drinks it becomes troubled by them. This is part of the benefit of the medicine, for it stirs them up in order to expel them, and it neither joins with them nor shares with them. Likewise, Allah strikes forth truth and falsehood.

Then He mentioned the parable of fire, saying: ﴿And from what they heat in the fire seeking an ornament or goods, there is similar foam﴾. This is the dross that emerges when gold, silver, copper and iron are smelted. The fire brings it out, distinguishes it and separates it from the substance that is useful, so it is cast off and thrown away and passes away as scum. Likewise, desires and doubts are rejected by the heart of the believer, which casts them off and pushes them away, just as the torrent and the fire cast away that foam, debris and dross. And there settles at the bottom of the valley the pure water from which people drink, irrigate their crops and water their livestock. Likewise, there settles in the depths and root of the heart pure, sincere faith, which benefits its possessor and from which others also benefit. Whoever does not understand these two parables, does not reflect upon them, and does not recognise what is intended by them, is not among their people. And Allah is the Granter of success.

And he said in Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam﴾.

This is the parable of water. He likened the revelation that He sent down for the life of hearts to the water that He sent down from the sky, and He likened the hearts that carry it to the valleys that carry the torrent. A great heart holds great knowledge, like a great valley holds much water, and a small heart, like a small valley, holds little knowledge. The hearts carried of this knowledge according to their measure, just as the valleys flowed according to their measure.

Since the valleys are the channels of torrents, in which there is debris and the like that the torrent passes over, the torrent carries it along, and it floats on the surface of the water as high foam that passes over, piled up. But beneath it is the sweet water in which is the life of the earth. The valley casts that debris to its sides until none of it remains, and the water beneath the foam remains, with which Allah, exalted is He, irrigates the earth, giving life thereby to the lands, the people, the trees and the animals. The foam passes away as scum, cast aside on the edge of the valley. Likewise, knowledge and faith, which He sent down into hearts, were carried by them, and through their mixing with the hearts they stirred up what was in them of the debris of desires and the foam of false doubts, which floats to the top. Knowledge, faith and guidance settle at the root of the hearts. That debris and foam continue to pass away as scum and gradually disappear until all of it is gone, and there remains beneficial knowledge and pure faith in this heart, which people come to, drink from, irrigate with, and through which their land becomes green.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 13, verse 18:

When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, had struck these two parables, He mentioned the ruling for the one who responded to Him and whose head was raised by His guidance, and the ruling for the one who did not respond to Him and did not raise his head by His guidance. He said: ﴿For those who responded to their Lord is the best (reward). But those who did not respond to Him—if they had all that is in the earth entirely, and the like thereof with it, they would surely offer it for ransom. Those will have a terrible account, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ (13:18)

The purpose is that Allah, exalted is He, made life where there is light, and death where there is darkness. The life of both the spiritual and the bodily existence is through light, and it is the substance of life just as it is the substance of illumination. There is no life without it, just as there is no illumination without it. Just as the life of the heart is through it, its expansion, its openness, and its breadth are also through it, as in al-Tirmidhi: "From the Prophet ﷺ: When the light enters the heart, it expands and opens." They said: "What is the sign of that?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it descends."

The light of the servant is what raises his deeds and his words up to Allah, for Allah does not receive from words except the good, and it is a light and it emanates from light.

Nor from deeds except the righteous, nor from spirits except the good ones, which are the spirits of the believers that were illuminated by the light that He sent down upon His Messenger ﷺ, and the angels, who were created from light, as in Sahih Muslim from ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from smokeless fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you." So since the substance of the angels is from light, they are the ones who ascend to their Lord, blessed and exalted is He. Likewise the spirits of the believers are those that ascend to their Lord at the time the angels take them. The gate of the lowest heaven is opened for them, then the second, the third, and the fourth, until it reaches the seventh heaven. It then stands before Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and He commands that its book be written in ʿIlliyyin. Since this spirit is a pure, good, luminous, and radiant spirit, it ascends to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, along with the angels.

As for the dark, evil, and turbid spirit, the gates of heaven are not opened for it and it does not ascend to Allah. Rather, it is returned from the lowest heaven to its world and its origin, because it is earthly and lowly, while the other is heavenly and celestial. Thus every spirit returns to its element and to what it came from. This is explicitly stated in the lengthy hadith of al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, which Imam Ahmad narrated, and Abu ʿAwanah al-Isfara'ini in his Sahih, and al-Hakim and others, and it is a sound hadith.

The purpose is that Allah, mighty and majestic is He, does not receive from the deeds, the words, and the spirits except what is luminous, and those nearest to Him and most honored by Him are the most luminous.

In the Musnad, from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet ﷺ:

"Indeed Allah created His creation in darkness, and cast upon them some of His light. Whoever is struck by some of that light is guided, and whoever misses it goes astray."

Therefore I say: the pen has dried over the knowledge of Allah. This great hadith is a foundation of faith, and through it opens a great gate of the secret of destiny and its wisdom. And Allah is the Granter of success.

This light which He cast upon them, glorified and exalted is He, is what gave them life and guided them, and the natural disposition (fitrah) received its share from it.

But since it was not sufficient by itself in its completeness and perfection, He completed it for them and perfected it with the spirit which He cast upon His messengers, peace be upon them, and the light which He revealed to them. So the fitrah grasped it through that earlier light which it had obtained on the day the light was cast. Thus the light of revelation and prophethood was added to the light of the fitrah: light upon light. The hearts shone through it, the faces were illumined by it, the spirits came alive by it, and the limbs submitted to acts of obedience willingly and by choice. Thus the hearts increased by it in the highest attributes, in which every other light is extinguished, and they witnessed it with the insight of faith, a witnessing whose relation to the heart is like the relation of visible things to the eye, because certainty had taken hold of them and the realities of faith were unveiled to them, until it is as if they look upon the Throne of the Merciful, blessed and exalted is He, manifest, and upon His ascending over it, as He, glorified is He, told in His Book, and as His Messenger ﷺ told of Him.

He manages the affairs of the kingdoms, commands and forbids, creates and provides, causes to die and gives life, decrees and executes, grants honor and humiliation, alternates the night and the day, rotates the days among the people, and overturns dynasties, taking away one dynasty and bringing another. The angels, the messengers, peace be upon them, go between ascending to Him with the command and descending from Him with it, and His orders and decrees follow one another in succession as the verses do, executed according to His will: whatever He wills, as He wills, at the time He wills, in the manner He wills, without increase or decrease, without advance or delay. His command and authority are effective in the heavens and their regions, in the earth and what is upon it and beneath it, in the seas and the air, and in all parts and particles of the world.

He turns them, directs them, and brings about in them whatever He wills. He encompasses everything in knowledge, has counted everything in number, and His mercy and wisdom encompass everything. His hearing encompasses voices, so they do not differ for Him nor become confused for Him. Rather, He hears their clamor in the variety of their languages despite the multitude of their needs; no hearing distracts Him from another hearing, the multitude of questions does not confuse Him, and He is not wearied by the insistence of those in need. His sight encompasses all visible things: He sees the crawl of the black ant on the solid rock in the darkest night. The unseen is witnessed by Him, and the secret is open to Him. He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret: the secret is what the servant's inner self conceals and what occurs to his heart without his lips moving, and what is more hidden than that is what has not yet occurred, so He knows that it will occur to his heart such and such at such and such a time. To Him belong the creation and the command; to Him belong the dominion and the praise; to Him belong this world and the Hereafter; to Him belong the blessing and the grace and the good praise. To Him belongs all the dominion, to Him belongs all the praise, in His hand is all the good, and to Him all matters return. His power encompasses everything, His mercy has embraced everything, and His bounty has reached every living thing.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 13, verse 19:

He gathered for them the stations of Islam and faith in these attributes. He described them as fulfilling their covenant with Him, the covenant He made with them, and this encompasses His command and His prohibition, which He entrusted to them, between themselves and Him and between themselves and His creation. Then He reported their continuous fulfillment of it, that breaking it does not occur from them. Then He described them as joining what Allah has commanded to be joined, and included in this is the outward and inward religion, and the right of Allah and the right of His creation. So they join what is between them and their Lord through worshiping Him alone without partner, standing in obedience to Him, turning to Him in repentance, relying upon Him, loving Him, fearing Him, hoping in Him, repenting to Him, humbling themselves before Him, submitting and abasing themselves to Him, acknowledging His blessing and thanking Him for it, and confessing their sin and seeking forgiveness for it. This is the connection between the Lord and the servant, and Allah has commanded that these bonds between Him and His servant be joined. He also commanded that we join what is between us and His Messenger by believing in him, affirming him, making him the judge in everything, being content with his judgment, submitting to him, and giving his love precedence over the love of the self, the child, the parent, and all people, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. Included in this is standing by his right and the right of His Messenger.

He commanded that we join what is between us and our parents and relatives through righteousness and kinship, for He commanded kindness to parents and maintaining ties of kinship, and this is among what He commanded to be joined. He commanded that we join what is between us and our wives by fulfilling their rights and living with them in kindness. He commanded that we join what is between us and our slaves by feeding them from what we eat, clothing them from what we wear, and not burdening them beyond their capacity. He commanded that we join what is between us and the near and distant neighbor by observing his right and guarding him in his person, his wealth, and his family, with the same care by which we guard our own selves, our families, and our wealth. He commanded that we join what is between us and the companion on a journey and at home. He commanded that we join what is between us and people in general by treating them with what we would like them to treat us with. He commanded that we join what is between us and the noble recording angels by honoring them and being shy before them as a man is shy before his companion and whoever is with him among those he respects and honors.

All of this is among what Allah has commanded to be joined. Then He described them by that which moves them to this joining, which is their fear of Him and their fear of the evil reckoning on the Day of Return. It is impossible for anyone ever to join what Allah has commanded to be joined except through fear of Him, and whenever fear departs from the heart, these bonds are severed. Then He, glorified is He, gathered all of that for them into one root, which is the foundation of it, its basis, and the axis upon which it turns, and that is patience. So He said: ﴿And those who patiently seek the face of their Lord﴾. He did not suffice with mere patience from them until it was sincerely for His face.

Then He mentioned to them what helps them in patience, which is prayer, so He said: ﴿and establish prayer﴾. These two are the two aids for the interests of this world and the Hereafter, and they are patience and prayer. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humble﴾, and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their goodness toward others by spending on them secretly and openly. They were good to themselves through patience and prayer, and good to others through spending on them. Then He mentioned their state when they are treated ignorantly and harmed: they do not repay that with its like, but rather they repel evil with good, so they show kindness to whoever mistreats them. He said: ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾. This "repelling" has been explained as: they counter a sin with a good deed after it, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾.

The Prophet said: "Follow the bad deed with a good deed, and it will erase it."

The verified view is that the verse encompasses both types.

The purpose is that these verses encompass all the stations of Islam and faith. They comprise doing what is commanded, avoiding what is forbidden, and patience with what is decreed. Allah, the Exalted, mentioned these three foundations in His saying: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears [Allah] and is patient﴾, and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient, endure, remain stationed, and fear Allah that you may be successful﴾. Thus every place where taqwa (God-consciousness) is paired with patience includes these three matters, for the reality of taqwa is doing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden.

**(Issue)**
**"Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah"** (سلام عليكم ورحمة الله)

In this greeting there are twenty-eight questions:

**First question:** What is the meaning of *salam* (peace), and what is its reality?

**Second question:** Is it a verbal noun (*masdar*) or a noun (*ism*)?

**Third question:** Is the Muslim's saying *salamun 'alaykum* a statement of fact (*khabar*) or a performative utterance (*insha'*)?

**Fourth question:** What is the meaning of the peace that is sought in greeting? If it is a supplication and a request, what is the wisdom in seeking it at meeting and in correspondence, rather than other meanings?

**Fifth question:** If it derives from *al-salama* (safety), it is known that the verb from it is not transitive with *'ala* (upon). So one does not say *salamah 'alayka* or *sallamtu 'alayka* with a kasra on the lam, but rather *salam laka*, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So peace be to you from the companions of the right hand﴾?

**Sixth question:** What is the wisdom in beginning with *salam* when the predicate is a prepositional phrase (*jar wa majrur*), while the rule of Arabic is to place the predicate first in such constructions, as in *fi al-dar rajul* (there is a man in the house)?

**Seventh question:** Why is the one who responds to the greeting singled out with this structure, and why is the prepositional phrase placed before *salam* in the reply? Why was his reply not with *salam* placed first in absolute form, like his initial greeting?

**Eighth question:** What is the wisdom in the initiator's greeting being with an indefinite noun (*nakira*), while the response to it is with a definite noun (*ma'rifa*)? Likewise, what is the wisdom in the greeting at the beginning of a letter being with an indefinite noun, and at its end with a definite noun, so that one says at first *salamun 'alaykum*, and at the close of the letter *wa's-salamu 'alaykum*? Is this definiteness for the sake of the known (*'ahd*) and the prior mention of *salam*, or for some other wisdom?

**Ninth question:** What is the benefit of the conjunctive *wa* (and) entering the second greeting? One says first *salamun 'alaykum*, and at the end *wa's-salamu 'alaykum*. Upon what is this conjunction based?

**Tenth question:** What is the secret in *salam* being in the accusative (*nasb*) in the angels' greeting, and in the nominative (*raf'*) in Abraham's greeting? Is it as the grammarians say, that the greeting of Abraham is more complete because it contains a nominal sentence indicating permanence, while the greeting of the angels contains a verbal sentence indicating occurrence? Or is there some other secret?

**Eleventh question:** What is the secret in *salam* being in the accusative in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, and in the nominative in His words: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you"﴾? And what is the difference between the two places?

**Twelfth question:** What is the wisdom in Allah's greeting upon His prophets and messengers, when *salam* is in fact a request for safety for the one greeted? How can this meaning be conceived with regard to Allah? This is one of the most important and finest of questions.

**Thirteenth question:** If the wisdom of His greeting upon them has become clear, what is the wisdom in His greeting them with an indefinite noun, while He legislated for His servants to greet His Messenger with a definite noun, saying: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings" (as-salamu 'alayka ayyuha an-nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh), and likewise their greeting of themselves, and of the righteous servants of Allah?

**Fourteenth question:** What is the secret in Allah's greeting upon Yahya with an indefinite noun in His words: ﴿And peace be upon him﴾, and Jesus's greeting upon himself with a definite noun in his words: ﴿And peace is upon me﴾? Which of the two greetings is more complete and more comprehensive?

**Fifteenth question:** What is the wisdom in restricting these two greetings to these three days: ﴿The day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾, especially since greeting is required at all times? If it had been stated absolutely, would it not have been more comprehensive? Does this restriction not confine the greeting to these days alone?

**Sixteenth question:** What is the wisdom in the Prophet's greeting (ﷺ) upon those who follow guidance in the letter to Heraclius being with an indefinite noun, while Moses's greeting upon those who follow guidance is with a definite noun, as it occurs in the Qur'an? Why was the Prophet's greeting (ﷺ) not with a definite noun, so as to match the Qur'an? What is the difference between them?

**Seventeenth question:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾. Is this a peace from Allah, so that the speech contains two sentences: an imperative, which is the command in His words ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾, and a declarative, which is Allah's peace upon His servants? On this view, it would be a case of conjoining a declarative sentence to an imperative. Or is it a command from Allah to greet them with peace? On this view, He has commanded two things: one, saying "Praise be to Allah," and the second, saying "Peace upon His servants whom He has chosen," with both being objects governed by the verb "say." Which of the two meanings is more fitting for the verse?

**Eighteenth question:** Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Juray al-Hujaymi, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Upon you be peace, O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' He said: 'Do not say "Upon you be peace," for "Upon you be peace" is the greeting of the dead.'" It is authentic. At-Tirmidhi said: "It is a hadith that is authentic." It is also established from him regarding greeting the dead, both in deed and command: "Peace be upon you, O abode of believing people." Related by Muslim. What is the meaning of this hadith, and how is it reconciled with the authentic hadiths?

**Nineteenth question:** What is the meaning of the entry of the *wa* (and) in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "When the People of the Book greet you, say, 'And upon you' (wa 'alaykum)." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Many people have found this *wa* problematic, and some of the skilled scholars even denied that it is authentic. He said: "Because the *wa* in such a case requires the affirmation of the first and its confirmation, as when you say, 'Zayd is a writer,' and the addressee says, 'and a jurist,' for it implies the affirmation of the first and an additional attribute, 'jurist.'" So how did it enter this context, and what is its meaning?

**Twentieth question:** What is the secret in mercy and blessing being joined with the greeting, rather than other attributes such as forgiveness, righteousness, kindness, and the like?

**Twenty-first question:** Why does the greeting end at the words "and His blessings," and why is no addition legislated beyond them?

**Twenty-second question:** What is the wisdom in attributing mercy and blessing to Allah the Exalted, while the greeting is stripped of this attribution? Why were they not all attributed, or all left unattributed?

**Twenty-third question:** What is the wisdom in making *salam* and *rahma* singular, while *barakah* is plural?

**Twenty-fourth question:** What is the wisdom in emphasizing the command to greet the Prophet with the verbal noun (*masdar*) rather than with the word "prayer," in His words: ﴿O you who believe, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace (taslima)﴾? Why did He not say "salu salat"?

**Twenty-fifth question:** What is the wisdom in placing the greeting upon him before the blessing upon him in the prayer? Could the beginning not have been with the blessing upon him first, followed by the greeting, so that the beginning would be with what Allah began with, namely placing the blessing before the greeting?

**Twenty-sixth question:** What is the wisdom in the greeting upon him in prayer being in the form of direct address (*khitab al-mawajaha*), while the blessing upon him comes in the third-person form (*ghayba*), mentioning him by his proper name?

**Twenty-seventh question:** This is what the consistency of the speech leads to: What is the wisdom in the praise of Allah being in the form of the third person in our saying "At-tahiyyatu lillah" (all greetings are for Allah), although He, glory be to Him, is the one addressed in intimate conversation, who hears our speech and sees our place? And the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) came in the form of direct address, although the situation would seem to require the opposite. What is the wisdom in this?

**Twenty-eighth question:** This is the conclusion of the questions: What is the secret in the greeting being the conclusion of the prayer, and why was it not at its beginning? And if it is so, what is the secret in its coming definite, and why was it not indefinite?

As for the **first question**, which is: what is the reality of this word? Its reality is disavowal, freedom, and deliverance from evil and defects, and upon this meaning its derivations revolve. From it is your saying: "May Allah keep you safe (salamaka)," and "So-and-so was kept safe from evil (salama)." From it is also the supplication of the believers on the bridge: "O Lord, keep us safe, O Allah, keep us safe." From it is also *salima al-shay' li-fulan*, meaning it became purely his, so that it was freed from the harm of partnership in it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are associates in dispute, and a man belonging entirely to one man﴾, meaning purely to him alone, with no other owning it along with him. From it is also *al-silm*, the opposite of war. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾, because each of the two warring parties is freed and kept safe from the harm of the other. For this reason, it is formed with the pattern of mutual action (*mufa'ala*), so one says: *al-musalama* is like *al-musharaka* (partnership). From it is also "the sound heart" (al-qalb as-salim), which is the one purified of rancor and deceit. Its reality is one who has become wholly devoted to Allah the Exalted alone, so he is freed from the deceit and corruption of *shirk* and from the deceit of sins and transgressions. Indeed, he is the one who remains upright in the sincerity of his love and the goodness of his dealings. This is the one for whom deliverance from His punishment and success with His honor are guaranteed. From this root also comes *al-Islam*, for it is from this same root, since it is submission and surrender to Allah the Exalted and freedom from the impurities of *shirk*. He has submitted to his Lord and become purely His, like the slave who belongs wholly to his master, with no quarreling partners. For this reason, the Exalted has struck these two examples: the purely devoted believer, and the one who associates others with Him. From it also comes *al-salam* in the sense of advance payment for a debt (*al-salaf*), whose reality is the compensation delivered in the contract, because the one who owes it has guaranteed its safety for the creditor. Then the contract itself was called *salam*, and its reality is what we have mentioned.

If it is said: Does this not contradict their saying of the one bitten by a snake, "*saqim*" (sound/safe, by euphemism)?

It is answered: This is not a contradiction to it, but rather an application of what we have said. They called him *salim* on account of what concerns him, seeks it, and hopes that his condition will come to safety. Nothing is more important to him than safety, and he is no more eager for anything else than for it. So he was called *salim* for this reason. This is of the same kind as their naming the deadly desert *mafazah* (a place of salvation), because nothing is more important to the one who traverses it than his success in escaping it, that is, his deliverance. So it was called *mafazah* because he seeks success from it. This is better than their saying that it is called *mafazah* and the stung one is called *salim* as an omen of good. Although optimism is part of this meaning and is included in it, the explanation we have given is more general and better.

If it is said: How can you trace *al-silm* back to this root?

It is answered: That is clear, for the one who ascends to a high place, since he is exposed to falling and destruction and seeks safety, is hoping for it. The instrument by which he reaches his goal was called *sullam* (ladder), because it includes his safety. For if he climbed with effort and without a ladder, his destruction would be expected. So it is established that *al-sullam* derives from this meaning. From it also comes the naming of Paradise as "the Abode of Peace" (*dar as-salam*). Regarding its attribution to peace, there are three opinions. The first is that it is an attribution to its owner, who is *as-Salam*, glory be to Him. The second is that it is an attribution to the greeting of its people, for their greeting therein is peace. The third is that it is an attribution to the meaning of peace, that is, the abode of peace from every calamity, defect, and evil. All three are mutually entailed, though the third is the most evident. For if the attribution were to its owner, it would have been attributed to one of His names other than *as-Salam*, and it would have been said "the abode of the Merciful," "the abode of Allah," "the abode of the King," or the like. Since its attribution to Him is known, when "the abode of peace" is mentioned, it is understood as referring to what is known. Moreover, what is customary in the Qur'an is attributing it either to its qualities or to its people. As for the first, such as: the abode of permanence, the abode of glory, the garden of refuge, the gardens of bliss, the gardens of Paradise. As for the second, such as: the abode of the righteous. But its attribution to a name of Allah the Exalted is not known in the Qur'an. So it is better to understand the attribution in light of what is customary in the Qur'an. Likewise, its attribution to greeting is weak for two reasons. The first is that greeting with peace is shared between the abode of this world and the abode of the Hereafter, whereas what is attributed to Paradise is only that which is specific to it, such as eternity, permanence, and continuance. The second is that among its qualities there are others more perfect than greeting, such as its being everlasting and enduring, and being the abode of eternity, whereas greeting there is incidental, occurring at meeting and mutual visiting. This is unlike safety from every defect, loss, and evil, which is among its most perfect and intended qualities, one that is constant, and without which bliss in it is not complete. Therefore, attributing it to this is more fitting. And this is evident.

**(Section)**

Having understood these two matters, the naming of peace as one of Allah's names is more fitting than all of this, and more deserving of this name than anything else named by it, because He, glory be to Him, is free from every defect and deficiency in every respect. He is *as-Salam* in the true sense in every consideration. Created beings are peaceful only by comparison. He, glory be to Him, is peace in His essence, free from every defect and deficiency that could be imagined. He is peace in His attributes, free from every defect and deficiency. He is peace in His actions, free from every defect, evil, injustice, and act that occurs otherwise than in accordance with wisdom. Rather, He is the true peace in every respect and in every consideration. Thus it is known that His deserving this name is more perfect than the deserving of any other thing named by it. This is the very reality of the transcendence (*tanzih*) by which He declared Himself transcendent and by which His Messenger declared Him transcendent. He is peace from having a consort or a child, peace from having an equal, a peer, a namesake, or a like, and peace from having a partner. For this reason, when you consider the individual attributes of His perfection, you find that each attribute is a peace from what opposes its perfection. His life is peace from death, from drowsiness, and from sleep. Likewise, His self-subsistence and power are peace from fatigue and weariness. His knowledge is peace from anything escaping it, or from the occurrence of forgetfulness, or from any need for recollection or reflection. His will is peace from departing from wisdom and benefit. His words are peace from falsehood and injustice; rather, His words are perfect in truth and justice. His self-sufficiency is peace from any need for other than Him in any way; rather, everything other than Him is in need of Him, while He is independent of all that is other than Him. His dominion is peace from any disputant over it, any partner, any aide, any manifest supporter, or any intercessor with Him without His permission. His divinity is peace from any partner in it; rather, He is Allah, there is no god but Him. His forbearance, pardon, forgiveness, and overlooking are peace from being due to need or to anything of that sort, or to flattery, as is the case with others. Rather, it is pure bounty, goodness, and generosity. Likewise, His punishment, vengeance, severity of grip, and swiftness of retribution are peace from being injustice, or vindictiveness, or harshness, or cruelty. Rather, they are pure wisdom, justice, and the placing of things in their proper places. They are also among the things for which He deserves praise and thanks, just as He deserves them for His goodness, reward, and blessings. Indeed, if He were to place reward in the place of punishment, that would contradict His wisdom and His might. So His placing punishment in its place is part of His justice, wisdom, and might. He is peace from what His enemies and those ignorant of Him imagine, such as contradiction to His wisdom. His decree and His measure are peace from futility, oppression, and injustice, and from any supposition that they occur contrary to the perfect wisdom. His legislation and religion are peace from contradiction, discord, confusion, and what opposes the benefit and mercy of His servants and goodness to them, and what opposes His wisdom. Rather, all His legislation is wisdom, mercy, benefit, and justice. Likewise, His giving is peace from being an exchange or from any need of the one who receives it, and His withholding is peace from miserliness and from fear of poverty. Rather, His giving is pure goodness, without exchange or need; and His withholding is pure justice and wisdom, unmixed with miserliness or incapacity. His establishment (*istiwa'*) upon His Throne and His exaltation above it are peace from needing what would carry Him or what He would be established upon. Rather, the Throne is in need of Him, and its bearers are in need of Him. He is the Independent of the Throne, of its bearers, and of everything other than Him. So His establishment and exaltation are free from being confined, from any need for a throne or for anything else, and from anything encompassing Him, glory be to Him and exalted. Indeed, He, glory be to Him, was when there was no throne, and He had no need of it, for He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. Rather, His establishment upon His Throne and His dominance over His creation are among the requirements of His dominion and His subjugation, without any need for a place or anything else in any way. His descent to the lowest heaven every night is peace from what contradicts His exaltation, and peace from what contradicts His self-sufficiency and perfection. He is peace from everything that a denier (*mu'attil*) imagines or a likener (*mushabbih*) asserts. He is peace from ever being beneath anything or confined within anything. Exalted is our Lord above everything that contradicts His perfection and His self-sufficiency. His hearing and His seeing are peace from everything that a likener imagines or a denier asserts. His allegiance to His friends is peace from being like the allegiance of one created being to another; rather, it is an allegiance of mercy, goodness, benevolence, and kindness, as He said: ﴿And say, "Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has not had a partner in the dominion, and has not had any protector out of humiliation"﴾. He did not deny that He could have a protector absolutely, but He denied that He has a protector out of humiliation. Likewise, His love for those who love Him and His friends is peace from the accidents of created love, whether it be love of need, or flattery, or benefit from nearness to Him, and peace from what the deniers say about it. Likewise, what He attributed to Himself, such as the hand and the face, is peace from what a likener imagines or a denier asserts. So reflect on how His name *as-Salam* encompasses everything from which He, blessed and exalted, is declared free. How many have memorized this name without knowing what these secrets and meanings it contains are! And Allah is the One sought for help, the One asked to grant success in commenting upon the Beautiful Names in this manner; He is near and responsive. Let us stop the discussion here on the first question.

**(Section)**

As for the **second question**, which is: Is *al-salam* a verbal noun or a noun that functions as a verbal noun?

The answer: *al-salam*, which is the greeting, is a noun of verbal action (*ism masdar*) derived from *sallama*. Its verbal noun (*masdar*) that is regularly used is *taslim*, as with *'allama* producing *ta'lim*, *fahhama* producing *tafhim*, and *kallama* producing *taklim*. And *as-salam* from *sallama* is like *al-kalam* from *kallama*.

If it is said: What is the difference between a verbal noun (*masdar*) and a noun of verbal action (*ism masdar*)?

Qur'an study app translation of Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 13, verses 23–24 (part 2 of 10):

We say: there is a difference between them, both verbal and semantic. The verbal difference is that the **masdar** (verbal noun) follows the regular pattern of its verb, which is its standard form, like the verbal nouns of *af'ala* (*if'āl*), *fa''ala* (*taf'īl*), *infa'ala* (*infi'āl*), *tafa''ala* (*tafa''ul*), and their pattern. The words *salām* and *kalām*, however, do not follow the regular pattern of their verbs. If they did, one would say *taslīm* and *taklīm*. The semantic difference is that the masdar indicates the action and its agent. So when you say *takhlīm*, *taslīm*, *ta'līm*, and similar words, they indicate the action and the one who performs it. *Taslīm* therefore indicates both the greeting (*salām*) and the one who greets (*muslim*). The same applies to *taklīm* and *ta'līm*. The **ism al-masdar** (noun of the verbal action), however, indicates only the action by itself. So *salām* and *kalām* do not, by their form, indicate a greeter (*muslim*) or a speaker (*mukallim*), unlike *taklīm* and *taslīm*. The secret of this distinction is that the masdar in your saying *sallama taslīman* and *kallama taklīman* functions like repeating the verb, as though you said *sallama sallama* and *takallama takallama*, and the verb is never without its agent.

As for the noun of the verbal action, they stripped it down to indicate only the action itself. This subtle point is one of the secrets of the Arabic language. This *salām* that is the greeting (*tahiyya*) is of this type. As for the *Salām* that is one of the names of Allah, there are two opinions about it:

The first: it is likewise a noun of the verbal action, and its application to Him is like the application of *'adl* (justice) to Him. The meaning is "the One possessing peace," and "the One possessing justice," with an omitted possessive construction (*hadhf al-muḍāf*).

The second: the masdar here carries the meaning of the active participle, i.e., *al-sālim* (the one who is free from defect), just as the Night of Decree was called *salām* meaning "free from every evil," for it is good and contains no evil.

The better of the two opinions, and the more consistent with Arabic grammar, is that *al-Salām* itself is one of His names, like *al-'Adl*. This is an instance of applying a masdar to the agent because it is predominant in him and repeatedly manifested by him, as in the expressions *rajulun ṣawm* (a man who fasts constantly), *'adl* (a just man), *zūr* (a man who often lies), and similar forms.

As for *salām* in the sense of *salāma* (safety, soundness), it is a masdar of its own kind, similar to *jalāl* and *jalāla*. When you drop the *tā'* (*jalāl*), the intended meaning is the masdar itself. When you add the *tā'* (*jalāla*), it signals specification with respect to a single instance of the masdar, like *ḥubb* and *ḥubba*. Thus *salām*, *jamāl*, and *jalāl* are like the general genus, since they lack the *tā'* of specification. *Salāma*, *jalāla*, *malāḥa*, and *faṣāḥa* all indicate a single quality. Do you not see that *malāḥa* (charm) is one of the qualities of perfection, and *jalāla* (majesty) is one of the qualities of grandeur? For this reason they did not say *kamāla* as they said *malāḥa* and *faṣāha*, because *kamāl* (perfection) is a comprehensive term for the attributes of nobility and excellence. If they had said *kamāla*, they would have defeated the purpose intended by the noun *kamāl*. Reflect on this.

On this same pattern come *ḥalāwa* (sweetness), *aṣāla* (nobility of origin), *razāna* (gravity), and *rajāḥa* (sound judgment), because each is a specific quality within absolute perfection and beauty, so they used the *tā'* that indicates specification. The opposite forms are *ḥamāqa* (foolishness), *ruqāʿa* (baseness), *nadhāla* (meanness), and *safāha* (folly), for they are specific qualities within absolute defect and imperfection. They used the form without *tā'* for the genus that encompasses the types, and they used the *tā'* for its types and individual instances. This meaning has already been established, and there is no need to repeat it. Now consider how *salām* came without the *tā'* to signal the attainment of the complete notion, since the intended purpose is achieved only through it. If someone is safe from one calamity but falls into another, he has not attained *salām*. It is therefore clear that *salām* has not left the category of the masdar in any of its aspects.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in its coming as a noun of the verbal action and not in the form of the masdar proper?

The answer: this secret is wonderful. The intention is that the meaning of safety be attained for the one greeted, in an absolute sense, without restriction to an agent. Since the intended meaning is absolute safety without reference to an agent, they used the noun of the verbal action, which indicates the action alone, and did not use the masdar, which indicates the action together with its agent. Reflect on this.

**(Section)**

As for the third question: is the Muslim's saying *salāmun 'alaykum* an expression of an injunctive act (*inshā'*) or a declarative statement (*khabar*)?

Its answer: this and similar expressions of supplication contain both the injunctive and the declarative. The aspect of declaration in it does not contradict the aspect of injunction. This is a subtle point that requires explanation and clarification. We say: speech has two relations: a relation to the speaker himself, and a relation to the matter he speaks about, whether as a request or as a report. It also has a third relation, to the addressee, which does not bear on this discussion. Its verification depends on the first two relations. The division into declarative and injunctive arises from these two relations, and one can know where they meet and where they separate. By its relation to the speaker's intention and will, bringing about the content of the statement, it is characterized as injunctive. By its relation to the matter spoken of and informing about its realization in external reality, it is characterized as declarative. The two relations sometimes coincide and sometimes diverge. Every case in which the meaning is established solely through the speaker's intention and will does not allow the declarative and injunctive to combine. Examples are the statements "I have sold you such-and-such," "I have given it to you," "I have freed," and "I have divorced." These meanings have no external existence except through the speaker's will and intention, so they are injunctive acts. Their declarative character arises from another aspect: they include the speaker's report of this relation's existence in his mind. However, this is not the declarative character for which the word "khabar" was established. Every case in which the meaning is realized from a source other than the speaker, and where the speaker has nothing but to supplicate for its realization and to desire it, does not contradict the injunctive. The declarative in it does not conflict with the injunctive. This is the case with *salām 'alaykum*, for the desired safety was not achieved by the action of the greeter, and the greeter has nothing but to supplicate for it and desire it. So when he says *salām 'alaykum*, it includes a report of the realization of safety, and an injunctive act of supplicating for it, willing it, and wishing for it. Likewise *waylun lahu* (woe to him). Sibawayh said: "It is supplication and declaration." Many people did not understand Sibawayh's statement as he intended it, and distorted it from his meaning. What Sibawayh meant is this: "It includes a report of the realization of woe for him together with a supplication for it." Reflect on this point, which you will not find clearly stated elsewhere. Rather, you will find that they divide speech into declarative and injunctive without clarifying the places where they combine and separate. You have now understood that their saying *salām 'alaykum*, *waylun lahu*, and similar expressions is more eloquent than putting the utterance in the bare form of a request, such as *Allāhumma sallimhu* (O Allah, grant him safety).

**(Section)**

As for the fourth question: what is the meaning of the *salām* that is sought in the greeting?

There are two well-known opinions on this:

The first: the meaning is "the name *al-Salām* upon you," with *al-Salām* here referring to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of the statement is that the blessing of His name descends upon you and settles upon you, and similar expressions. Among His names, the name *al-Salāma* was chosen over others for reasons that will be explained in the answer to the next question. The proponents of this view argued with several proofs, including what is established in the authentic collections, that they used to say in the prayer: "Peace be upon Allah before His servants; peace be upon Jibril; peace be upon so-and-so." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not say 'Peace be upon Allah,' for Allah Himself is *al-Salām*. Rather say: 'All greetings, prayers, and good things are for Allah. Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.'" Sahih. So the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them to say "Peace be upon Allah," because *salām* here is a supplication for the one greeted and a request that he be made safe. Allah, exalted is He, is the one from whom it is requested, not the one for whom it is requested. He is the one invoked, not the one for whom invocation is made. It is therefore impossible to greet Him with *salām*. Rather, He is the One who greets His servants, as He greeted them in His Book, saying: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers.﴾ And His saying: ﴿Peace be upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin.﴾ He said of Yahya: ﴿And peace be upon him.﴾ And He said to Noah: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you."﴾ And on the Day of Resurrection He will greet the people of Paradise, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they request. [They will have] peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful.﴾ Here *qawlan* (a word) is in the accusative as a cognate accusative (*maṣdar*), and its verb is what is implied by *salām*, which is a kind of speech, because *salām* is speech.

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light suddenly shines upon them from above. They raise their heads, and behold, the Majestic, whose majesty is great, has looked down upon them from above and said: 'O people of Paradise, peace be upon you.' Then he recited: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful.﴾ Then He withdraws from them, and His mercy and blessing remain upon them in their dwellings." Da'if (weak).

In Sunan Ibn Majah, it is related with a raised chain (*marfū'*): "The first one to be greeted with peace by the Truth on the Day of Resurrection is 'Umar." Da'if jiddan (very weak), and it contains a rejected element (*nakāra*).

Allah, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be peace.﴾ This is their greeting on the day they meet Him, blessed and exalted is He. It is impossible that this is a greeting from them to Him, for they know Him too well to greet Him, and they were forbidden from doing so in this world. Rather, this is a greeting from Him to them. The greeting here is attached to the object (*mudāf ilā al-maf'ūl*), so it is the greeting with which they are greeted, not the greeting with which they greet Him. Had it not been for His saying in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful, Merciful,﴾ it could have been possible that the greeting to them comes from the angels, as Allah said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, saying, "Peace be upon you."﴾ But this is the angels' greeting when they enter upon them in their dwellings in Paradise, entering with greetings of peace upon them.

As for the greeting mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be peace,﴾ it is a greeting to them at the time of meeting, just as a beloved greets his beloved upon meeting him. What then have those who are veiled from their Lord lost on that day?

*Yakfī alladhī ghāba 'anka ghaybatuhu* ∗∗∗ *fadhāka dhanbun 'iqābuhu fīhi*

It suffices that the one who has been absent from you is absent; that is a sin, and its punishment is within it.

The point is that Allah, exalted is He, requests *salām* from Him, so there is no impossibility regarding Him greeting His servants, and He is not requested to give it to Himself. Therefore He is not greeted. His saying, "Allah Himself is *al-Salām*," is explicit that *al-Salām* is one of His names. They said: when the Muslim says *salām 'alaykum*, its meaning is "the name *al-Salām* upon you."

Among their proofs is what Abu Dawud related from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "A man greeted the Prophet (ﷺ), but he did not return the greeting until he faced a wall and performed tayammum, and then returned it, saying: 'I disliked mentioning Allah except in a state of purity.'" Sahih. They said: this hadith shows that *salām* is a remembrance of Allah, and it is a remembrance only when it includes one of His names.

Among their proofs as well is that the People of the Book who are disbelievers do not initiate greetings of *salām*, so one does not say to them *salām 'alaykum*. It is known that there is no objection to saying to one of them *salamaka Allāh* (may Allah grant you safety). This is only because *salām* is a name of Allah, so it is not permissible to request for a disbeliever the blessing of that name upon him.

These arguments, as you see, are strong and evident.

The second opinion: *salām* is a masdar meaning *salāma* (safety), and it is the requested object invoked in the greeting. Among the proofs of the proponents of this view is that it is mentioned without the definite article (*alif lām*). The Muslim says *salām 'alaykum*. Had it been one of Allah's names, it would not have been used this way, but would have been stated in the definite form, as all His other beautiful names are stated, such as: ﴿Al-Salām, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-'Azīz, al-Jabbār, al-Mutakabbir.﴾ Indefiniteness does not direct the word to a specific referent, let alone direct it to Allah alone, unlike the definite form, which is directed to Him by specification when His beautiful names are mentioned.

Among their proofs also is that the conjunction of mercy and blessing with it in the expression *salām 'alaykum wa raḥmatullāhi wa barakātuh* shows that the intended meaning is a masdar. For this reason, two masdars similar to it were conjoined to it.

Among their proofs also is that if *salām* here were one of Allah's names, the statement could not be correct except by supplying an implied element that would restrict it, so that the meaning would be "the blessing of the name *al-Salām* upon you," for the name itself is not upon them. If you said "the name of Allah upon you," the meaning would be "the blessing of this name," and similar supplied elements. It is known that such an implied element contradicts the original form and has no evidence.

Among their proofs also is that the purpose of *salām* is not this meaning. Rather, its purpose is to announce safety, both as a report and as a supplication, as will be explained in the answer to the question following this one. For this reason *salām* is a protection, since it contains the meaning of safety, and the safety of both the greeter and the one who returns the greeting from one another.
