Another reason: His saying, ﴿Say: Praise be to God, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen,﴾ clearly indicates that the one who says "Praise be to God" is the Muslim. This is why the pronoun is in the third person and He did not say "peace upon My servants."

Evidence that the peace is from God Most High includes several things. The first is that it matches its counterparts in the Qur'an, His peace upon His chosen servants Himself, such as His saying: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds,﴾ ﴿Peace upon Abraham,﴾ ﴿Peace upon Moses and Aaron,﴾ ﴿Peace upon the family of Yasin.﴾

Another is that His chosen servants are the messengers, and God joins His glorifying of Himself with His peace upon them, and His praising of Himself with His peace upon them. As for the first, He said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace upon the messengers.﴾ He mentioned His exalting Himself above what does not befit His majesty, and then His peace upon His messengers. In the joining of peace upon them with His glorifying of Himself there is a great secret of the Qur'an, which contains the refutation of every falsifier and innovator. He exalted Himself absolutely, as He exalted Himself above what His creation says about Him, and then He gave peace to the messengers. This requires their safety from everything the deniers and opponents say about them. If they are safe from everything their enemies accuse them of, then everything they brought is safe from lies and corruption. The greatest of what they brought is tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), the knowledge of God, and describing Him with what befits His majesty, of what He described Himself with on their tongues. When this is safe from lies, impossibility and corruption, it is pure truth, and what contradicts it is falsehood and impossible lie.

This very meaning is in His saying: ﴿Say: Praise be to God, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen,﴾ for it includes His praise with what He has of the attributes of perfection, the qualities of majesty, the praiseworthy acts and the most beautiful names, and the safety of His messengers from every defect, deficiency and lie. That includes the safety of what they brought from all falsehood. So reflect on this secret of joining peace upon His messengers with His praise and glorification. This indicates that the peace here is from God Most High, as it is at the end of the chapter al-Saffat.

As for conjoining a report to an imperative, how much of it there is! Among it is His saying: ﴿He said: My Lord, judge with truth. Our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought.﴾ And His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful.﴾ And His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of deciders.﴾ Its counterparts are very numerous.

The decisive statement on this is that the verse includes both matters together and encompasses them in one arrangement. The Messenger is the one who conveys God's speech from Him, and there is nothing in his role but conveying, and the speech is the speech of the Lord, blessed and exalted. He is the one who praised Himself and gave peace upon His servants, and He commanded His Messenger to convey that. So when the Messenger says, "Praise be to God and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen," he has praised God and given peace upon His servants with what God praised Himself with and gave peace with. Thus it is peace from God originally, from the conveyer by conveying, and from the servants by following and obedience. So we say, as our Lord, blessed and exalted, commanded us: ﴿Praise be to God, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen.﴾

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Say: He is God, the One.﴾ It is His affirmation of His own oneness and a command to the addressee to affirm His oneness. When the servant says, ﴿Say: He is God, the One,﴾ he has affirmed God with what He affirmed Himself with, and he included the word "say" to realize this meaning, and that he is a pure conveyer, saying what he was commanded to say. And God knows best.

This is different from His saying: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak,﴾ and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind.﴾ For this is a pure command to perform the act of seeking refuge, not a conveying of His speech, since God does not seek refuge from anyone, and that is impossible for Him. It is unlike ﴿Say: He is God, the One,﴾ which is a report about His oneness, and He, glory be to Him, reports about Himself that He is the One, the Unique. So reflect on this wondrous subtlety. And God is the one whose help is sought.

(Section)

As for the eighteenth question: the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the one who said to him "Upon you (alayka) be peace" from saying that, and said: "Do not say 'upon you is peace,' for 'upon you is peace' is the greeting of the dead." How many have strayed from the truth regarding its meaning, and its purpose and secret were hidden from them, so they resorted to various strained, unpleasant interpretations. Some rejected the hadith and said: it is authentically established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that in greeting the dead he said, "Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people," narrated by Muslim. They said: this is more authentic than the hadith of prohibition, and it contains the mention of the word "peace" first, so it must be adopted. A group imagined that the sunnah (the prophetic practice) in greeting the dead is to say "upon you peace," to distinguish between greeting the living and greeting the dead. All of these have only come to what they came to because they failed to understand the intent of the hadith.

His (ﷺ) saying, "upon you is peace, the greeting of the dead," is not legislation, nor a report of a legal ruling. It is a report of the common reality that was on the tongues of poets and people, for they used to put the name of the deceased before the supplication, as one of them said:

"Upon you is the peace of God, Qays ibn Asim, and His mercy, whatever mercy He wills."

And the saying of the one who elegized Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him:

"Upon you is peace from a commander, and blessed be the hand of God in that torn hide."

This is more common in their poetry than we can mention here. Reporting a reality does not indicate its permissibility, let alone that it is a sunnah. Rather, his prohibiting it while reporting that it occurs indicates that it is not legislated. The sunnah in greeting is to place its word (salam) before the word of the one greeted, and this applies to greeting both the living and the dead. Just as one does not say "upon you is peace" in greeting the living, so one does not say it in greeting the dead, as authentic sunnah has indicated for both.

What the people imagined as a distinction seems to be this: the one greeting another expects a reply, and it is said to him, "and upon you peace," so they began with the name of peace upon the one prayed for, anticipating his saying "and upon you peace." As for the dead, since they did not expect a reply from them, they placed the one prayed for before the supplication and said, "upon you peace." If this distinction were valid, it would be evidence for equating the living and the dead in greeting, for the one greeting his dead brother also expects a reply.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man passes by the grave of his brother, whom he knew in the world, and greets him, except that God returns his spirit to him until he returns his greeting." It is sound.

In sum, this imagination has been refuted by authentic sunnah, which legislated greeting both the living and the dead. Here is a wondrous subtlety that should be noticed. Greeting was legislated for the living and the dead with its name placed before the one greeted, because it is a supplication for good, and the better practice in supplicating for good is that the supplication precede the one prayed for, as in His saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings upon you, people of the house,﴾ and His saying: ﴿Peace upon Abraham,﴾ ﴿Peace upon Noah,﴾ ﴿Peace upon the family of Yasin,﴾ ﴿Peace upon you for what you patiently endured.﴾

As for supplication for evil, the one cursed is generally placed before the curse, as in His saying to Iblis: ﴿And indeed upon you is My curse,﴾ and His saying: ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse,﴾ and His saying: ﴿Upon them is the evil turn of fortune,﴾ and His saying: ﴿And upon them is wrath.﴾

The secret of this, and God knows best, is that in supplication for good they place the name of the desired thing first, which souls crave and seek, and whose word is pleasing to the hearing. The hearing begins with mention of the beloved, sought thing, and the heart begins to imagine it. So the heart and hearing are opened to it, and the listener remains as one awaiting who will attain this and upon whom it will descend. Then the speaker brings its name and says, "upon you" or "for you," and the listener gains joy and delight that stirs love, affection and compassion, which is the purpose of greeting.

As for supplication against someone, placing the one cursed first signals that he is singled out for that supplication, and that it is upon him alone, as if it were said to him: "This is upon you alone; the listeners do not share in it with you." This is unlike supplication for good, where what is sought is its generality, and whatever the supplicant includes in it is better. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, say: "The excellence of general supplication over specific supplication is like the excellence of the heavens over the earth." He mentioned in this regard a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) through Ali, that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him while he was supplicating, and said: "O Ali, make it general, for the excellence of the general over the specific is like the excellence of the heavens over the earth."

There is a second benefit in it as well: in supplication against someone, when one says to him "upon you," his hearing opens and his heart becomes eager to know what will be upon him. When the name of the one supplicated against is mentioned to him, it meets a heart that is empty and eager to know it, so it is more effective in harming him. Whoever understands this understands the secret of the omission of the particle waw in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened,﴾ so that its torment and what God has prepared in it surprise and overwhelm them. They are like one who stands at a door without knowing what kind of evil will be opened for him, except that he expects a great evil from it. The door is opened in his face and he is surprised by what he was expecting.

This is like what you find in this world, where a man is led to prison, and its door is closed until he arrives, and then the door is opened in his face, and its horror and pain surprise him. This is unlike the case in which it would have been opened before he came. As for the people of Paradise, since they are being led to the abode of honor, and it is part of honoring a visiting guest that the door of the house be opened for him, so that when he comes he finds it open and suffers no pain of waiting, He said about the people of Paradise: ﴿Until, when they reach it, and its gates are opened,﴾ with the waw.

The omission of the response is to magnify its matter and glorify its importance, according to their custom of omitting responses for this purpose. This approach relieves you of the claim that the waw is extra, and of the claim that it is the waw of eight (waw al-thamaniyah), since the gates of Paradise are eight. For even if that were valid, it would only apply if the number eight were enumerated in speech one after another, so that they reach seven and then resume counting from eight with a waw. Here there is no mention of the word "eight" in the verse, nor any counting of it, so reflect on this.

Moreover, there is another discussion about whether the waw comes to denote eight, which we have mentioned in al-Fath al-Makki, and we explained the places where it has been claimed that the waw denotes eight, and where such a claim is possible and where it is impossible.

If it is said: this is refuted by the fact that the master of creation (ﷺ) comes to the gate of Paradise and finds it closed until he asks for it to be opened?

We say: this is part of showing his nobility and superiority over creation: that Paradise is closed so that it will be opened for its people only at his hands. If he came and found it open, and he and its people entered it, the entrants would not know that its opening was at his hands and that it was he who opened it for them. Do you not see that when people try to enter the gate of a city or fortress and cannot open it, until a man comes and opens it for them, at the time they most need it opened, there is in that a manifestation of his lordship over them and his superiority and nobility that would not be known had he come with them and found it open?

We have gone beyond the purpose, and how far we have gone!

Do not consider these subtleties too lengthy, for you will hardly find them outside this commentary. And God Most High is the One who bestows by His grace and generosity.

(Section)

As for the nineteenth question: the particle waw in his (ﷺ) saying, "When the People of the Book greet you, say: 'and upon you,'" narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Many people have found it problematic, as the question mentions, and said: the correct version is to omit the waw and say "upon you." Al-Khattabi said: most of the narrators transmit it with the waw, while Ibn Uyaynah transmits it without it, and that is the correct version. For if the waw is omitted, their saying becomes exactly what they said, returned to them. But with the waw, one joins them and enters into what they said, since the waw is a conjunction.

I say: The meaning of what al-Khattabi pointed to is that the waw in such a case establishes the sentence and adds a second element to it. For example, if you say "Zayd is a writer," and the addressee says, "and a poet," this affirms writing for him and adds the description of poetry. Likewise, if you say to a man, "So-and-so loves you," and he says, "and does good to me." Al-Suhayli in al-Rawd derived from this that the number of the People of the Cave is seven, saying: "God Most High conjoined the dog to them with the waw," and said: ﴿And their eighth is their dog,﴾ and did not mention the waw in what preceded it of their speech. The waw establishes the first sentence. What he derived is good, except that it only benefits if the item conjoined by the waw is not part of their saying, but rather God reports that they said "seven," and then informs that their eighth is the dog. In that case it is an establishment of what they said and a report that the dog is the eighth. But if the report about the dog is part of their speech, and they said "this and this," then what he said does not hold, and the waw in this does not indicate establishment or confirmation. So reflect on this.

As for his saying that the hadith-scholars transmit it with the waw, this hadith was transmitted by Abdullah ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of the Jews greets you, he only says 'al-sam alaykum' (death be upon you), so say: 'and upon you.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim and Abu Dawud. Abu Dawud said: "Likewise Malik transmitted it from Abdullah ibn Dinar, and al-Thawri transmitted it from Abdullah ibn Dinar and said in it: 'and upon you.'" End of his words. Al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i also reported it in this way. Muslim reported it, and in some of its chains it says: "say: 'upon you,'" without mentioning the waw. The hadith of Malik that Abu Dawud mentioned is in al-Bukhari's Sahih, and the hadith of Sufyan al-Thawri is agreed upon; they are all with the waw. As for what al-Khattabi pointed to from the hadith of Ibn Uyaynah, al-Nasa'i reported it in his Sunan without the waw.

Having understood this, the inclusion of the waw in the hadith does not entail any objection whatsoever. The purpose of the greeting they used toward the Muslims is ultimately to announce that death has befallen them and to request it, since al-sam means death. So when they greet a Muslim with it and he returns it to them, this is by way of retaliation and justice, and the meaning of his return is: "We do not die before you; rather, you too will die. What you wished upon us has befallen you." Better than this is to say: the inclusion of the waw does not confirm the content of their greeting; rather, it returns it to them and affirms it for them, meaning: "and we too pray against you with what you prayed against us." For their supplication had already taken effect. So when the one who answers returns it to them with "and upon you," the waw conveys a subtle meaning: that what you asked for us and prayed for is the very same thing returned upon you, not any other greeting. Thus the inclusion of the waw serves this great benefit. Reflect on this in contrast with supplication for good, when one says, "May God forgive you," and he replies, "and you," meaning: this very supplication is from me to you. If you said "May God forgive you" and he said "you" alone, it would not indicate that the second supplication is the very same as the first. So reflect on it, for it is very subtle.

On this basis, the correct version is to retain the waw, as it is established in the Sahih and the Sunan. This is what has become clear to me regarding this word. Whoever finds something should add it in the margin, and God will reward him and his servants will thank him for his effort, for the aim is to reach the truth. When the truth becomes clear, whatever contradicts it is trodden underfoot. We have treated this question fully, to the extent we were able, in the book Tahdhib al-Sunan.

(Section)

As for the twentieth question: what is the wisdom in joining mercy and blessing with peace?

The answer to this is: since a person can only benefit from life through three things, the first being his safety from evil and from everything that opposes his life and livelihood, the second the attainment of good for him, and the third its continuation and permanence for him, his benefit from life is complete only through these three. The greeting (tahiyyah, a salutation) was prescribed to include all three. His saying ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ includes safety from evil. His saying "and the mercy of Allah" includes the attainment of good. His saying "and His blessings" includes its continuation and permanence, as the word *barakah* (blessing) is designed to mean abundance of good and its continuity. From here the wisdom in the pairing of His name *al-Ghafur* (the Forgiving) with His name *al-Rahim* (the Merciful) throughout most of the Qur'an can be known.

Since these three are sought by everyone, indeed they include all of a person's aims, and every aim falls short of them and is a means to them and a cause for attaining them, the word *tahiyyah* came to signify them: sometimes by correspondence (*mutabaqah*), since it is their completion; sometimes by inclusion (*tadammun*); and sometimes by implication (*iltizam*). Thus the word signifies them by correspondence when they are mentioned by their own names, by inclusion when peace and mercy are mentioned, since these two include the third, and by implication when only peace is mentioned, since it necessitates the attainment and continuation of good, for if good were absent, absolute safety would not be achieved. Peace necessitates the attainment of mercy, as has already been established. It is thereby known that this greeting excels and is complete above all the greetings of the nations, and for this reason Allah chose it for His servants and made it their greeting among themselves in this world and in the Abode of Peace (Paradise). It has also become clear to you that it is among the excellences and perfections of Islam. If this is the case in one branch of Islam's branches, namely the greeting known to the elite and the common alike, then what do you think of the rest of Islam's excellences, its majesty, its greatness, and its radiance, which reason and natural disposition bear witness to? Indeed, they are among the greatest proofs and clearest demonstrations indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), the perfection of his religion, its excellence, its nobility above all religions, and that its miraculousness lies in the very content of his call. Had he relied on it alone, it would have been a sign and proof of his truthfulness, and he would not need, along with it, any extraordinary act or separate sign. Rather, his religion, his law, his call, and his conduct are among the greatest of his miracles in the eyes of the elite of his community, so much so that their faith in him rests upon these, while signs with respect to them are strengthening supports, like the convergence of evidences. Whoever understands this, a great door of knowledge and faith is opened to him, indeed a door of the immediate Paradise, where the heart dances with joy and wishes that it were his in exchange for this world and all that is in it. Perhaps Allah will bring a victory or a command from Him, and that will assist in composing a book that includes mention of some of the excellences of the Sharia and the profound wisdoms and dazzling secrets within it, which are among the greatest proofs of the perfect knowledge, wisdom, mercy, goodness to His servants, and kindness to them of the Lord, the Exalted. It also includes the explanation of the benefits of both abodes and the guidance towards them, and the explanation of the corruptions of both abodes and the prohibition of them. He, glory be to Him, has not shown mercy to them in this world with any mercy, nor has He bestowed upon them any favour greater than His favour to them through this upright religion and this perfect Sharia. For this reason the word *mann* (a favour bestowed) is not mentioned in the Qur'an as a favour upon them except in the context of its mention, such as His saying: ﴿Allah has truly conferred a favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, though before that they were certainly in clear error﴾, and His saying: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me. Rather, Allah confers a favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful﴾. Thus it is pure goodness towards them, compassion for them, and guidance to what is good for them in this world and the next, not merely a mere obligation and trial devoid of the praiseworthy consequences and ends that cannot be reached except through this means. It is, for its aims which are tested and sought, like eating for satiety, drinking for quenching thirst, and intercourse for seeking offspring, and other causes to which their effects are linked by the requirement of wisdom and might. Therefore this straight path was established as a means and a way to the greatest triumph and happiness, and there is no way to reach it except by this path, just as there is no way to enter Paradise except by crossing the bridge (sirat). The Sharia is the life of hearts, the radiance of souls, and the delight of spirits. The hardship that arises in it and the obligation occur as a secondary intention, like their occurrence in the causes leading to the desired ends, not that they are sought for their own sake, let alone that they should be the sole aim to the exclusion of all else. So reflect on this point and give it its due thought in its sources and its arrivals, and it will open for you a wide door of knowledge and faith, and you will be among those firmly rooted in knowledge, not among those who know only an outward appearance of the life of this world, while they are heedless of the Hereafter.

And just as it is a sign bearing witness to Him regarding the perfect attributes by which He described Himself, it is also a sign bearing witness to His messenger that he is truly a messenger, and that he is the most knowing of creation, the most perfect, the most excellent, and the strongest in means of reaching Allah, and that no servant has been given the like of what he has been given. Woe to me for the one who would help in treading this path, unlocking this door, and reaching what lies beyond it, even with half a word! Nay, woe to the one who does not undertake to cut through the road and to turn away from this great aim, who abandons the mount and its driver, and surrenders the bow to its maker! But when the goal is great, helpers become few, and opponents and adversaries become many. When reliance is placed on the mere gifts and bounty of Allah, what a person bears for its sake becomes insignificant to him. So let not the hatred of one who turns away from the path and tells the truth deter you, nor let the one who has grown weary of persisting in the night journey and stopped be a reason for you to break off, for it is only one life, so consider where you place its loss and on whom you count its reward.

> You are slain by everyone you love, so look to your own soul in passion and choose well.

Spend your breaths on whatever you wish, for that expenditure will be returned to you precisely, and it will arrive to you and to no other. Between the servant and happiness and success lies an hour's patience for the sake of Allah and enduring blame in the way of Allah.

> It is but an hour, then it passes, and all this goes away and vanishes.

We have gone on at length, but we have not wearied. For a heart in which there is even a little life trembles when Allah and His messenger are mentioned, and wishes that the speaker were entirely tongues reciting and the listener entirely attentive ears. And whoever does not find his heart so—then, then—let him occupy himself with what suits him, for each is made easy for what he was created for, and each acts according to his own disposition.

> Every person yearns towards whom he loves, and every person inclines towards what suits him.

**(Section)**

Through this you have come to know the answer to the twenty-first question: that the perfection of the greeting lies in the mention of the blessings, since these three words comprehend all aims: the repelling of evil, the attainment of good, its permanence, its abundance, and its continuation. Hence there is no sense in adding to them. For this reason the well-known report says: "The greeting ends at *and His blessings*."

**(Section)**

As for the twenty-second question, namely: what is the wisdom in attributing mercy and blessing to Allah the Exalted, and in leaving the peace unattributed? Its answer is that since *al-Salam* (Peace) is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, it suffices to mention it without attribution to the one named. As for mercy and blessing, were they not attributed to Allah, one would not know whose mercy or whose blessing is being sought. So if one said "upon you be mercy and blessing," this phrase would contain no indication of the Merciful, the Blessed, from whom mercy and blessing are sought. Therefore it is said: "the mercy of Allah and His blessings." A second answer: *peace* is meant as the saying of the Muslim, "peace be upon you," and this is in reality attributed to him, but it is also meant as the real safety sought from *al-Salam*, glory be to Him and exalted, and this is attributed to Allah. So this verbal noun is attributed to the seeker who remembers, sometimes, and to the one from whom it is sought, sometimes, and so it is stated absolutely without attribution. Mercy and blessing, however, are attributed only to Allah the Exalted alone. For this reason one does not say "my mercy and my blessing upon you," but one says "peace from me upon you," and "peace from so-and-so upon so-and-so." The secret of this is that the word *salam* is the name of the verbal utterance, unlike mercy and blessing, which are names of their meanings rather than of their wording. So reflect upon it, for it is marvellous. A third answer: mercy and blessing are more complete than mere safety, for safety is a distancing from evil, whereas mercy and blessing are the attainment of good, its continuation, establishment, growth, and increase. This is more perfect, since it is the thing sought for its own sake, while the first is a means to it. For this reason, the bliss which the people of Paradise attain is more perfect than their mere safety from the Fire. Therefore the most perfect and complete of the two meanings was attributed to the Lord, blessed and exalted, in wording, and the other was stated absolutely, its attribution being understood in meaning from the context and the circumstance. So the wording came in the most perfect order and the finest arrangement.

**(Section)**

As for the twenty-third question, namely: what is the wisdom in using the singular for peace and mercy, and the plural for blessing?

Its answer: *peace* is either a pure verbal noun, which is one thing, so there is no sense in pluralising it, or it is a name of Allah the Exalted, and then it is likewise impossible to pluralise it. Under either assumption, there is no way to pluralise it. As for mercy, it is also a verbal noun meaning tenderness and compassion, so it too is not pluralised. The *ta'* in it is like its counterpart in *khullah* (friendship), *mahabbah* (love), and *ruqqah* (tenderness). It is not for delimiting a unit, as it is in *darbah* (a blow) and *tamrah* (a date). Just as one does not say *ruqqat*, *khullat*, or *ra'fat*, so one does not say *rahamat*. Moreover, the introduction of the plural suggests delimitation and restriction by number, while the singular suggests the named meaning absolutely, without delimitation. Thus the singular here is more complete and richer in meaning than the plural. This is a marvellous point, that the meaning of the singular should be greater than the meaning of the plural. For this reason, His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Say: To Allah belongs the conclusive proof﴾ is more general and more complete in meaning than saying "the conclusive proofs." And His saying: ﴿If you count the favour of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾ is more complete in meaning than saying "the favours of Allah, you will not enumerate them." And His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ is more complete in meaning than saying "good deeds." Likewise His saying: ﴿They rejoice in a favour from Allah and grace﴾, and its like are very numerous. We shall mention the secret of this later, if Allah wills.

As for blessing, since its named meaning is abundance of good and its continuation, one thing after another, such that whenever one unit of it passes, another unit follows it, it is a continuous good that succeeds through units perpetually, one thing after another. The plural form is therefore more appropriate for it, since it indicates the meaning intended by it. For this reason it came in the Qur'an in this way, in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾. So He made *mercy* singular and *blessings* plural. Likewise with peace in the tashahhud: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings."

**(Section)**

Know that mercy attributed to Allah the Exalted is of two kinds. The first is attributed to Him as the object of an action is attributed to its agent. The second is attributed to Him as an attribute is attributed to the one it describes. From the first kind is His saying in the authentic hadith: "The Garden and the Fire disputed..." and the hadith continues, in which it says: "He said to the Garden: You are only My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will." This was related by Muslim and Ahmad. This is a created mercy, attributed to Him in the way that a created thing that is through mercy is attributed to its Creator, the Exalted. It was named *mercy* because it was created through mercy and for mercy, and the people of mercy are specially singled out for it, for only the merciful enter it. From the same kind is His saying (ﷺ): "Allah created mercy on the day He created it as a hundred mercies, each mercy of which is as wide as the space between heaven and earth." This was related by Muslim and al-Hakim, and al-Bukhari related something similar. From the same kind is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us﴾, and from it is His naming of rain as mercy in His saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾. On this basis, the widely known supplication among people, past and present, which is the saying of the one who supplicates, "O Allah, gather us in the abode of Your mercy," is not impermissible. Al-Bukhari mentioned it in his *al-Adab al-Mufrad* from some of the early generations, and he reported the disapproval of it, saying: "The abode of His mercy is His essence." This is based on the premise that mercy is an attribute. But the intent of the supplicant is not that; rather, his intent is the created mercy, which is the Garden. Yet those who disliked it have a very subtle view, namely that if the intended meaning of mercy is the Garden itself, it is not proper to attribute "abode" to it. For this reason it is not proper to say "gather us in the abode of Your Garden," for the Garden itself is the abode of settling, and it is the very abode, as He said: ﴿How good as a place of settling and a station﴾. How then is the abode attributed to it, when the abode is the place in which a thing settles, and it is not valid for the supplicant to seek gathering in the place where the Garden settles? Therefore it was said: "The abode of His mercy is His essence." But the correct view is that this is not impermissible at all, and even if one said plainly, "gather us in the abode of Your Garden," it would not be impermissible. This is because the abode is more general than being mercy or punishment, so when it is attributed to one of its kinds, it is attributed to what distinguishes it from others, as though it were said: "in the abode which is Your mercy, not in the other abode." A parallel is to say: "sit in the abode of the mosque," meaning the abode which is the mosque, and attribution in such a case is neither impermissible nor disliked. Furthermore, even though the Garden is called mercy, it is not impermissible to call what is in it of various kinds of bliss mercy too. There is no doubt that the abode of that bliss is the Garden. So the supplicant asks that Allah gather him and those he loves in the place where that created mercy in the Garden settles. This is very clear, so the supplication is not impermissible in any respect, and Allah knows best. This is unlike the saying of the supplicant, "O Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek aid," for here mercy is His attribute, blessed and exalted, and it is the object of seeking aid, since one does not seek aid from a created being. For this reason this supplication is among the supplications for distress, because it contains tawhid and seeking aid through the mercy of the Most Merciful, appealing to Him through two names upon which all the Most Beautiful Names depend, and to which all their meanings return, namely the name *al-Hayy al-Qayyum* (the Living, the Self-Subsisting). For life necessitates all the attributes of perfection, and no attribute of perfection is absent from it except through weakness of life. So when His life, exalted be He, is the most perfect and complete life, its affirmation necessitates the affirmation of every perfection that contradicts the negation of the perfection of life. By this rational path, the speculative theologians of the Affirmers (*ahl al-ithbat*) affirmed for Him the attributes of hearing, sight, knowledge, will, power, speech, and all other attributes of perfection. As for *al-Qayyum*, it includes the perfection of His self-sufficiency and the perfection of His power, for He is the one who subsists in His own essence, needing none to sustain Him in any way, and this is the perfection of His self-sufficiency in Himself above all else. He is also the one who sustains others, so no other has subsistence except through His sustaining it, and this is the perfection of His power and might. These two names thus combine the attributes of perfection, complete self-sufficiency, and complete power. So the one who seeks aid through these two names is as though he seeks aid through every name of the Lord and every attribute of His. How fitting it is that seeking aid through these two names should be in the place of expectation for the relief of distresses, the rescue of the afflicted, and the granting of requests!

The point is that the mercy sought for aid is an attribute of the Lord, exalted be He, and not any of His creatures, just as one who seeks refuge in His might, saying, "I seek refuge in Your might," is seeking refuge in His might which is His attribute, not in a might which He created and by which He grants honour to His believing servants. All of this confirms the view of the people of the Sunnah, that the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah" indicates that His words, blessed and exalted, are uncreated, for one does not seek refuge in a created thing. As for His saying, exalted be He, relating the words of His angels: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy﴾, this is the mercy of attribute which encompassed everything, as He said, exalted be He: ﴿And My mercy has encompassed all things﴾. Its encompassing is the generality of its connection to everything, just as the vastness of His knowledge is the generality of its connection to every known thing.

**(Section)**

As for blessing, it is likewise of two kinds. The first is blessing which is His act, blessed and exalted. From it the verb is *barak*, which is transitive sometimes directly, sometimes with a particle *ʿala* (upon), and sometimes with a particle *fi* (in). Its passive participle is *mubarak*, which is that which has been made so, and thus it is blessed by His making it.

The second type: a blessing attributed to Him in the sense of mercy, might, and action. From this comes *tabaraka* (blessed is He), and for this reason it is not said of anyone else. It is fitting only for Him, glory be to Him. He is *al-Mubarak* (the Blessed One), and His servant and messenger is blessed as the Messiah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I am﴾. Whoever God blesses, and upon whom He bestows blessing, is blessed. As for His attribute *tabaraka*, it is specific to Him, exalted is He, as He applied it to Himself in His saying: ﴿Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ ﴿And blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned﴾ ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾. Do you not see how it recurs throughout the Qur'an, applied to Him alone, not to be used of anyone else? It comes in the pattern of abundance and intensity, like *ta'ala* (He is exalted) and *ta'aẓẓama* (He is magnified) and similar forms. So the pattern of *tabaraka* follows the pattern of *ta'ala*, which indicates the perfection and utmost height of loftiness. Likewise *tabaraka* indicates the perfection of His blessing, its greatness, and its vastness.

This is the meaning of the statement of some of the salaf: "*Tabaraka* means *ta'aẓẓama* (He is magnified)."

Another said: its meaning is that blessings come from Him, so all blessing is from Him.

Another said: "His goodness and benevolence to His creation abound."

It was said: "His compassion and mercy toward them have widened."

It was said: "He has exceeded everything and is exalted above it in His attributes and actions."

From here it was said: "Its meaning is *ta'ala* and *ta'aẓẓama*."

It was said: "*Tabaraka* means *taqaddasa* (He is sanctified), and *al-qudus* means purity."

It was said: "*Tabaraka* means by His name He blesses everything." It was also said: "*Tabaraka* means He is elevated, and *al-mubarak* is the one whose mention is elevated," narrated by al-Baghawi.

It was said: "*Tabaraka* means blessing is acquired and attained through mentioning Him."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He brought every blessing."

It was said: "Its meaning is that He remained and endured, with what has not ceased and does not cease, and His mention." Also al-Baghawi.

The reality of the word is that *al-barakah* (blessing) is the abundance of good and its continuity, and no one is more deserving of this in attribute and action than Him, blessed and exalted is He.

The interpretation of the salaf revolves around these two meanings, and they are mutually entailing. But the more fitting meaning for the word is the sense of attribute, not action, since it is an intransitive verb like *ta'ala*, *taqaddasa* and *ta'aẓẓama*. The meaning of such words is not that He made others lofty, holy, or great. This is not something the word can bear in any way. Rather, their meaning lies in the one to whom they are ascribed: He is the Exalted, the Sanctified. So likewise *tabaraka* cannot mean that He blessed others. How far apart are the two, in form and meaning! This is intransitive and that is transitive. You know, then, that whoever interprets *tabaraka* as "He cast blessing and blessed others" has not hit its meaning, even though this is a necessary consequence of His being blessed. *Tabaraka* follows the pattern of *majada* (to be glorious), and *al-majd* is the abundance of attributes of majesty, vastness, and grace. *Baraka* follows the pattern of *a'ṭā* and *an'ama* (to give and to bestow). Since the transitive entails the intransitive but not vice versa, those among the salaf who interpreted the word in the transitive sense did so to encompass both meanings. So they said: "the coming of all blessing is from Him," or "all blessing is from Him." This is a branch from *tabaraka* in itself.

We have elaborated on this at length in the book *al-Fath al-Makki*, and there we showed that all blessing belongs to Him, exalted is He, and comes from Him. He is the Blessed One, and whoever He casts His blessing upon becomes blessed. For this reason His Book is blessed, His House is blessed, and the times and places that He honored and distinguished above others are blessed. The Night of Power is blessed, and what surrounds al-Aqsa is blessed, and He described the land of Syria with blessing in four or five places in His Book. Reflect on the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Thawban, which Muslim narrated in his Sahih, when he finished the prayer:

"O God, You are peace, and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, O Possessor of majesty and honor."

Narrated by Muslim, Abu Dawud and Ahmad.

Contemplate these noble words: how they combined the two kinds of praise, namely praise of transcendence and glorification, and praise of commendation and exaltation, in the most eloquent, concise, and complete meaning. He informed that He is Peace, and from Him is peace. So peace belongs to Him in attribute and in dominion. The explanation of this has already passed in His description as *al-Salam* (the Peace), and that all His attributes of perfection, qualities of majesty, actions, and names are all peace. Likewise all praise belongs to Him in attribute and dominion. He is the Praised in His essence, and He makes whichever of His servants He wills to be praised, bestowing praise from Himself. Likewise all might belongs to Him in attribute and dominion, and He is the Mighty, than whom nothing is mightier, and whoever among His servants is made mighty is so by His making him mighty. Likewise all mercy belongs to Him in attribute and dominion. Likewise blessing: He is the One blessed in His essence, who blesses whomever He wills of His creation, and by that they become blessed. ﴿So blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿And blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned﴾.

This is a vast carpet, and the furthest knowledge of the scholars reaches only the outer edges and borders of it.

As for what lies beyond that, it is as the most knowledgeable of creation about God, the closest of them to God, and the most honored of them in His sight said:

"I cannot enumerate praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself."

Narrated by Muslim.

And in the long hadith of intercession he said: "I will fall prostrate before my Lord, and He will then open to me of His praises what I do not know well now." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim. And in the supplication for distress and grief: "I ask You by every name that is Yours, by which You named Yourself, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept hidden in the knowledge of the unseen with You."

(Sahih)

This shows that God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, has names and attributes which He has kept to Himself in the knowledge of the unseen with Him, which no near angel nor sent prophet knows. Our sufficiency is to acknowledge our incapacity and to stop at what He has permitted us of that. We neither exceed in it nor neglect it. And success is from God.

(Section)

As for the twenty-fourth question: what is the wisdom in emphasizing the command to greet the Prophet (ﷺ) with the verbal noun, but not in the case of prayer upon him, in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, pray upon him and greet him with peace﴾?

Its answer: the emphasis falls upon both the prayer and the greeting, though the direction of the emphasis differs. At the beginning of the verse, God informed of His own prayer upon him and the prayer of His angels upon him, emphasizing this report with the particle *inna* (indeed), and reporting about the angels in the plural form attached to a pronoun, which indicates generality and comprehensiveness. When souls sense that his station with God and His angels is this station, they hasten to pray upon him even if they are not commanded to do so. A mere reminder and slight allusion suffices for them. When they are commanded, there is no need to emphasize the command. Rather, when a bare command comes, they hasten and rush to agree with God and His angels in praying upon him, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him. So there was no need to emphasize the verb with the verbal noun. As for the greeting, since it lacks this meaning and comes in the context of a bare command, not a report, it is fitting to emphasize it with the verbal noun, to indicate the realization and affirmation of the meaning. The emphasis of the verb takes the place of its repetition, just as repetition occurred in the prayer, in report and in command. So likewise the honoring occurred in the greeting, in action and in verbal noun. Reflect on this, for it is very wondrous. And God knows best.

We have mentioned some of the secrets and wondrous wisdoms in this verse in the book *Ta'zim Sha'n al-Salat wa-al-Salam 'ala Khayr al-Anam*, and we brought in it benefits equal to the least of them, a journey of benefits found nowhere else. To God be praise. So we will limit ourselves to this one point.

(Section)

As for the twenty-fifth question: what is the wisdom in placing the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) before the prayer upon him in the sentence? Could the beginning not have been with what God began with in the verse?

This too is a question with its own importance, which should not be dismissed carelessly or passed over. The Prophet (ﷺ) was extremely careful to put first what God put first, and to begin with what He began with. For this reason he began with al-Safa in the sa'i (ritual running), and said: "We begin with what God began with." (Sahih). He began with the face, then the hands, then the head in ablution, and he never neglected this once; rather, this was his ablution until he departed this world. Then he would put last what came last, and never put first what should come later. No one can transmit from him any contrary practice, neither with a sound chain, nor a fair one, nor a weak one. Nevertheless, in the matter of the prayer and greeting upon him, the greeting came first and the prayer came later. This is due to a secret of the prayer which we point to briefly as the situation allows. The prayer comprises worship of all the limbs and organs along with worship of the heart. Each limb has its share of worship. All the members and limbs of the worshipper move in the prayer as worship to God, in humility and submission. When the worshipper completes this worship and his movements end, he concludes by sitting before the Lord, exalted is He, in a sitting of humility, brokenness, and submission to His majesty, mighty and majestic is He, just as a humble servant sits before his master. The sitting of prayer is the most humble of sittings and the greatest in submission and abasement. So in this state the servant is permitted to praise God, blessed and exalted is He, with the most eloquent kinds of praise, namely *al-tahiyyat lillah wa-al-salawat wa-al-tayyibat* (greetings, prayers and good things belong to God). It is their custom, when they enter upon their kings, to greet them with what befits them, and that greeting is exaltation of them and praise of them. God is more deserving of exaltation and praise than any of His creatures. So the servant, in saying "the greetings, the prayers and the good things," gathered the kinds of praise upon God, and reported that these belong to Him in attribute and dominion. Likewise all prayers belong to God; He is the One to whom prayer is offered, alone, not to another. Likewise all good things, words and deeds, belong to Him. His words are good, and His actions likewise. He is good, and only the good ascends to Him, and ﴿to Him ascends the good word﴾. So all good things belong to Him and come from Him and return to Him: they belong to Him in dominion and attribute, they come from Him and begin with Him, and to Him they ascend and end. The prayer comprises righteous deeds and good words, and ﴿the good word ascends to Him, and righteous deeds raise it﴾. So it is fitting to mention this at the close of the prayer, at the time of its ascent to God, exalted is He. Then the secret of greeting the Prophet (ﷺ): when he had brought this praise of the Lord, he turned to the status of the Messenger through whom this good came. So he greeted him with the most complete greeting, defined with the *alif-lam* of comprehensiveness, joined with mercy and blessing. This is the most authentic thing said in greeting him. So do not be stingy with the *alif-lam* in this station. Then he moved to greeting himself and the righteous servants of God, beginning with himself, since it is most important, and a person begins with himself, then with those he supports. Then he concluded this station with the bond of Islam, which is the testimony of truth, the first and last of matters, and in it is all praise. Then he moved to another kind, supplication and request. So the *tashahhud* combines both kinds of supplication: supplication of praise and goodness, and supplication of request and asking. The first is nobler of the two, because it is the right of the Lord and His attribute, and the second is the portion and benefit of the servant. In a report: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." (Weak).

But since prayer is the most complete of acts of worship in servitude and the most perfect, both kinds are prescribed in it, and the first of them is put first for its excellence. Then he moved to the second kind, supplication and request, beginning with what is most important, most sublime, and most beneficial to him, namely asking God for prayer upon His Messenger (ﷺ). This is one of the most excellent supplications of the servant and the most beneficial for him in this world and the Hereafter, as we have mentioned in the book *Ta'zim Sha'n al-Salat 'ala al-Nabi*. In it also is that the supplicant makes it a prelude before his need and his request for himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this meaning in his saying: "Then let him choose from supplication what pleases him most." Likewise in the hadith of Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd: "When one of you supplicates, let him begin with praising God and extolling Him, then let him pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then let him supplicate." So reflect on how the *tashahhud*, from beginning to end, corresponds to this and is arranged in the finest order. The hadith of Fadalah is what uncovered and clarified this meaning for us. So may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, through whom He completed our religion, perfected His favor upon us by his message, made him a mercy to the worlds, and a sorrow to the disbelievers.

(Section)

As for the twenty-sixth question: what is the wisdom in the greeting being in the second-person address while the prayer is in the third-person form? Its answer is apparent from what preceded. Prayer upon him is a request and supplication from God that He pray upon him, so in it only the third-person form is possible, since one does not say "O God, pray upon You." As for greeting him, it came in the form of present address, treating him as one who is face to face, for a very wondrous wisdom: when he (ﷺ) was dearer to the believer than his own self between his two sides, and more fitting for him and nearer, and his mental reality and ideal image existed in his heart such that nothing is absent from it except his person, as the poet said:

"Your likeness is before my eyes, your mention is on my tongue,
And your abode is in my heart, so where could you be absent?"

One who is in this state is truly present, and whoever else, even if present to the eye, is absent from the heart. So addressing him in direct address and presence, greeting him, was more fitting than greeting in absence, treating him as one face to face and visible, because of his nearness to the heart and his indwelling in all its parts, such that no part of the heart is left except that his love and mention are in it, as it is said:

"If my heart were split open, you would see your mention in its midst."

The declaration of *There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God* is in a single line. Do not be surprised at the beloved's domination over the heart of the lover and his overpowering of it, to the extent that it is as though he sees him. This is why you find them, in addressing their beloved, relying on direct address and witnessing, along with the utmost physical distance, because of the perfection of spiritual nearness. Bodily distance did not prevent them from conversing with spirits and addressing them. Whoever is coarse in temperament is far removed from all this. Love may reach some of its people such that they see their beloved, in nearness to them, as nearer to them than their own soul, than which nothing is nearer. As it is said:

"O you who remain in my heart through all time, and distant from my sight and my vision,
You are my soul, even if you are not seen; it is nearer to me than any near thing."

And another said:

"O you who dwell between my ribs and my inner heart,
Though far away, your abode is near to me."

Love refines its matter so much that the lover sees it as nearer and closer to him than his own soul. Here are verses that touch on this:

"It is nearer to the passionate lover than his own self, though it is absent from his eye,
And whoever has love like this, how could he be one who forgets?"

Then it refines its affair and subdues its authority, until the lover is absent with his beloved from himself, feeling nothing but his beloved and not feeling himself. From this arose the Sufi *shathahat* (ecstatic utterances), whose source is the strength of the inspired state and weakness of discernment. Its author judges by the state over knowledge, makes the judgment rest with it, and removes his knowledge from the matter. The preserved ones judge by knowledge over the authority of the state. They know that any state over which knowledge does not rule should not be relied upon or trusted, except as one relies on the defeated and subdued in what overtakes him that he cannot repel. This is the condition of the perfected among the people, who combined the light of knowledge with states of practice. The storms of their states did not extinguish the light of their knowledge, and their knowledge did not hold them back from ascending to the stations of faith and excellence beyond it. These are the judges over both groups. As for others, they are either veiled by a knowledge that has no authority over them, or deceived by a state with no knowledge of its soundness from its corruption. And God, exalted is He, is asked for His bounty; He is near and responsive.

So the perfected person is the one who makes knowledge rule over the state, acting in his state by his knowledge, and makes knowledge the light by which he distinguishes the sound from the corrupt, not the one who disparages knowledge by the state and makes the state a standard and scale over it. What agrees with his state from knowledge he accepts, and what contradicts it he rejects and negates. This is the root of error in this domain. Rather, the obligation is to make knowledge the judge and to return to its ruling. On this basis all the gnostic shaykhs of the path enjoined, and urged most strongly toward knowledge, because of their awareness of the dangers and ruin in the bare state divorced from it: ﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

(Section)

As for the twenty-seventh question: what is the wisdom in the praise of God in the *tashahhud* coming in the third-person form, though He, glory be to Him, is the one addressed, whom the servant confides in, while the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) comes in the second-person form, though he is absent?

Its answer: praise of God generally comes attached to His beautiful names in their apparent form, not with a pronoun, unless the apparent name has been mentioned earlier, and then the pronoun follows it. Such is the worshipper's saying: ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone we worship﴾, and his saying in bowing, "Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty," and in prostration, "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

This is part of Ibn al-Qayyim's discussion of the secret in the divine names and the choice of the names used in praise and supplication. Within it, the sayings of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the verses of the Qur'an are quoted as the author cites them.

The secret in this is that praise is attached to His Most Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna) because their meanings include the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty. So He is named by the apparent noun that signifies the meaning by which and for which He is praised, exalted be He. The pronoun carries no indication of this. For this reason, when praise must be addressed to Him directly, the apparent noun is used together with the plural suffix *mim* (the sign of the plural), which signifies all the names and attributes. An example is his saying when he raised his head from bowing (ruku'): "O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs the praise" (*Allahumma Rabbana laka al-hamd*). Sometimes he confines himself to mentioning the Lord, exalted be He, because the word itself indicates this meaning. So reflect upon it, for its line of thought is very subtle. Consider also how the supplication that includes both praise and request is opened with the word "Allahumma" (O Allah), as in the Master of Forgiveness (*sayyid al-istighfar*): "O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me, and I am Your servant..." (the hadith).

Narrated by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i.

The bare supplication (du'a' mujarrad) is introduced with the word "Lord" (Rabb), as in the words of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, and the words of Adam: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾, and the words of Moses: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, and the words of Noah: ﴿My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say between the two prostrations: "Lord, forgive me, Lord, forgive me" (sahih). The secret of this is that God is asked by His lordship, which includes His power, His beneficence, His nurturing of His servant and the rectification of his affairs, and He is praised by His divinity (uluhiyyah), which includes the affirmation of what is due to Him of the exalted attributes and the most beautiful names. Reflect upon the method of the Qur'an and you will find it as I have mentioned to you. As for supplication, we have mentioned examples of it; wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, it almost never comes except introduced by the name "Lord." As for praise, wherever it occurs, it is introduced by the Most Beautiful Names, and the most important with which it is introduced is the name of Allah, majestic is His majesty, as in ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ wherever it comes, and ﴿So glory be to Allah﴾, and ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might﴾, and similar to it ﴿Glorify Allah, whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ wherever it occurs, and ﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, and their likes.

In the supplication of the Messiah there came: ﴿O Allah, our Lord, send down upon us a table from the heaven﴾, so he mentioned both matters, and nothing else like it is found in the Qur'an. I have not seen anyone address this or draw attention to it. It is a wondrous secret that indicates the Messiah's perfect knowledge of his Lord and his glorification of Him. This request came after his people had said to him: ﴿Is your Lord able to send down upon us a table from the heaven?﴾. So Allah caused them to fear and informed them that this is something that it is not fitting to ask about, and that faith rejects it. When they persisted in the demand, and the Messiah feared that doubt would enter them if they were not granted what they asked, he began his request with the word ﴿Allahumma﴾ (O Allah), which signifies praise of Allah by all His names and attributes. Within that is the representation of himself as one who praises, extols, and remembers the names of his Lord, and who glorifies Him by them. The purpose of this supplication and the fulfilment of this need is that the Lord be praised with that, glorified by it, that His favours be mentioned, and that the signs of His power and lordship be made manifest, and that it be a proof of the truthfulness of His messenger. Thereby there is achieved an increase in faith and in praise of Allah, an affair that makes the request fitting and serves as an excuse for it. So he used the two names: the name Allah, by which He is praised, and the name Lord, by which He is called upon and asked, because the situation was one that required both.

So reflect upon this wondrous secret, and do not let your understanding slip past it, for it is of the understanding that Allah gives to whom He wills in His Book. And to Him belongs all praise.

As for greeting the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of direct address, we have mentioned its secret in the aspect before this, so its context is near.

(Section)

As for the twenty-eighth question: it includes two questions. The first: what is the secret in the greeting (*salam*) being at the end of the prayer? The second: why was it definite (*ma'rifah*)?

The answer: as for concluding the prayer with it, Allah has made for every act of worship a means of exiting from it (*tahlil*). Thus exiting from the pilgrimage (*hajj*) is by stoning and what follows it, and likewise exiting from fasting is by breaking the fast after sunset. So He made the greeting the exit from the prayer, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Its entry is the takbir and its exit is the taslim" (sahih). Its entry (*tahrim*) here is its gate by which one enters into it, and its exit (*tahlil*) is its gate by which one leaves it. So He made the takbir the gate of entry and the taslim the gate of exit, for a wondrous and far-reaching wisdom that is understood by one who comprehends from Allah, and who obliges himself to contemplate the excellences of this great religion, whose thought travels far in extracting its rulings, secrets and marvels, and who is removed from the world of habit and familiarity. He is not content with mere forms until he knows the spirits that are sustained by them. For Allah does not legislate anything in vain, nor devoid of profound wisdom; rather, within the folds of what He has legislated and commanded there are wisdoms and secrets that dazzle the intellects, by which the observer is guided to what lies behind them, so the heart prostrates in submission and acceptance.

We say, and with Allah is success: since the worshipper has withdrawn from distractions, cut off all attachments, purified himself, taken his adornment, and prepared himself to enter upon Allah, exalted be He, and to converse with Him, it was prescribed for him to enter upon Him as servants enter upon kings, entering with glorification and reverence. So He prescribed for him the most eloquent expression that signifies this meaning, which is the saying "Allahu Akbar" (Allah is greatest). For in this utterance there is glorification, specification, and an absoluteness in the omitted object governed by *min* that is not found in any other. For this reason the correct view is that no other expression can take its place, convey its meaning, or validly establish the prayer except with it, as is the position of the people of Madina and the people of hadith (*ahl al-hadith*). So this utterance, and the apprehension of its meaning, is the gate of the prayer through which the servant enters upon his Lord. When he feels in his heart that Allah is greater than anything that may occur to the mind, he will be ashamed to occupy his heart in prayer with anything else. Otherwise he would not fulfil the meaning of "Allah is greatest," nor render the due of this utterance, and he would not have come to the House by its door; rather, the door would be shut against him. This is by the consensus of the early generations (*salaf*): the servant has from his prayer only what he understands of it and what is present in his heart.

How excellent is what Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi said in some of his admonitions: "Presence of heart is the first station of the prayer. When you have alighted at it, you pass on to the desert of meaning. When you depart from it, you kneel at the gate of intimate conversation (*munajah*). The first hospitality for the guest is wakefulness and the unveiling of the veil from the eye of the heart. How can one who has not gone out into the desert hope to enter Mecca? You have sent your heart into every valley, so the prayer may surprise you while your heart is not with you. Then you send the messenger after it, but he does not find it, and you enter into prayer without a heart."

The point is that it is ugly for the servant to say with his tongue "Allah is greatest" while his heart is filled with other than Allah. He takes it as the direction of his heart in prayer, and perhaps he is not present before his Lord in any part of it. Had he fulfilled the due of "Allah is greatest" and come to the House by its door, he would have entered and departed with kinds of gifts and blessings. This is the gate through which the worshipper enters, which is the *tahrim*. As for the gate through which he exits, it is the gate of the greeting (*salam*), which contains one of the Most Beautiful Names. So he opens his prayer with the name of the Blessed and Exalted, and closes it with His name. Thus he mentions the name of his Lord at the beginning and at the end of the prayer: its beginning is with His name, and its end is with His name. He entered into it with His name and departed from it with His name, together with what the name *al-Salam* (The Source of Peace) has of distinctive property and wisdom suited to the worshipper's departure from before Allah, exalted be He. For as long as the worshipper is in his prayer before his Lord, he is within His sanctuary, which no one can violate; indeed he is within a sanctuary protected from all calamities and evils. When he departs from before Him, blessed and exalted be He, calamities, afflictions and trials rush upon him from every side, and Satan comes to him with his snares and his troops. So he is exposed to kinds of afflictions and trials. But when he departs from before Allah accompanied by the greeting, a guardian from Allah does not cease to protect him until the time of the next prayer. And it is part of the completion of the blessing upon him that his departure from before his Lord be with a peace that he carries with him, that remains for him and stays with him.

So reflect upon this secret, for even if there were nothing else in this connection, it would be sufficient. How much more so, when it contains secrets and benefits not found among the people of this age. Praise for this belongs to Allah alone. Just as the One who bestows the blessing is Allah alone, so the One praised for it is Allah alone.

By this, the answer to the second question has also become known: the greeting comes here in definite form so that it signifies His name *al-Salam*.

Let this be the end of the discussion on the matter of "Peace be upon you" (*salamun 'alaykum*).

Had it not been for the intention of brevity, it would have come out as a huge volume. We have not touched in it upon the derivative issues of the greeting and its rulings that are recorded in the books, for they are full of them; whoever wants them should take them from there. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

**(Issue)**
**"Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah"** (سلام عليكم ورحمة الله)

In this greeting there are twenty-eight questions:

**First question:** What is the meaning of *salam* (peace), and what is its reality?

**Second question:** Is it a verbal noun (*masdar*) or a noun (*ism*)?

**Third question:** Is the Muslim's saying *salamun 'alaykum* a statement of fact (*khabar*) or a performative utterance (*insha'*)?

**Fourth question:** What is the meaning of the peace that is sought in greeting? If it is a supplication and a request, what is the wisdom in seeking it at meeting and in correspondence, rather than other meanings?

**Fifth question:** If it derives from *al-salama* (safety), it is known that the verb from it is not transitive with *'ala* (upon). So one does not say *salamah 'alayka* or *sallamtu 'alayka* with a kasra on the lam, but rather *salam laka*, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So peace be to you from the companions of the right hand﴾?

**Sixth question:** What is the wisdom in beginning with *salam* when the predicate is a prepositional phrase (*jar wa majrur*), while the rule of Arabic is to place the predicate first in such constructions, as in *fi al-dar rajul* (there is a man in the house)?

**Seventh question:** Why is the one who responds to the greeting singled out with this structure, and why is the prepositional phrase placed before *salam* in the reply? Why was his reply not with *salam* placed first in absolute form, like his initial greeting?

**Eighth question:** What is the wisdom in the initiator's greeting being with an indefinite noun (*nakira*), while the response to it is with a definite noun (*ma'rifa*)? Likewise, what is the wisdom in the greeting at the beginning of a letter being with an indefinite noun, and at its end with a definite noun, so that one says at first *salamun 'alaykum*, and at the close of the letter *wa's-salamu 'alaykum*? Is this definiteness for the sake of the known (*'ahd*) and the prior mention of *salam*, or for some other wisdom?

**Ninth question:** What is the benefit of the conjunctive *wa* (and) entering the second greeting? One says first *salamun 'alaykum*, and at the end *wa's-salamu 'alaykum*. Upon what is this conjunction based?

**Tenth question:** What is the secret in *salam* being in the accusative (*nasb*) in the angels' greeting, and in the nominative (*raf'*) in Abraham's greeting? Is it as the grammarians say, that the greeting of Abraham is more complete because it contains a nominal sentence indicating permanence, while the greeting of the angels contains a verbal sentence indicating occurrence? Or is there some other secret?

**Eleventh question:** What is the secret in *salam* being in the accusative in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, and in the nominative in His words: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you"﴾? And what is the difference between the two places?

**Twelfth question:** What is the wisdom in Allah's greeting upon His prophets and messengers, when *salam* is in fact a request for safety for the one greeted? How can this meaning be conceived with regard to Allah? This is one of the most important and finest of questions.

**Thirteenth question:** If the wisdom of His greeting upon them has become clear, what is the wisdom in His greeting them with an indefinite noun, while He legislated for His servants to greet His Messenger with a definite noun, saying: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings" (as-salamu 'alayka ayyuha an-nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh), and likewise their greeting of themselves, and of the righteous servants of Allah?

**Fourteenth question:** What is the secret in Allah's greeting upon Yahya with an indefinite noun in His words: ﴿And peace be upon him﴾, and Jesus's greeting upon himself with a definite noun in his words: ﴿And peace is upon me﴾? Which of the two greetings is more complete and more comprehensive?

**Fifteenth question:** What is the wisdom in restricting these two greetings to these three days: ﴿The day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾, especially since greeting is required at all times? If it had been stated absolutely, would it not have been more comprehensive? Does this restriction not confine the greeting to these days alone?

**Sixteenth question:** What is the wisdom in the Prophet's greeting (ﷺ) upon those who follow guidance in the letter to Heraclius being with an indefinite noun, while Moses's greeting upon those who follow guidance is with a definite noun, as it occurs in the Qur'an? Why was the Prophet's greeting (ﷺ) not with a definite noun, so as to match the Qur'an? What is the difference between them?

**Seventeenth question:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾. Is this a peace from Allah, so that the speech contains two sentences: an imperative, which is the command in His words ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾, and a declarative, which is Allah's peace upon His servants? On this view, it would be a case of conjoining a declarative sentence to an imperative. Or is it a command from Allah to greet them with peace? On this view, He has commanded two things: one, saying "Praise be to Allah," and the second, saying "Peace upon His servants whom He has chosen," with both being objects governed by the verb "say." Which of the two meanings is more fitting for the verse?

**Eighteenth question:** Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Juray al-Hujaymi, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Upon you be peace, O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' He said: 'Do not say "Upon you be peace," for "Upon you be peace" is the greeting of the dead.'" It is authentic. At-Tirmidhi said: "It is a hadith that is authentic." It is also established from him regarding greeting the dead, both in deed and command: "Peace be upon you, O abode of believing people." Related by Muslim. What is the meaning of this hadith, and how is it reconciled with the authentic hadiths?

**Nineteenth question:** What is the meaning of the entry of the *wa* (and) in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "When the People of the Book greet you, say, 'And upon you' (wa 'alaykum)." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Many people have found this *wa* problematic, and some of the skilled scholars even denied that it is authentic. He said: "Because the *wa* in such a case requires the affirmation of the first and its confirmation, as when you say, 'Zayd is a writer,' and the addressee says, 'and a jurist,' for it implies the affirmation of the first and an additional attribute, 'jurist.'" So how did it enter this context, and what is its meaning?

**Twentieth question:** What is the secret in mercy and blessing being joined with the greeting, rather than other attributes such as forgiveness, righteousness, kindness, and the like?

**Twenty-first question:** Why does the greeting end at the words "and His blessings," and why is no addition legislated beyond them?

**Twenty-second question:** What is the wisdom in attributing mercy and blessing to Allah the Exalted, while the greeting is stripped of this attribution? Why were they not all attributed, or all left unattributed?

**Twenty-third question:** What is the wisdom in making *salam* and *rahma* singular, while *barakah* is plural?

**Twenty-fourth question:** What is the wisdom in emphasizing the command to greet the Prophet with the verbal noun (*masdar*) rather than with the word "prayer," in His words: ﴿O you who believe, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace (taslima)﴾? Why did He not say "salu salat"?

**Twenty-fifth question:** What is the wisdom in placing the greeting upon him before the blessing upon him in the prayer? Could the beginning not have been with the blessing upon him first, followed by the greeting, so that the beginning would be with what Allah began with, namely placing the blessing before the greeting?

**Twenty-sixth question:** What is the wisdom in the greeting upon him in prayer being in the form of direct address (*khitab al-mawajaha*), while the blessing upon him comes in the third-person form (*ghayba*), mentioning him by his proper name?

**Twenty-seventh question:** This is what the consistency of the speech leads to: What is the wisdom in the praise of Allah being in the form of the third person in our saying "At-tahiyyatu lillah" (all greetings are for Allah), although He, glory be to Him, is the one addressed in intimate conversation, who hears our speech and sees our place? And the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) came in the form of direct address, although the situation would seem to require the opposite. What is the wisdom in this?

**Twenty-eighth question:** This is the conclusion of the questions: What is the secret in the greeting being the conclusion of the prayer, and why was it not at its beginning? And if it is so, what is the secret in its coming definite, and why was it not indefinite?
