As for the **first question**, which is: what is the reality of this word? Its reality is disavowal, freedom, and deliverance from evil and defects, and upon this meaning its derivations revolve. From it is your saying: "May Allah keep you safe (salamaka)," and "So-and-so was kept safe from evil (salama)." From it is also the supplication of the believers on the bridge: "O Lord, keep us safe, O Allah, keep us safe." From it is also *salima al-shay' li-fulan*, meaning it became purely his, so that it was freed from the harm of partnership in it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are associates in dispute, and a man belonging entirely to one man﴾, meaning purely to him alone, with no other owning it along with him. From it is also *al-silm*, the opposite of war. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾, because each of the two warring parties is freed and kept safe from the harm of the other. For this reason, it is formed with the pattern of mutual action (*mufa'ala*), so one says: *al-musalama* is like *al-musharaka* (partnership). From it is also "the sound heart" (al-qalb as-salim), which is the one purified of rancor and deceit. Its reality is one who has become wholly devoted to Allah the Exalted alone, so he is freed from the deceit and corruption of *shirk* and from the deceit of sins and transgressions. Indeed, he is the one who remains upright in the sincerity of his love and the goodness of his dealings. This is the one for whom deliverance from His punishment and success with His honor are guaranteed. From this root also comes *al-Islam*, for it is from this same root, since it is submission and surrender to Allah the Exalted and freedom from the impurities of *shirk*. He has submitted to his Lord and become purely His, like the slave who belongs wholly to his master, with no quarreling partners. For this reason, the Exalted has struck these two examples: the purely devoted believer, and the one who associates others with Him. From it also comes *al-salam* in the sense of advance payment for a debt (*al-salaf*), whose reality is the compensation delivered in the contract, because the one who owes it has guaranteed its safety for the creditor. Then the contract itself was called *salam*, and its reality is what we have mentioned.

If it is said: Does this not contradict their saying of the one bitten by a snake, "*saqim*" (sound/safe, by euphemism)?

It is answered: This is not a contradiction to it, but rather an application of what we have said. They called him *salim* on account of what concerns him, seeks it, and hopes that his condition will come to safety. Nothing is more important to him than safety, and he is no more eager for anything else than for it. So he was called *salim* for this reason. This is of the same kind as their naming the deadly desert *mafazah* (a place of salvation), because nothing is more important to the one who traverses it than his success in escaping it, that is, his deliverance. So it was called *mafazah* because he seeks success from it. This is better than their saying that it is called *mafazah* and the stung one is called *salim* as an omen of good. Although optimism is part of this meaning and is included in it, the explanation we have given is more general and better.

If it is said: How can you trace *al-silm* back to this root?

It is answered: That is clear, for the one who ascends to a high place, since he is exposed to falling and destruction and seeks safety, is hoping for it. The instrument by which he reaches his goal was called *sullam* (ladder), because it includes his safety. For if he climbed with effort and without a ladder, his destruction would be expected. So it is established that *al-sullam* derives from this meaning. From it also comes the naming of Paradise as "the Abode of Peace" (*dar as-salam*). Regarding its attribution to peace, there are three opinions. The first is that it is an attribution to its owner, who is *as-Salam*, glory be to Him. The second is that it is an attribution to the greeting of its people, for their greeting therein is peace. The third is that it is an attribution to the meaning of peace, that is, the abode of peace from every calamity, defect, and evil. All three are mutually entailed, though the third is the most evident. For if the attribution were to its owner, it would have been attributed to one of His names other than *as-Salam*, and it would have been said "the abode of the Merciful," "the abode of Allah," "the abode of the King," or the like. Since its attribution to Him is known, when "the abode of peace" is mentioned, it is understood as referring to what is known. Moreover, what is customary in the Qur'an is attributing it either to its qualities or to its people. As for the first, such as: the abode of permanence, the abode of glory, the garden of refuge, the gardens of bliss, the gardens of Paradise. As for the second, such as: the abode of the righteous. But its attribution to a name of Allah the Exalted is not known in the Qur'an. So it is better to understand the attribution in light of what is customary in the Qur'an. Likewise, its attribution to greeting is weak for two reasons. The first is that greeting with peace is shared between the abode of this world and the abode of the Hereafter, whereas what is attributed to Paradise is only that which is specific to it, such as eternity, permanence, and continuance. The second is that among its qualities there are others more perfect than greeting, such as its being everlasting and enduring, and being the abode of eternity, whereas greeting there is incidental, occurring at meeting and mutual visiting. This is unlike safety from every defect, loss, and evil, which is among its most perfect and intended qualities, one that is constant, and without which bliss in it is not complete. Therefore, attributing it to this is more fitting. And this is evident.

**(Section)**

Having understood these two matters, the naming of peace as one of Allah's names is more fitting than all of this, and more deserving of this name than anything else named by it, because He, glory be to Him, is free from every defect and deficiency in every respect. He is *as-Salam* in the true sense in every consideration. Created beings are peaceful only by comparison. He, glory be to Him, is peace in His essence, free from every defect and deficiency that could be imagined. He is peace in His attributes, free from every defect and deficiency. He is peace in His actions, free from every defect, evil, injustice, and act that occurs otherwise than in accordance with wisdom. Rather, He is the true peace in every respect and in every consideration. Thus it is known that His deserving this name is more perfect than the deserving of any other thing named by it. This is the very reality of the transcendence (*tanzih*) by which He declared Himself transcendent and by which His Messenger declared Him transcendent. He is peace from having a consort or a child, peace from having an equal, a peer, a namesake, or a like, and peace from having a partner. For this reason, when you consider the individual attributes of His perfection, you find that each attribute is a peace from what opposes its perfection. His life is peace from death, from drowsiness, and from sleep. Likewise, His self-subsistence and power are peace from fatigue and weariness. His knowledge is peace from anything escaping it, or from the occurrence of forgetfulness, or from any need for recollection or reflection. His will is peace from departing from wisdom and benefit. His words are peace from falsehood and injustice; rather, His words are perfect in truth and justice. His self-sufficiency is peace from any need for other than Him in any way; rather, everything other than Him is in need of Him, while He is independent of all that is other than Him. His dominion is peace from any disputant over it, any partner, any aide, any manifest supporter, or any intercessor with Him without His permission. His divinity is peace from any partner in it; rather, He is Allah, there is no god but Him. His forbearance, pardon, forgiveness, and overlooking are peace from being due to need or to anything of that sort, or to flattery, as is the case with others. Rather, it is pure bounty, goodness, and generosity. Likewise, His punishment, vengeance, severity of grip, and swiftness of retribution are peace from being injustice, or vindictiveness, or harshness, or cruelty. Rather, they are pure wisdom, justice, and the placing of things in their proper places. They are also among the things for which He deserves praise and thanks, just as He deserves them for His goodness, reward, and blessings. Indeed, if He were to place reward in the place of punishment, that would contradict His wisdom and His might. So His placing punishment in its place is part of His justice, wisdom, and might. He is peace from what His enemies and those ignorant of Him imagine, such as contradiction to His wisdom. His decree and His measure are peace from futility, oppression, and injustice, and from any supposition that they occur contrary to the perfect wisdom. His legislation and religion are peace from contradiction, discord, confusion, and what opposes the benefit and mercy of His servants and goodness to them, and what opposes His wisdom. Rather, all His legislation is wisdom, mercy, benefit, and justice. Likewise, His giving is peace from being an exchange or from any need of the one who receives it, and His withholding is peace from miserliness and from fear of poverty. Rather, His giving is pure goodness, without exchange or need; and His withholding is pure justice and wisdom, unmixed with miserliness or incapacity. His establishment (*istiwa'*) upon His Throne and His exaltation above it are peace from needing what would carry Him or what He would be established upon. Rather, the Throne is in need of Him, and its bearers are in need of Him. He is the Independent of the Throne, of its bearers, and of everything other than Him. So His establishment and exaltation are free from being confined, from any need for a throne or for anything else, and from anything encompassing Him, glory be to Him and exalted. Indeed, He, glory be to Him, was when there was no throne, and He had no need of it, for He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. Rather, His establishment upon His Throne and His dominance over His creation are among the requirements of His dominion and His subjugation, without any need for a place or anything else in any way. His descent to the lowest heaven every night is peace from what contradicts His exaltation, and peace from what contradicts His self-sufficiency and perfection. He is peace from everything that a denier (*mu'attil*) imagines or a likener (*mushabbih*) asserts. He is peace from ever being beneath anything or confined within anything. Exalted is our Lord above everything that contradicts His perfection and His self-sufficiency. His hearing and His seeing are peace from everything that a likener imagines or a denier asserts. His allegiance to His friends is peace from being like the allegiance of one created being to another; rather, it is an allegiance of mercy, goodness, benevolence, and kindness, as He said: ﴿And say, "Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has not had a partner in the dominion, and has not had any protector out of humiliation"﴾. He did not deny that He could have a protector absolutely, but He denied that He has a protector out of humiliation. Likewise, His love for those who love Him and His friends is peace from the accidents of created love, whether it be love of need, or flattery, or benefit from nearness to Him, and peace from what the deniers say about it. Likewise, what He attributed to Himself, such as the hand and the face, is peace from what a likener imagines or a denier asserts. So reflect on how His name *as-Salam* encompasses everything from which He, blessed and exalted, is declared free. How many have memorized this name without knowing what these secrets and meanings it contains are! And Allah is the One sought for help, the One asked to grant success in commenting upon the Beautiful Names in this manner; He is near and responsive. Let us stop the discussion here on the first question.

**(Section)**

As for the **second question**, which is: Is *al-salam* a verbal noun or a noun that functions as a verbal noun?

The answer: *al-salam*, which is the greeting, is a noun of verbal action (*ism masdar*) derived from *sallama*. Its verbal noun (*masdar*) that is regularly used is *taslim*, as with *'allama* producing *ta'lim*, *fahhama* producing *tafhim*, and *kallama* producing *taklim*. And *as-salam* from *sallama* is like *al-kalam* from *kallama*.

If it is said: What is the difference between a verbal noun (*masdar*) and a noun of verbal action (*ism masdar*)?

Qur'an study app translation of Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 13, verses 23–24 (part 2 of 10):

We say: there is a difference between them, both verbal and semantic. The verbal difference is that the **masdar** (verbal noun) follows the regular pattern of its verb, which is its standard form, like the verbal nouns of *af'ala* (*if'āl*), *fa''ala* (*taf'īl*), *infa'ala* (*infi'āl*), *tafa''ala* (*tafa''ul*), and their pattern. The words *salām* and *kalām*, however, do not follow the regular pattern of their verbs. If they did, one would say *taslīm* and *taklīm*. The semantic difference is that the masdar indicates the action and its agent. So when you say *takhlīm*, *taslīm*, *ta'līm*, and similar words, they indicate the action and the one who performs it. *Taslīm* therefore indicates both the greeting (*salām*) and the one who greets (*muslim*). The same applies to *taklīm* and *ta'līm*. The **ism al-masdar** (noun of the verbal action), however, indicates only the action by itself. So *salām* and *kalām* do not, by their form, indicate a greeter (*muslim*) or a speaker (*mukallim*), unlike *taklīm* and *taslīm*. The secret of this distinction is that the masdar in your saying *sallama taslīman* and *kallama taklīman* functions like repeating the verb, as though you said *sallama sallama* and *takallama takallama*, and the verb is never without its agent.

As for the noun of the verbal action, they stripped it down to indicate only the action itself. This subtle point is one of the secrets of the Arabic language. This *salām* that is the greeting (*tahiyya*) is of this type. As for the *Salām* that is one of the names of Allah, there are two opinions about it:

The first: it is likewise a noun of the verbal action, and its application to Him is like the application of *'adl* (justice) to Him. The meaning is "the One possessing peace," and "the One possessing justice," with an omitted possessive construction (*hadhf al-muḍāf*).

The second: the masdar here carries the meaning of the active participle, i.e., *al-sālim* (the one who is free from defect), just as the Night of Decree was called *salām* meaning "free from every evil," for it is good and contains no evil.

The better of the two opinions, and the more consistent with Arabic grammar, is that *al-Salām* itself is one of His names, like *al-'Adl*. This is an instance of applying a masdar to the agent because it is predominant in him and repeatedly manifested by him, as in the expressions *rajulun ṣawm* (a man who fasts constantly), *'adl* (a just man), *zūr* (a man who often lies), and similar forms.

As for *salām* in the sense of *salāma* (safety, soundness), it is a masdar of its own kind, similar to *jalāl* and *jalāla*. When you drop the *tā'* (*jalāl*), the intended meaning is the masdar itself. When you add the *tā'* (*jalāla*), it signals specification with respect to a single instance of the masdar, like *ḥubb* and *ḥubba*. Thus *salām*, *jamāl*, and *jalāl* are like the general genus, since they lack the *tā'* of specification. *Salāma*, *jalāla*, *malāḥa*, and *faṣāḥa* all indicate a single quality. Do you not see that *malāḥa* (charm) is one of the qualities of perfection, and *jalāla* (majesty) is one of the qualities of grandeur? For this reason they did not say *kamāla* as they said *malāḥa* and *faṣāha*, because *kamāl* (perfection) is a comprehensive term for the attributes of nobility and excellence. If they had said *kamāla*, they would have defeated the purpose intended by the noun *kamāl*. Reflect on this.

On this same pattern come *ḥalāwa* (sweetness), *aṣāla* (nobility of origin), *razāna* (gravity), and *rajāḥa* (sound judgment), because each is a specific quality within absolute perfection and beauty, so they used the *tā'* that indicates specification. The opposite forms are *ḥamāqa* (foolishness), *ruqāʿa* (baseness), *nadhāla* (meanness), and *safāha* (folly), for they are specific qualities within absolute defect and imperfection. They used the form without *tā'* for the genus that encompasses the types, and they used the *tā'* for its types and individual instances. This meaning has already been established, and there is no need to repeat it. Now consider how *salām* came without the *tā'* to signal the attainment of the complete notion, since the intended purpose is achieved only through it. If someone is safe from one calamity but falls into another, he has not attained *salām*. It is therefore clear that *salām* has not left the category of the masdar in any of its aspects.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in its coming as a noun of the verbal action and not in the form of the masdar proper?

The answer: this secret is wonderful. The intention is that the meaning of safety be attained for the one greeted, in an absolute sense, without restriction to an agent. Since the intended meaning is absolute safety without reference to an agent, they used the noun of the verbal action, which indicates the action alone, and did not use the masdar, which indicates the action together with its agent. Reflect on this.

**(Section)**

As for the third question: is the Muslim's saying *salāmun 'alaykum* an expression of an injunctive act (*inshā'*) or a declarative statement (*khabar*)?

Its answer: this and similar expressions of supplication contain both the injunctive and the declarative. The aspect of declaration in it does not contradict the aspect of injunction. This is a subtle point that requires explanation and clarification. We say: speech has two relations: a relation to the speaker himself, and a relation to the matter he speaks about, whether as a request or as a report. It also has a third relation, to the addressee, which does not bear on this discussion. Its verification depends on the first two relations. The division into declarative and injunctive arises from these two relations, and one can know where they meet and where they separate. By its relation to the speaker's intention and will, bringing about the content of the statement, it is characterized as injunctive. By its relation to the matter spoken of and informing about its realization in external reality, it is characterized as declarative. The two relations sometimes coincide and sometimes diverge. Every case in which the meaning is established solely through the speaker's intention and will does not allow the declarative and injunctive to combine. Examples are the statements "I have sold you such-and-such," "I have given it to you," "I have freed," and "I have divorced." These meanings have no external existence except through the speaker's will and intention, so they are injunctive acts. Their declarative character arises from another aspect: they include the speaker's report of this relation's existence in his mind. However, this is not the declarative character for which the word "khabar" was established. Every case in which the meaning is realized from a source other than the speaker, and where the speaker has nothing but to supplicate for its realization and to desire it, does not contradict the injunctive. The declarative in it does not conflict with the injunctive. This is the case with *salām 'alaykum*, for the desired safety was not achieved by the action of the greeter, and the greeter has nothing but to supplicate for it and desire it. So when he says *salām 'alaykum*, it includes a report of the realization of safety, and an injunctive act of supplicating for it, willing it, and wishing for it. Likewise *waylun lahu* (woe to him). Sibawayh said: "It is supplication and declaration." Many people did not understand Sibawayh's statement as he intended it, and distorted it from his meaning. What Sibawayh meant is this: "It includes a report of the realization of woe for him together with a supplication for it." Reflect on this point, which you will not find clearly stated elsewhere. Rather, you will find that they divide speech into declarative and injunctive without clarifying the places where they combine and separate. You have now understood that their saying *salām 'alaykum*, *waylun lahu*, and similar expressions is more eloquent than putting the utterance in the bare form of a request, such as *Allāhumma sallimhu* (O Allah, grant him safety).

**(Section)**

As for the fourth question: what is the meaning of the *salām* that is sought in the greeting?

There are two well-known opinions on this:

The first: the meaning is "the name *al-Salām* upon you," with *al-Salām* here referring to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of the statement is that the blessing of His name descends upon you and settles upon you, and similar expressions. Among His names, the name *al-Salāma* was chosen over others for reasons that will be explained in the answer to the next question. The proponents of this view argued with several proofs, including what is established in the authentic collections, that they used to say in the prayer: "Peace be upon Allah before His servants; peace be upon Jibril; peace be upon so-and-so." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not say 'Peace be upon Allah,' for Allah Himself is *al-Salām*. Rather say: 'All greetings, prayers, and good things are for Allah. Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.'" Sahih. So the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them to say "Peace be upon Allah," because *salām* here is a supplication for the one greeted and a request that he be made safe. Allah, exalted is He, is the one from whom it is requested, not the one for whom it is requested. He is the one invoked, not the one for whom invocation is made. It is therefore impossible to greet Him with *salām*. Rather, He is the One who greets His servants, as He greeted them in His Book, saying: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers.﴾ And His saying: ﴿Peace be upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin.﴾ He said of Yahya: ﴿And peace be upon him.﴾ And He said to Noah: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you."﴾ And on the Day of Resurrection He will greet the people of Paradise, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they request. [They will have] peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful.﴾ Here *qawlan* (a word) is in the accusative as a cognate accusative (*maṣdar*), and its verb is what is implied by *salām*, which is a kind of speech, because *salām* is speech.

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light suddenly shines upon them from above. They raise their heads, and behold, the Majestic, whose majesty is great, has looked down upon them from above and said: 'O people of Paradise, peace be upon you.' Then he recited: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful.﴾ Then He withdraws from them, and His mercy and blessing remain upon them in their dwellings." Da'if (weak).

In Sunan Ibn Majah, it is related with a raised chain (*marfū'*): "The first one to be greeted with peace by the Truth on the Day of Resurrection is 'Umar." Da'if jiddan (very weak), and it contains a rejected element (*nakāra*).

Allah, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be peace.﴾ This is their greeting on the day they meet Him, blessed and exalted is He. It is impossible that this is a greeting from them to Him, for they know Him too well to greet Him, and they were forbidden from doing so in this world. Rather, this is a greeting from Him to them. The greeting here is attached to the object (*mudāf ilā al-maf'ūl*), so it is the greeting with which they are greeted, not the greeting with which they greet Him. Had it not been for His saying in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful, Merciful,﴾ it could have been possible that the greeting to them comes from the angels, as Allah said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, saying, "Peace be upon you."﴾ But this is the angels' greeting when they enter upon them in their dwellings in Paradise, entering with greetings of peace upon them.

As for the greeting mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be peace,﴾ it is a greeting to them at the time of meeting, just as a beloved greets his beloved upon meeting him. What then have those who are veiled from their Lord lost on that day?

*Yakfī alladhī ghāba 'anka ghaybatuhu* ∗∗∗ *fadhāka dhanbun 'iqābuhu fīhi*

It suffices that the one who has been absent from you is absent; that is a sin, and its punishment is within it.

The point is that Allah, exalted is He, requests *salām* from Him, so there is no impossibility regarding Him greeting His servants, and He is not requested to give it to Himself. Therefore He is not greeted. His saying, "Allah Himself is *al-Salām*," is explicit that *al-Salām* is one of His names. They said: when the Muslim says *salām 'alaykum*, its meaning is "the name *al-Salām* upon you."

Among their proofs is what Abu Dawud related from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "A man greeted the Prophet (ﷺ), but he did not return the greeting until he faced a wall and performed tayammum, and then returned it, saying: 'I disliked mentioning Allah except in a state of purity.'" Sahih. They said: this hadith shows that *salām* is a remembrance of Allah, and it is a remembrance only when it includes one of His names.

Among their proofs as well is that the People of the Book who are disbelievers do not initiate greetings of *salām*, so one does not say to them *salām 'alaykum*. It is known that there is no objection to saying to one of them *salamaka Allāh* (may Allah grant you safety). This is only because *salām* is a name of Allah, so it is not permissible to request for a disbeliever the blessing of that name upon him.

These arguments, as you see, are strong and evident.

The second opinion: *salām* is a masdar meaning *salāma* (safety), and it is the requested object invoked in the greeting. Among the proofs of the proponents of this view is that it is mentioned without the definite article (*alif lām*). The Muslim says *salām 'alaykum*. Had it been one of Allah's names, it would not have been used this way, but would have been stated in the definite form, as all His other beautiful names are stated, such as: ﴿Al-Salām, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-'Azīz, al-Jabbār, al-Mutakabbir.﴾ Indefiniteness does not direct the word to a specific referent, let alone direct it to Allah alone, unlike the definite form, which is directed to Him by specification when His beautiful names are mentioned.

Among their proofs also is that the conjunction of mercy and blessing with it in the expression *salām 'alaykum wa raḥmatullāhi wa barakātuh* shows that the intended meaning is a masdar. For this reason, two masdars similar to it were conjoined to it.

Among their proofs also is that if *salām* here were one of Allah's names, the statement could not be correct except by supplying an implied element that would restrict it, so that the meaning would be "the blessing of the name *al-Salām* upon you," for the name itself is not upon them. If you said "the name of Allah upon you," the meaning would be "the blessing of this name," and similar supplied elements. It is known that such an implied element contradicts the original form and has no evidence.

Among their proofs also is that the purpose of *salām* is not this meaning. Rather, its purpose is to announce safety, both as a report and as a supplication, as will be explained in the answer to the question following this one. For this reason *salām* is a protection, since it contains the meaning of safety, and the safety of both the greeter and the one who returns the greeting from one another.

They said: all of this shows that *salām* is a masdar meaning *salāma*, and its *tā'* was dropped because what is sought is the genus, not a single instance of it, and the *tā'* indicates specification, as has already been explained.

The decisive resolution of this question is this: the truth lies in both opinions together. Each of them contains part of the truth, and the correct view is in combining them. We clarify this by a principle that we have pointed out repeatedly: whoever calls upon Allah, exalted is He, by His beautiful names should ask for each desired object, and seek nearness to Him by the name that implies that object and is suited to its attainment, as though the supplicant is interceding with Him and seeking nearness to Him through it. So if he says: "My Lord, forgive me and turn to me, for You are the Ever-Returning, the Oft-Forgiving," he has asked Him for two things and sought nearness to Him through two of His names that imply the attainment of his request. Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'A'isha, when she asked him what she should supplicate with if she happened upon the Night of Decree: "Say: O Allah, You are the Pardoner, the Generous. You love pardon, so pardon me." Sahih. Likewise, when al-Siddiq asked him to teach him a supplication to make, he said: "O Allah, I have wronged myself greatly, and no one forgives sins but You, so forgive me with forgiveness from You, and have mercy upon me, for You are the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Such examples are very numerous, so we will not lengthen the discussion by citing their instances.

Once this is established, since the situation is one of seeking safety, which is the most important thing a person possesses, it was expressed with the form of one of Allah's names, *al-Salām*, from whom safety is sought. The word *salām* thus contains two meanings: first, the remembrance of Allah, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar; and second, the request for safety, which is the Muslim's aim. So *salām 'alaykum* includes one of Allah's names and the request for safety from Him. Reflect on this benefit.

A similar point is what has been reported from some of the early scholars, that he said regarding *āmīn* that it is one of Allah's names, blessed and exalted is He. Many people rejected this view, saying: "There is no *Āmīn* among His names," and they did not understand the meaning of his statement. He meant that this word includes His name, blessed and exalted is He, for its meaning is "answer and give what we have asked You." It thus contains His name while also indicating a request. This inclusion is more evident in *salām 'alaykum*, because *al-Salām* is one of His names, exalted is He. This explains the secret of the matter.

**(Section)**

Having understood this, the ruling regarding its use as a request at the time of meeting, rather than any other form of supplication, is as follows. The customary practice among people is that they greet one another upon meeting. Each group has its own greetings and expressions that they have agreed upon. In the pre-Islamic period, the Arabs used to say to each other in their greetings: *an'ama ṣabāḥan* (may you have a pleasant morning) and *an'amū ṣabāḥan* (may you all have a pleasant morning). They used the word *an'amū*, from *ni'ma* (with a fatha on the nun), meaning a pleasant life and wellbeing, and they joined it with *ṣabāḥan*, because morning is the beginning of the day. If blessing is attained in it, its effect remains and continues throughout the day. So they specified it to the beginning of the day, signaling that it be hastened and not delayed until the day has risen high. Likewise they said *an'amū masā'an* (may you have a pleasant evening), for time consists of morning and evening. Morning is the beginning of the day until about midday, and evening is from after midday until night. For this reason people say *ṣabbaḥaka Allāhu bi-khayr* (may Allah greet you with good in the morning) and *massāka Allāhu bi-khayr* (may Allah greet you with good in the evening). This is the meaning of *an'ama ṣabāḥan* and *masā'an*, except that it contains mention of Allah. The Persians used to say in their greeting *hazā rasāla mīmāyī*, meaning "may you live a thousand years." Every nation has a greeting of this kind or similar to it. They also had greetings reserved for their kings, with particular postures when entering upon them, such as prostration and similar things, and special expressions that distinguished the greeting of the king from the greeting of the common people. All of these were intended to express life, its blessings, and its permanence. For this reason it was called *taḥiyya*, which is of the form *taf'ila* from *ḥayāh* (life), like *takrima* from *karāma* (honor), but the two similar letters were assimilated, so it became *taḥiyya*. Then the King, the Holy, the Giver of Peace, blessed and exalted is He, legislated for the people of Islam a greeting among themselves: *salām 'alaykum*. It was more worthy than all the greetings of the nations, some of which were impossible and false, such as their saying "may you live a thousand years," and some of which were limited in meaning, such as *an'ama ṣabāḥan*, and some of which belong only to Allah, such as prostration. The greeting with *salām* was therefore more deserving than all of these, because it includes the safety without which there is no life and no success. It is thus the foremost foundation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 13, verses 23–24 (part 3 of 10):

over everything. The servant's goal in life is achieved through two things: being safe from every evil, and attaining all good. Safety from evil takes precedence over attaining good, and it is the foundation. For this reason a person, indeed every animal, is concerned first with its safety and then with its gain. Moreover, absolute safety includes the attainment of good, for if a person loses good, destruction and ruin, or deficiency and weakness, befall him. Thus the loss of good prevents the attainment of absolute safety. Safety therefore includes deliverance from every evil and success in attaining good. It combines the two foundations without which life is not complete. It is derived from His name al-Salam (the Peace) and includes it. The ta' (feminine marker) has been dropped from it for the reason we mentioned, which is that it denotes the genus and not a single instance of safety. Since Paradise is the abode of safety from every defect, evil and affliction, and indeed is free from everything that disturbs living and life, its inhabitants' greeting there is "salam" (peace), and their Lord greets them there with peace: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home."﴾ This is the secret of greeting with "salam" upon meeting.

As for greeting in writing: since each of the two correspondents is absent from the other, and the letter is his messenger to him, the letter takes the place of his speech to him. So in writing to him he uses the same salam he would use if he were addressing him, since the letter stands in the place of the address.

(Section)

As for the fifth question, which concerns the construction of this meaning with ʿalā ("upon"), its answer requires a preliminary point: what is the meaning of your saying "sallamtu" (I greeted)? Once its meaning is known, it becomes clear that the particle ʿalā is the most suitable for it. Know that the expressions "sallamtu ʿalayhi," "ṣallaytu ʿalayhi," and "laʿantu fulānan" are formulas whose content is performative sentences (jumal ṭalabiyyah), not individual meanings. The content of your saying "sallamtu" is that you said "as-salāmu ʿalayka." The content of "ṣallaytu ʿalayhi" is that you said "Allāhumma ṣalli ʿalayhi," or "I supplicated for him." The content of "laʿantuhu" is that you said "Allāhumma ulʿanhu" (O God, curse him). Similar to this is "sabbaḥtu Allāh," whose content is that you said "subḥāna Allāh." Similar to this too, though derived from the formula itself, are: "hallaltu" when one says "lā ilāha illā Allāh"; "ḥamdaltu" when one says "al-ḥamdu lillāh"; "ḥawqaltu" when one says "lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh"; "ḥayʿaltu" when one says "ḥayya ʿalā al-ṣalāh"; and "basmaltu" when one says "bismillāh." He said:

Layla has said "bismillāh" the morning I met her,
how sweet is that beloved who says "bismillāh."

Once this is established, your saying "sallamtu ʿalayhi" means that you uttered this formula to him and placed it upon him, signalling that its meaning encompasses him, just as a garment encompasses its wearer. The particle ʿalā was the most fitting particle for this, so reflect on it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he was of the companions of the right hand, then [there is] peace for you from the companions of the right hand﴾, this is not a greeting of salutation. Had it been a greeting, it would have said "fa-salāmun ʿalayhi," as in ﴿Peace upon Abraham﴾ and ﴿Peace upon Noah﴾. Rather, the verse includes mention of the ranks and categories of people at the minor resurrection, upon arrival before God. It mentions three categories: the one brought near, for whom there is rest, provision and the Garden of Bliss; the companion of the right hand, who is among the moderate, for whom there is safety; and the wrongdoer who denies and goes astray, for whom there is a welcome of boiling water and the burning of Hell. It promised the companion of the right hand safety, and promised the one brought near gain and success, though each of them is safe and a gainer. Since the context was not one of greeting but of reporting his state, it mentioned what he would obtain of safety.

If it is said: this is a sound distinction, but what is the meaning of the lām in His saying "lak" (for you), who is the addressee of this address, and what is the meaning of the particle min in ﴿from the companions of the right hand﴾? These are three questions about the verse.

It is said: With God's praise, we have fulfilled the purpose by mentioning the difference between this salam in the verse and the salam of greeting, which was the aim. These questions, although connected to the verse, lie outside our purpose. Nevertheless, we answer them to complete the benefit, by God's power and might. Although we have not seen any of the exegetes satisfy the thirst in this place, or reveal the reality of the meaning and wording, some of them say the meaning is "it is granted to you that you are of the companions of the right hand," while others say other things that hover around its meaning without reaching it. Know, then, that whatever is invoked of good or evil is annexed to its possessor by the lām of annexation, which indicates that it befalls him. Among this is His saying: ﴿Those—for them is the curse﴾. He did not say "ʿalayhim al-laʿnah," signalling that its meaning occurs and is established for them. Likewise His saying: ﴿And woe to you because of what you describe﴾. In its opposite, one says "lak al-raḥmah" (for you is mercy), "lak al-taḥiyyah" (for you is greeting), and "lak al-salām" (for you is peace). Among this is this verse, ﴿fa-salāmun laka﴾, meaning that safety is established for you and has come to you. On this basis the address is to everyone of this kind, so it is an address to the genus: "so safety for you, O one who is of the companions of the right hand," just as you say "hanīʾan laka" to one who is among them. For this reason, and God knows best, He brought the particle min in ﴿min aṣḥāb al-yamīn﴾, and the prepositional phrase stands in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that is, "safety for you, being from the companions of the right hand," just as you say "hanīʾan laka min ittibāʿ Rasūl Allāh (ﷺ) wa ḥizbihi," meaning "being among them." A prepositional phrase following a definite noun is put in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, just as you say "uḥibbuka min ahl al-dīn wa al-ʿilm," meaning "being among them." This is the meaning of this verse. Although the books of the exegetes are devoid of it, some of them hovered around it, and what was transmitted did not disclose its meaning or clarify it, so review what they said. And God is the Granter of success, the Bestower of His bounty.

(Section)

As for the sixth question: what is the wisdom in beginning here with an indefinite noun (nakirah), although the rule is to place the predicate before it? This question contains two questions. The first: what is the wisdom of beginning with an indefinite noun in this place? The second: since it has been begun with, why not place the predicate (khabar) before the subject (mubtadaʾ), since that is the analogy of the chapter, as in "fī al-dār rajul" (in the house there is a man)?

The answer to the first question: the grammarians said that when the indefinite noun carries the sense of supplication, as in "salāmun laka" and "waylun lahu," it is permissible to begin with it, because supplication is one of the meanings of speech, and so the indefinite is specified by a kind of specification and may therefore be begun with. This statement has no real substance beneath it. The predicate is also a kind of speech, yet the predicative sense does not permit beginning with an indefinite. How, then, could the supplicatory sense permit it? As for the claim that the supplication is a type, the predicate a type, and the request a type, does that not specify the referent of the indefinite so that it may be predicated? What prevents predicating of it is its commonness and vagueness, which keep it from being fixed in the hearer's mind until he gains the predicative attribution to it. There is no difference in this between the speech being supplication or predication. As for the saying of those who claim that beginning with an indefinite is forbidden only where it does not yield benefit, such as "rajul fī al-dunyā" (a man in the world) and "rajul māta" (a man died), and the like, so that when it yields benefit it is permissible to begin with it without any restriction by rule or limit: a better course than restricting it by whether the speech is supplication, or in the sense of another speech, or by the other rules mentioned, is the method of the imam of grammar Sībawayh. In his book he did not make a rule for beginning with it, nor did he limit it by number. Rather, he made benefit the criterion of validity. This is the truth, which does not stand up to examination except as he stated. Everyone who burdens himself with a rule will find expressions outside it that come back at him. Either he strains to return them to that rule, or he singles them out with other rules. The matter reached some grammarians to the point that they made thirty rules in this chapter, and others perhaps added to them. All this is a needless burden. You are relieved of the trouble of "sharru aḥharu dhā nāb" (the worst is what provokes the one with fangs) and its chapter, by a comprehensive principle regarding beginning [with an indefinite].

If you say: what rule do you have if you follow their path in this? I say: listen now to a comprehensive principle in this chapter from which almost nothing deviates. The subject (mubtadaʾ) is originally to be definite, or specified by some kind of specification through which the benefit of the predication is obtained. If all modes of specification are absent from it, then one does not predicate of it, except where the predicate is a prepositional phrase that yields a definite meaning and is placed before it, under these four conditions. Because when it comes first and is definite, it is as if the discourse is about it, and as if the delayed subject were its predicate. An example: when you say "ʿalā Zayd dayn" (upon Zayd is a debt), you find this sentence in effect equal to your saying "Zayd is in debt" (mudayyan or mudin). The focal point of benefit is the debt, and it is what is gained from the predication. So do not get stuck in the restrictions of word-order. You say "ʿalā Zayd jār wa majrūr" (upon Zayd is a prepositional phrase), so how can it be the subject? You see that it is in fact the thing spoken about. The aim is not predication about the debt, but about Zayd, that he is in debt. If your mind is dull to this, review the conditions of the subject and the conditions of the predicate. If the predicate is not beneficial, the matter yields nothing, and there is no difference between fronting and delaying the predicate. When you say "fī al-dunyā rajul," it is in lack of benefit like your saying "rajul fī al-dunyā." Here benefit is not prevented by fronting or delaying, but by the predicate's failure to be beneficial. Similar to this is your saying "fī al-dār imraʾah" (in the house there is a woman), which is a beneficial utterance, because it is like your saying "al-dār fīhā imraʾah" (the house has in it a woman). You predicated of the house, in wording and meaning, the presence of a woman in it. For you did not intend predication about the woman that she is in the house. Had you intended that, you would have first made the referent of the subject concrete, and then predicated to it. Rather, your aim is predication about the house, that it is occupied by a woman and contains a woman. This degree is what made predicating about the indefinite here sound, for it is not really a predicate. In reality it is a predicate about the preceding definite. This is the real meaning of the statement. As for its grammatical parsing (iʿrāb), the prepositional phrase is the fronted predicate, and the indefinite is the subject, raised by the beginning. It is a condition for beginning with an indefinite that it be qualified.

If you say: then from where does the prohibition on fronting this subject in wording come, so that one does not say "imraʾah fī al-dār" and "dayn ʿalā Zayd"? I say: because the indefinite strongly demands a qualifier, so the mind runs ahead to suppose that the prepositional phrase is a qualifier of it and not a predicate about it. It is not its custom to be predicated about except after a qualifier. So the mind remains eager for the predicate which is to arrive upon it. It has already reached the hearing, but there is no certainty that it is the predicate; it may be a qualifier, so no benefit results, and the hearer remains in the pain of waiting and anticipation for the predicate. So when you front the prepositional phrase before it, it becomes impossible for it to be a qualifier, because a qualifier does not precede what it qualifies. His thought goes to the fronted prepositional phrase being the predicate and the discourse being about the indefinite, which is the focal point of benefit.

Once you know this, among the specifications that permit beginning with an indefinite are: that it be qualified, as in ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾; or general, as in "mā aḥadun khayrun min Rasūl Allāh (ﷺ)" (no one is better than the Messenger of God (ﷺ)) and "hal aḥadun ʿindaka?" (is there anyone with you?). Among these is that it occurs within a comparative context, as in ʿUmar's saying: "tamratun khayrun min jarādah" (a date is better than a locust). Comparison is a kind of specification by generality, since the intent is not one unspecified unit of this genus. Rather, the intent is that this genus is better than that genus. He brought the ta' (which indicates unity) to signal that this preference holds for each individual of the genus. Among these is Sībawayh's interpretation of His saying: ﴿Obedience and fair speech﴾. He estimated it as "obedience is better, and fair speech is more fitting for you, and this is best." Some people said that what permits beginning with it here is its being coordinated upon, because the coordinated-upon element is qualified and so may be begun with. Sībawayh's view is better, because qualifying the conjoined does not require qualifying what it is conjoined to. Had you said "ṭāʿatun amthal" (a better obedience), it would be permissible even without coordination. Among these also is an indefinite occurring within a context of detailed explanation after a summary. For example, when you say: "divide these garments among these people: a garment for Zayd, a garment for ʿAmr, and a garment for Bakr," the indefinite here is specified and determined, and its indefiniteness and commonness within the genus of garments disappears. Rather, it is specified by those particular garments, as if you said "a garment of them for Zayd, and a garment of them for ʿAmr." This is restriction and specification. Among these also is beginning with an indefinite when the speech is not a pure statement but carries the sense of praise and commendation, as in their saying: "ʿamat fī al-ḥajr lā fīk" (ʿamat, a plant, is in the stone, not in you). They did not say "ʿamat fī al-ḥajr" and stop, until they joined to it "lā fīk." So the meaning of the speech became that the attribution of ʿamat to the stone is closer than its attribution to you, and ʿamat is more suited to the stone than to you. For they intended to commend the addressee and to negate fault from him, and they did not intend a predication about ʿamat that it is in the stone. Rather it is in the sense of negation from the stone and from the addressee together, though its negation from the addressee is more emphatic. When the speech takes on the sense of negation, there is no wonder in beginning with an indefinite, because of the generality and benefit it carries.

Among these is their saying "sharru aḥharu dhā nāb" (the worst thing provoking the fanged one). It has two estimations. The first is that it is in the manner of a qualifier: a great evil, or a frightening evil, provokes him. The second is that it is in the sense of another speech: "what provokes the fanged one is only evil," or "only evil provokes him." There is no doubt about the soundness of the matter in the manner of the subject. Likewise, when it is in the manner of subject and predicate with its implied meaning. Among these is their saying "sharru mā jāʾa bihi" (the worst of what he brought), because the meaning of the speech is "what he brought is only evil." Here the superfluous (zāʾidah) "mā" delivers the meaning of two things: negation and affirmation. It delivers them as it does in your saying "innamā jāʾa bihi sharr" (he brought only evil), and in His saying: ﴿So they believe only a little﴾, meaning "they believe only a little"; and ﴿little do they remember﴾; and His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them﴾, meaning "We cursed them only for their breaking of their covenant"; and similarly His saying: ﴿It is by mercy from God that you were lenient with them﴾, meaning "you were lenient with them only by mercy from God." Do not listen to the saying of some grammarians that "mā" is superfluous in these places, for that comes from lack of reflection.

If it is said: from where did "mā" here get these two meanings, negation and affirmation? If it were on its literal sense, pure negation, it would yield only one meaning, negation. If negation is not explicit in it, how can it yield two meanings?

It is said: We did not claim that it yields negation and affirmation by itself. Rather, that came from it together with the contextual indicators associated with it in the speech. As for their saying "sharru mā jāʾa bihi": since it combined with the indefinite noun, and an indefinite is not begun with, when they intended to front it, it became known that the benefit of the predicate is restricted to it. This restriction was reinforced by "mā," so the predication was negated from anything other than this subject, and it was not except for it, until the addressee understands from it what he understands from "mā jāʾa bihi illā sharr." Here they dispensed with "mā" as a negative particle by means of beginning with an indefinite, and with "illā" by means of the beginning with the indefinite. As for your saying "innamā Zayd qāʾim" (only Zayd is standing): "anna" was combined with it and merged into it, and the two became one word. "Anna" gives the affirmation that "illā" gives, and "mā" gives the negation that "illā" gives. That is why one may say "innamā yaqūmu anā" (only I stand), but "anā" cannot be its agent except when separated from the verb by "illā." You say "mā yaqūmu illā anā" (only I stand), and you do not say "yaqūmu anā." So when you say "innamā qāma anā," it is as if you had pronounced "mā" with "illā." He said:

I defend the honour of my people, and only defends their honour I or someone like me.

So when you know that its superfluity together with "anna," and its connection to it, required this negation and affirmation, transfer this meaning to its connection with the prepositional particle, in His saying: ﴿It is by mercy from God﴾ and ﴿For their breaking of their covenant﴾.

Consider how you find the difference between this construction and saying "fa-biraḥmatin min Allāh" and "fa-binaqḍihim mīthāqahum." From the composition of the verse you understand: "you were lenient with them only by a mercy from God," and "We cursed them only for their breaking of their covenant." Likewise His saying: ﴿So little do they believe﴾ indicated negation by its wording and affirmation by the fronting of an element which should be delayed, namely the object (maʿmūl), together with the connection of "mā" to it along with the fronting, as established in their saying "sharru mā jāʾa bihi."

We have expounded this in our book al-Fatḥ al-Makkī (The Meccan Conquest), and explained there that there is no superfluous letter in the Qur'an. We discussed everything mentioned concerning that and showed that every word has a fresh benefit, additional to the basic structure. The pen has run on to this point, though it was not our aim, for it is more important than some of what we are concerned with and about.

Let us return to the purpose and say: what validated beginning with the indefinite in "salāmun ʿalaykum" is that the one greeting is a supplicant, and the indefinite subject is the thing sought by the supplication. So it becomes the intended and cared-for object, and it stands in the place of your saying "ask God for peace upon you" and "seek from God peace upon you." So the salam is the very thing you seek and intend. Do you not see that if you said "ask God upon you for peace," it would not be permissible? This is its strength and meaning, so reflect on it.

It is most wondrous.

Then if it is strong enough in its own right, why was it not put in the accusative like *saqyan* and *ra'yan*, since it carries the sense of *saqaaka Allahu saqyan wa ra'aaka Allahu ra'yan* ("may God give you drink, and may God shepherd you")? I answer that the answer to this will come in the answer to the tenth question, on the difference between Abraham's greeting and the greeting of his guest, God willing. Moreover, what makes it good to begin with an indefinite noun here is that it has the status of a qualified noun, because when the Muslim says *salamun 'alaykum*, what he means is "a peace from me upon you," as God says: ﴿Descend with peace from Us﴾. Do you not see that the Muslim's purpose in greeting the one he greets is to inform him that the greeting and the peace come from himself, because in this there is the attainment of the purpose of greeting: affection, friendship and compassion? So you have understood the answer to both questions: why it begins with an indefinite noun, and why it is placed before the predicate, unlike the usual pattern in such cases. God knows best.

(Section)

As for the seventh question, which is: why in the case of the one greeting is the greeting placed first, while in the case of the one replying the one greeted is placed first?

The answer to it: in this there are several benefits. The first: the distinction between the reply and the initiation. For if he said to him in the reply *as-salamu 'alaykum* or *salamun 'alaykum*, it would not be known whether this is a reply to his greeting or the initiation of a greeting from him. But when he says *'alayka as-salam*, it is known that he has returned his greeting. What the one greeting seeks from the one greeted is that he return his greeting; his aim is not that he should begin with a greeting as he himself began. For this reason, and God knows best, the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the one greeted, who said *'alayka as-salam*, to do so, saying: "Do not say *'alayka as-salam*, for *'alayka as-salam* is the greeting of the dead." (Authentic. The discussion of this hadith and its meaning will come in its proper place.) Do you not see how the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade him to begin the greeting with the wording of the reply, which is only used after a greeting has been given? And there is nothing in his saying "for it is the greeting of the dead" that indicates that what is prescribed for the greetings of the dead is the same, as we will mention. Since they relied on the distinction between the greeting of the initiator and the greeting of the one replying, they singled out the initiator with placing the greeting first, because it is the purpose, and singled out the replier with placing the prepositional phrase first.

The second benefit: the greeting of the replier follows the manner of an answer, and for this reason a single word indicating its counterpart suffices in it. So if he said *wa 'alayka* ("and upon you"), it would include the reply, as is prescribed in replying to the People of the Book. Yet we are commanded to return to whoever greets us a greeting like his greeting, and this is a kind of justice that is obligatory for everyone. This shows that the replier's *wa 'alayka* is equivalent to the initiator's *salamun 'alaykum*. But for the Muslim, it is preferred to repeat the first wording exactly, to achieve equivalence and to prevent the suspicion that the one greeted has not returned his greeting, given the possibility that he means something else by "upon you." As for the People of the Book: since they distort the greeting, do not act justly in it, and sometimes give a correct greeting that is not distorted, while the matter becomes confused for the replier, he was directed to a single word that includes a reply corresponding to what they said, and a complete sentence was not prescribed for him, because it would either contain distortion like what they said, and it is not fitting for a Muslim to distort the greeting, which is the greeting of the people of peace, especially since it is a mention of God, as has passed, because of the unbeliever's distortion of it; or he would return a correct greeting that is not distorted while the Muslim is distorting the greeting, and so he does not deserve a correct reply. Therefore turning to the singular word, which is *'alayka*, was the requirement of justice and wisdom, together with its safety from distorting the mention of God. So reflect on this remarkable benefit. The point is that for the reply it is sufficient for you to say *wa 'alayka*, and it was only completed as a perfecting of justice and a cutting off of suspicion.

The third benefit, which is stronger than what has preceded: since the Muslim's greeting includes the supplication of peace for the one greeted, that peace should fall upon him and settle upon him, and since the reply includes a request that there should settle upon him of that peace the same as what he prayed for, when he says *wa 'alayka as-salam*, its meaning is "and upon you of that the same as what you asked for me." This is like when he says *ghafara Allahu ta'ala laka* ("may God forgive you"), and you reply *wa laka yaghfiru* (and may He forgive you too). This is better than your saying *wa ghafara laka*. Likewise if he says *rahmatu Allahi 'alayka* you say *wa 'alayka*, and if he says *'afaa Allahu 'anka* you say *wa 'anka*, and similar cases. For the purpose is to share with the one supplicated for in that supplication for the one who supplicates, not to create a supplication like the one he made. It is as if he said: "and for you too, and upon you too," meaning "you share with me in that, and are equal to me in it, not that I am alone in it apart from you, nor that I am singled out for it over you." There is no doubt that this meaning requires placing first the sharer who is equal. So reflect on it.

(Section)

As for the eighth question, which is: what is the wisdom in beginning the greeting with an indefinite wording and answering it with a definite wording? For you say *salamun 'alaykum*, and the replier says *wa 'alayka as-salam*?

This is a question that includes two issues. The first is this one; the second is: the specificity of the indefinite in beginning a letter, and of the definite at its end.

The answer to them is by mentioning a principle that prepares the ground, to which the positions of definiteness and indefiniteness in the greeting return, which is that the greeting is a supplication and a request, and people, in words of supplication and request, only use the indefinite, either in the nominative on the basis of the subject, or in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*). Of the first kind: *waylun lahu* ("woe to him"). Of the second: *khaybatan lahu*, *jadma'an*, *'aqran*, *tarban*, *jandalan* (curses meaning "may he be ruined," "may he be cut off," "may he be struck down," "may he be destroyed"). This is for supplication against someone. For supplication in his favor there are *saqyan*, *ra'yan*, *karaamatan* and *masarratan*. So *salamun 'alaykum* came in the indefinite, as the other words of supplication came. The secret of this is that these expressions take the place of speaking the verb. Do you not see that *saqyan* and *ra'yan* and *khaybatan* take the place of *saqaaka Allahu* and *ra'aaka*? Likewise *salamun 'alayka* takes the place of *salamaka Allahu*, and the verb is indefinite. So they preferred to make the expression which takes its place, and is like a substitute for it, indefinite like it.

As for the definiteness of the greeting on the part of the replier, we will also mention a principle by which its secret and wisdom are known, which is that when the article *al-* enters the noun *salam*, it carries four benefits:

The first: an indication of the mention of God the Exalted, because the definite *as-salam* is one of His names, as has been established above.

The second benefit: its indication of seeking for the one greeted the meaning of safety from Him, because when you mention one of His names you have approached Him by it and used it as a means to attain the meaning from which that name is derived.

The third benefit: the article *al-* carries in some places the meaning of generality in what it is attached to, and inclusiveness.

The fourth benefit: it stands in the place of pointing to a specific thing, as you say: "Hand me the book," "give me the water," "give me the garment," referring to what is present before you; you dispense with saying "this" by it, so it conveys the meaning of pointing.

When you know these four benefits, the replier's *wa 'alayka as-salam* with the definite article includes an indication that his intention in the reply is the same greeting with which he was greeted, the very same. It is as if he said: "that peace which you asked for me is returned to you and falls upon you." If he had given the reply indefinitely, there would be no indication of this, because the definite, even if its mention is repeated and its wording is the same, is one thing, unlike the indefinite. Whoever understands this understands the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Hardship will never overcome two ease(s)." (It is a *mursal* report, and it has supporting chains that strengthen it.) For he was alluding to God's saying: ﴿So indeed with hardship is ease. Indeed, with hardship is ease﴾. So *'usr* (hardship), though repeated twice, is repeated in the definite form, so it is one; and *yusr* (ease) is repeated in the indefinite form, so there are two eases. Thus hardship is enclosed between two eases: an ease before it and an ease after it, so hardship will never overcome two eases.

A second benefit: the positions of returning the greeting are three: a position of excellence, a position of justice, and a position of wrong. Excellence is to return to him something better than his greeting; justice is to return to him its equivalent; and wrong is to withhold his right and diminish it. So the replier was given the more complete of the two wordings, which is the one defined by the article that is frequently used for totality and generality, so that he may be able to reach the position of excellence.

A third benefit: it has been established that the appropriate thing for the one greeted, in regard to the greeting, is to place him first. So if it were indefinite and he said *'alayka salam*, it would be like your saying "upon you is a debt," or "in the house is a man." It would be expressed as a pure statement, and once it becomes a statement, the meaning of greeting is lost, because its meaning is supplication and request. Whoever says *'alayka salam* is not one who greets; the one who greets is the one who says *salamun 'alayka*. So the replier's peace was defined with the article *al-*, as an indication of supplication for the addressee, and that he is returning the greeting to him, seeking for him safety through the name *as-Salam*. God knows best.

(Section)

As for the second issue, which is the beginning of the greeting in writing with the indefinite and its conclusion with the definite: its beginning with the indefinite is the same as its beginning in the spoken greeting, as has been mentioned, since writing takes the place of speech. As for its definiteness at the end of the letter, it has three benefits:

The first: the initial greeting has already established intimacy between them, and it announces that the greeting is a special one from him to him. So it is as if he said: "a peace from me upon you," as has been mentioned. This is also one of the benefits of making the initial greeting indefinite, to announce that it is a particular greeting from the one greeting. Once this is settled and known at the beginning of the letter, it is better that he greet him with a greeting more general than the first, so that it does not remain a pure repetition. Rather he brings a wording that combines his greeting and the greeting of others, so he has combined for him two greetings: the particular one from him, and the general one from him and from others. For this benefit they considered it good that the writer's phrase "so-and-so sends you greetings" (*wa fulan yuqri'uka as-salam*) and "so-and-so" should come after "and peace upon you" at the end of the letter, for this purpose.

The second benefit: it has been established that the definite *as-Salam* is one of God's names, and the writer began his letter with the mention of God, so it is appropriate that he end it with one of His names, which is *as-Salam*, so that His name is at the beginning and at the end of the letter. This is a remarkable benefit.

The third benefit, which is very remarkable, and is the answer to the ninth question that follows this one: the entry of the conjunctive *wa* in the writer's phrase *wa as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatu Allah* has two possible explanations. One is the view of Ibn Qutayba: that it is coordinated with the *salam* that was begun with, as if he said: "and the greeting mentioned before, upon you."

The second view: that it is for coordinating the sections of the letter with one another, so that the sentence of greeting is coordinated with the sentences before it, as *wa* enters among the sections of a letter. This is better than Ibn Qutayba's view, for several reasons:

Among them: the speech between the two greetings has been long, so coordinating its end after its long span with its beginning is ugly and not understood from the context.

The second reason: if he interprets it in that way, the second greeting would be exactly the first, so it would add no new benefit. This involves stinginess with a renewed greeting, and a failure to serve the aims of the correspondents, who enumerate sentences and sections, each sentence requiring a benefit different from the earlier benefit. So that the reader of the letter, whenever he reads a sentence containing a benefit other than the earlier one, his heart's longings reach out to acquire what comes after it; but if one benefit is repeated for him twice, his soul grows weary of it. So the fitting thing for this aim is that he should renew for him a greeting other than the first, which gladdens him as the first gladdened him, namely the general and comprehensive greeting. When the writer has finished the sections of his letter and concluded them, he brings the conjunctive *wa* with the definite greeting, and says: *wa as-salamu 'alaykum*, meaning: "and after all this, peace upon you." It has been established that when the greeting is built on a preceding prepositional phrase, and it is a greeting of reply and not of initiation, it is made definite, as in *wa 'alayka as-salam*. But since the writer's greeting here is not a greeting of reply, he placed the greeting before the prepositional phrase and said *wa as-salamu 'alaykum*, and brought the article *al-* to indicate the renewal of another greeting. God the Exalted knows best. This is a strange eloquence and an inherited wisdom from the predecessors of the community, and from the Companions in their letters, and thus they used to write to their Prophet (ﷺ), may God's blessings and peace be upon him. And we have finished the answer to the ninth question, which concerns the conjunctive *wa*.

(Section)

As for the tenth question, which is: what is the secret in the accusative of *salaman* in the greeting of the angels to Abraham's guests, and the nominative in Abraham's greeting?

The answer: you have known the view of the grammarians on it, that the angels' *salaman* implies a verbal sentence, because the accusative of the greeting indicates "we greeted you with a greeting" (*salamna 'alayka salaman*), while Abraham's *salamun* implies a nominal sentence, because its nominative indicates that the meaning is *salamun 'alaykum* ("peace upon you"). A nominal sentence indicates stability and fixedness, while a verbal sentence indicates occurrence and renewal. So his greeting to them was more complete than their greeting to him, and he had from the positions of the reply what befits his station, which is the position of excellence, since he greeted them with something better than their greeting. This is an account of what they said.

But in my view there is an answer better than this one: he did not intend to report the angels' greeting. So *salaman* in the accusative is the object of a simple verb of speech, as if it were said: "they said a saying, 'Peace,'" and "they said a word of rectitude and correctness," and similar. For the verb of saying is only used to report sentences; a single word is not reported by it, but is rather governed by it as the object. From this is God's saying: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. It does not mean that they uttered this single word in the accusative; rather its meaning is that they said a saying, *salaman*, like *sidadan* and *sawaban*. The saying was called "peace" because it expresses the meaning of greeting and includes what it contains of dispelling loneliness and achieving friendliness.

And he (Abraham) related the wording of their greeting and gave it in its own wording, in the nominative as a subject, reported by the verb of saying. Had he not intended reporting, he would have said *salaman* in the accusative, because when what follows the verb of saying is in the nominative, reporting is the only option. So from the difference between the two statements, in the reporting of Abraham's greeting and its nominative form, and the accusative form of that, there arises a very subtle indication, which is that his saying *salamun 'alaykum* is from the religion of Islam received from the leader of the Hanifs and father of the prophets, and that it is from the creed of Abraham, which God commanded us to follow and to adhere to. So He related to us his saying so that we might follow his example and adhere to him; He did not relate the saying of his guests, but reported it only in general, not in detail. God knows best. Weigh this answer and the one before it on a fair scale, and the stronger of the two will become clear to you. And success is from God.

(Section)

As for the eleventh question, which is: the accusative of *salaman* in God's saying ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, and its nominative in His saying, reporting from the believers among the People of the Book: ﴿"Peace be upon you; we do not seek out the ignorant"﴾?

Ibn al-Qayyim's answer to this is that Allah, glorified is He, praised His servants whom He mentioned in these verses by their finest qualities and deeds, and said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. Here "salaman" (peace) is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, so the meaning is "a saying of peace." Then comes the following. Allah conceals His servant's sin, while Satan strives to expose it and disgrace him. The servant is then deceived and says, "This is a sin that no one has seen but Allah," and he does not realise that his enemy is working to spread it and disgrace him. Few people perceive this subtle point. Among Satan's evils is that when the servant sleeps, he ties three knots on the back of his head, and strikes each knot, saying: "For you is a long night, so sleep." If the servant wakes and remembers Allah, one knot is undone; if he performs ablution, another is undone; if he prays, all the knots are undone, and he becomes energetic and content in the morning. Otherwise he becomes evil-spirited and lazy in the morning. This is related by al-Bukhari (Sahih al-Bukhari) and Muslim (Sahih Muslim), from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Satan ties three knots on the back of the head of one of you when he sleeps..." (as above).

Among his evils is that he urinates into the ear of the servant until he sleeps until morning. This is confirmed from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a man was mentioned in his presence who slept through the night until morning, and he said: "That is a man into whose ears Satan urinated," or he said: "in his ears." Related by al-Bukhari.

Among his evils is that he sits in wait for the son of Adam on all the paths of goodness. There is no path of goodness except that Satan lies in ambush on it, trying with all his effort to prevent him from taking it. If he disobeys him and takes it, Satan hinders him, obstructs him, and confuses him with objections and obstacles. If he completes his deed and finishes it, Satan prepares for him what will nullify its effect and turn him back on his heels.

It is enough of his evil that he swore by Allah that he would indeed sit in wait for the children of Adam on His straight path, and swore that he would come to them from before them, behind them, from their right and from their left. His evil has reached the point that he devised plots and exerted every effort to deceive until he expelled Adam from the Garden. Still that did not satisfy him, until he demanded from Adam's descendants a portion of the Fire, one out of every thousand, and nine hundred and ninety-nine. Still that did not satisfy him, until he worked to nullify the call to Allah on earth, and intended that the worship be for himself and that he be worshipped instead of Allah. He strives with his utmost effort to extinguish the light of Allah, nullify His call, establish the call to disbelief and polytheism, and erase tawhid (monotheism) and its signs from the earth.

It is enough of his evil that he confronted Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful, until his people threw him into the fire by catapult. Allah turned back his plot against him and made the fire cool and safe for His friend. He also confronted the Messiah (ﷺ) until the Jews intended to kill and crucify him, but Allah repelled their plot, protected the Messiah, and raised him to Himself. He also confronted Zakariyya and Yahya, [and the text continues with the verse] ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾. This is a description of a group of believers among the People of the Book who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Makkah and believed in him. The polytheists then reproached them and said: "Wretched is the delegation your people sent to you to learn the news of this man. You have abandoned your religion, followed him, and turned away from your people's religion." So Allah informed about them that they addressed them with a speech of disengagement, avoidance, and gracious abandonment, and they said: ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant﴾.

The raising of "salam" (peace) was necessary because it recounts what had actually occurred, whereas the accusative "salaman" in the verse of al-Furqan was necessary because it is instruction and guidance toward what is most perfect and most fitting for the believer to adopt when the ignorant address him. So reflect on these secrets; the least of them is worth a journey. And Allah, alone, is praised for what He bestowed and granted.

Such are the gifts from the Lord of the servants,
so do not say "if," "would that," or "so," for these are of no use.

(Section)

As for the twelfth question: what is the wisdom in Allah's sending peace upon His prophets and messengers, when peace is a request and a supplication, so how can it be conceived from Allah?

This is a question of great importance that deserves attention and should not be neglected, and few grasp its secret except one whom Allah has granted special understanding and care. This is not the concern of the people of this age, whose best scholars in transmission can only relay sayings and debates, and whose best in research can only propose possibilities and raise difficulties.

As for the genuine verification of knowledge as it should be:

For wars there are people who stand to them,
and for the registers there is a writer and an account.

We should have restrained ourselves, held back the reins of the pen, entered their arena, and addressed them in what they are accustomed to, and not unveiled the brides of meanings before the blind, nor unveiled their faces before the impotent. But this is a commodity and merchandise that has its own sheen; it is a bride that has its suitor, and it will reach its people and be given to its husband. Let the sermon not be prolonged, for it is the sigh of one in anguish. So let us return to the subject and say:
