Then the secret of greeting the Prophet (ﷺ): when he had brought this praise of the Lord, he turned to the status of the Messenger through whom this good came. So he greeted him with the most complete greeting, defined with the *alif-lam* of comprehensiveness, joined with mercy and blessing. This is the most authentic thing said in greeting him. So do not be stingy with the *alif-lam* in this station. Then he moved to greeting himself and the righteous servants of God, beginning with himself, since it is most important, and a person begins with himself, then with those he supports. Then he concluded this station with the bond of Islam, which is the testimony of truth, the first and last of matters, and in it is all praise. Then he moved to another kind, supplication and request. So the *tashahhud* combines both kinds of supplication: supplication of praise and goodness, and supplication of request and asking. The first is nobler of the two, because it is the right of the Lord and His attribute, and the second is the portion and benefit of the servant. In a report: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." (Weak).

But since prayer is the most complete of acts of worship in servitude and the most perfect, both kinds are prescribed in it, and the first of them is put first for its excellence. Then he moved to the second kind, supplication and request, beginning with what is most important, most sublime, and most beneficial to him, namely asking God for prayer upon His Messenger (ﷺ). This is one of the most excellent supplications of the servant and the most beneficial for him in this world and the Hereafter, as we have mentioned in the book *Ta'zim Sha'n al-Salat 'ala al-Nabi*. In it also is that the supplicant makes it a prelude before his need and his request for himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this meaning in his saying: "Then let him choose from supplication what pleases him most." Likewise in the hadith of Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd: "When one of you supplicates, let him begin with praising God and extolling Him, then let him pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then let him supplicate." So reflect on how the *tashahhud*, from beginning to end, corresponds to this and is arranged in the finest order. The hadith of Fadalah is what uncovered and clarified this meaning for us. So may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, through whom He completed our religion, perfected His favor upon us by his message, made him a mercy to the worlds, and a sorrow to the disbelievers.

(Section)

As for the twenty-sixth question: what is the wisdom in the greeting being in the second-person address while the prayer is in the third-person form? Its answer is apparent from what preceded. Prayer upon him is a request and supplication from God that He pray upon him, so in it only the third-person form is possible, since one does not say "O God, pray upon You." As for greeting him, it came in the form of present address, treating him as one who is face to face, for a very wondrous wisdom: when he (ﷺ) was dearer to the believer than his own self between his two sides, and more fitting for him and nearer, and his mental reality and ideal image existed in his heart such that nothing is absent from it except his person, as the poet said:

"Your likeness is before my eyes, your mention is on my tongue,
And your abode is in my heart, so where could you be absent?"

One who is in this state is truly present, and whoever else, even if present to the eye, is absent from the heart. So addressing him in direct address and presence, greeting him, was more fitting than greeting in absence, treating him as one face to face and visible, because of his nearness to the heart and his indwelling in all its parts, such that no part of the heart is left except that his love and mention are in it, as it is said:

"If my heart were split open, you would see your mention in its midst."

The declaration of *There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God* is in a single line. Do not be surprised at the beloved's domination over the heart of the lover and his overpowering of it, to the extent that it is as though he sees him. This is why you find them, in addressing their beloved, relying on direct address and witnessing, along with the utmost physical distance, because of the perfection of spiritual nearness. Bodily distance did not prevent them from conversing with spirits and addressing them. Whoever is coarse in temperament is far removed from all this. Love may reach some of its people such that they see their beloved, in nearness to them, as nearer to them than their own soul, than which nothing is nearer. As it is said:

"O you who remain in my heart through all time, and distant from my sight and my vision,
You are my soul, even if you are not seen; it is nearer to me than any near thing."

And another said:

"O you who dwell between my ribs and my inner heart,
Though far away, your abode is near to me."

Love refines its matter so much that the lover sees it as nearer and closer to him than his own soul. Here are verses that touch on this:

"It is nearer to the passionate lover than his own self, though it is absent from his eye,
And whoever has love like this, how could he be one who forgets?"

Then it refines its affair and subdues its authority, until the lover is absent with his beloved from himself, feeling nothing but his beloved and not feeling himself. From this arose the Sufi *shathahat* (ecstatic utterances), whose source is the strength of the inspired state and weakness of discernment. Its author judges by the state over knowledge, makes the judgment rest with it, and removes his knowledge from the matter. The preserved ones judge by knowledge over the authority of the state. They know that any state over which knowledge does not rule should not be relied upon or trusted, except as one relies on the defeated and subdued in what overtakes him that he cannot repel. This is the condition of the perfected among the people, who combined the light of knowledge with states of practice. The storms of their states did not extinguish the light of their knowledge, and their knowledge did not hold them back from ascending to the stations of faith and excellence beyond it. These are the judges over both groups. As for others, they are either veiled by a knowledge that has no authority over them, or deceived by a state with no knowledge of its soundness from its corruption. And God, exalted is He, is asked for His bounty; He is near and responsive.

So the perfected person is the one who makes knowledge rule over the state, acting in his state by his knowledge, and makes knowledge the light by which he distinguishes the sound from the corrupt, not the one who disparages knowledge by the state and makes the state a standard and scale over it. What agrees with his state from knowledge he accepts, and what contradicts it he rejects and negates. This is the root of error in this domain. Rather, the obligation is to make knowledge the judge and to return to its ruling. On this basis all the gnostic shaykhs of the path enjoined, and urged most strongly toward knowledge, because of their awareness of the dangers and ruin in the bare state divorced from it: ﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

(Section)

As for the twenty-seventh question: what is the wisdom in the praise of God in the *tashahhud* coming in the third-person form, though He, glory be to Him, is the one addressed, whom the servant confides in, while the greeting upon the Prophet (ﷺ) comes in the second-person form, though he is absent?

Its answer: praise of God generally comes attached to His beautiful names in their apparent form, not with a pronoun, unless the apparent name has been mentioned earlier, and then the pronoun follows it. Such is the worshipper's saying: ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone we worship﴾, and his saying in bowing, "Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty," and in prostration, "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

This is part of Ibn al-Qayyim's discussion of the secret in the divine names and the choice of the names used in praise and supplication. Within it, the sayings of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the verses of the Qur'an are quoted as the author cites them.

The secret in this is that praise is attached to His Most Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna) because their meanings include the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty. So He is named by the apparent noun that signifies the meaning by which and for which He is praised, exalted be He. The pronoun carries no indication of this. For this reason, when praise must be addressed to Him directly, the apparent noun is used together with the plural suffix *mim* (the sign of the plural), which signifies all the names and attributes. An example is his saying when he raised his head from bowing (ruku'): "O Allah, our Lord, to You belongs the praise" (*Allahumma Rabbana laka al-hamd*). Sometimes he confines himself to mentioning the Lord, exalted be He, because the word itself indicates this meaning. So reflect upon it, for its line of thought is very subtle. Consider also how the supplication that includes both praise and request is opened with the word "Allahumma" (O Allah), as in the Master of Forgiveness (*sayyid al-istighfar*): "O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me, and I am Your servant..." (the hadith).

Narrated by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i.

The bare supplication (du'a' mujarrad) is introduced with the word "Lord" (Rabb), as in the words of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, and the words of Adam: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾, and the words of Moses: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, and the words of Noah: ﴿My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say between the two prostrations: "Lord, forgive me, Lord, forgive me" (sahih). The secret of this is that God is asked by His lordship, which includes His power, His beneficence, His nurturing of His servant and the rectification of his affairs, and He is praised by His divinity (uluhiyyah), which includes the affirmation of what is due to Him of the exalted attributes and the most beautiful names. Reflect upon the method of the Qur'an and you will find it as I have mentioned to you. As for supplication, we have mentioned examples of it; wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, it almost never comes except introduced by the name "Lord." As for praise, wherever it occurs, it is introduced by the Most Beautiful Names, and the most important with which it is introduced is the name of Allah, majestic is His majesty, as in ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ wherever it comes, and ﴿So glory be to Allah﴾, and ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might﴾, and similar to it ﴿Glorify Allah, whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ wherever it occurs, and ﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, and their likes.

In the supplication of the Messiah there came: ﴿O Allah, our Lord, send down upon us a table from the heaven﴾, so he mentioned both matters, and nothing else like it is found in the Qur'an. I have not seen anyone address this or draw attention to it. It is a wondrous secret that indicates the Messiah's perfect knowledge of his Lord and his glorification of Him. This request came after his people had said to him: ﴿Is your Lord able to send down upon us a table from the heaven?﴾. So Allah caused them to fear and informed them that this is something that it is not fitting to ask about, and that faith rejects it. When they persisted in the demand, and the Messiah feared that doubt would enter them if they were not granted what they asked, he began his request with the word ﴿Allahumma﴾ (O Allah), which signifies praise of Allah by all His names and attributes. Within that is the representation of himself as one who praises, extols, and remembers the names of his Lord, and who glorifies Him by them. The purpose of this supplication and the fulfilment of this need is that the Lord be praised with that, glorified by it, that His favours be mentioned, and that the signs of His power and lordship be made manifest, and that it be a proof of the truthfulness of His messenger. Thereby there is achieved an increase in faith and in praise of Allah, an affair that makes the request fitting and serves as an excuse for it. So he used the two names: the name Allah, by which He is praised, and the name Lord, by which He is called upon and asked, because the situation was one that required both.

So reflect upon this wondrous secret, and do not let your understanding slip past it, for it is of the understanding that Allah gives to whom He wills in His Book. And to Him belongs all praise.

As for greeting the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of direct address, we have mentioned its secret in the aspect before this, so its context is near.

(Section)

As for the twenty-eighth question: it includes two questions. The first: what is the secret in the greeting (*salam*) being at the end of the prayer? The second: why was it definite (*ma'rifah*)?

The answer: as for concluding the prayer with it, Allah has made for every act of worship a means of exiting from it (*tahlil*). Thus exiting from the pilgrimage (*hajj*) is by stoning and what follows it, and likewise exiting from fasting is by breaking the fast after sunset. So He made the greeting the exit from the prayer, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Its entry is the takbir and its exit is the taslim" (sahih). Its entry (*tahrim*) here is its gate by which one enters into it, and its exit (*tahlil*) is its gate by which one leaves it. So He made the takbir the gate of entry and the taslim the gate of exit, for a wondrous and far-reaching wisdom that is understood by one who comprehends from Allah, and who obliges himself to contemplate the excellences of this great religion, whose thought travels far in extracting its rulings, secrets and marvels, and who is removed from the world of habit and familiarity. He is not content with mere forms until he knows the spirits that are sustained by them. For Allah does not legislate anything in vain, nor devoid of profound wisdom; rather, within the folds of what He has legislated and commanded there are wisdoms and secrets that dazzle the intellects, by which the observer is guided to what lies behind them, so the heart prostrates in submission and acceptance.

We say, and with Allah is success: since the worshipper has withdrawn from distractions, cut off all attachments, purified himself, taken his adornment, and prepared himself to enter upon Allah, exalted be He, and to converse with Him, it was prescribed for him to enter upon Him as servants enter upon kings, entering with glorification and reverence. So He prescribed for him the most eloquent expression that signifies this meaning, which is the saying "Allahu Akbar" (Allah is greatest). For in this utterance there is glorification, specification, and an absoluteness in the omitted object governed by *min* that is not found in any other. For this reason the correct view is that no other expression can take its place, convey its meaning, or validly establish the prayer except with it, as is the position of the people of Madina and the people of hadith (*ahl al-hadith*). So this utterance, and the apprehension of its meaning, is the gate of the prayer through which the servant enters upon his Lord. When he feels in his heart that Allah is greater than anything that may occur to the mind, he will be ashamed to occupy his heart in prayer with anything else. Otherwise he would not fulfil the meaning of "Allah is greatest," nor render the due of this utterance, and he would not have come to the House by its door; rather, the door would be shut against him. This is by the consensus of the early generations (*salaf*): the servant has from his prayer only what he understands of it and what is present in his heart.

How excellent is what Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi said in some of his admonitions: "Presence of heart is the first station of the prayer. When you have alighted at it, you pass on to the desert of meaning. When you depart from it, you kneel at the gate of intimate conversation (*munajah*). The first hospitality for the guest is wakefulness and the unveiling of the veil from the eye of the heart. How can one who has not gone out into the desert hope to enter Mecca? You have sent your heart into every valley, so the prayer may surprise you while your heart is not with you. Then you send the messenger after it, but he does not find it, and you enter into prayer without a heart."

The point is that it is ugly for the servant to say with his tongue "Allah is greatest" while his heart is filled with other than Allah. He takes it as the direction of his heart in prayer, and perhaps he is not present before his Lord in any part of it. Had he fulfilled the due of "Allah is greatest" and come to the House by its door, he would have entered and departed with kinds of gifts and blessings. This is the gate through which the worshipper enters, which is the *tahrim*. As for the gate through which he exits, it is the gate of the greeting (*salam*), which contains one of the Most Beautiful Names. So he opens his prayer with the name of the Blessed and Exalted, and closes it with His name. Thus he mentions the name of his Lord at the beginning and at the end of the prayer: its beginning is with His name, and its end is with His name. He entered into it with His name and departed from it with His name, together with what the name *al-Salam* (The Source of Peace) has of distinctive property and wisdom suited to the worshipper's departure from before Allah, exalted be He. For as long as the worshipper is in his prayer before his Lord, he is within His sanctuary, which no one can violate; indeed he is within a sanctuary protected from all calamities and evils. When he departs from before Him, blessed and exalted be He, calamities, afflictions and trials rush upon him from every side, and Satan comes to him with his snares and his troops. So he is exposed to kinds of afflictions and trials. But when he departs from before Allah accompanied by the greeting, a guardian from Allah does not cease to protect him until the time of the next prayer. And it is part of the completion of the blessing upon him that his departure from before his Lord be with a peace that he carries with him, that remains for him and stays with him.

So reflect upon this secret, for even if there were nothing else in this connection, it would be sufficient. How much more so, when it contains secrets and benefits not found among the people of this age. Praise for this belongs to Allah alone. Just as the One who bestows the blessing is Allah alone, so the One praised for it is Allah alone.

By this, the answer to the second question has also become known: the greeting comes here in definite form so that it signifies His name *al-Salam*.

Let this be the end of the discussion on the matter of "Peace be upon you" (*salamun 'alaykum*).

Had it not been for the intention of brevity, it would have come out as a huge volume. We have not touched in it upon the derivative issues of the greeting and its rulings that are recorded in the books, for they are full of them; whoever wants them should take them from there. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

(Section)

Know that Allah the Glorified's withholding from His believing, loving servant is a gift, and His trial of him is well-being.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "His withholding is a gift."

That is because He does not withhold out of stinginess or lack. Rather, He considers what is good for His believing servant and withholds from him by His choice and good judgment.

This is as he said. He does not decree for His believing servant any decree except that it is good for him, whether that decree displeases him or pleases him. So His decree of withholding for His believing servant is a gift, even if it appears as withholding. It is a blessing, even if it appears as an affliction. His trial is well-being, even if it appears as a calamity. But because of the servant's ignorance and wrongdoing, he counts as gifts, blessings, and well-being only what gives him pleasure in the immediate term and suits his nature. Had he been granted an abundant share of knowledge, he would count withholding a blessing and trial a mercy. He would take more pleasure in trial than in well-being, and more pleasure in poverty than in wealth, and in a state of scarcity he would be more thankful than in a state of abundance.

This was the state of the early pious predecessors (al-salaf).

So the wise and content person is one who counts trial as well-being, withholding as a blessing, and poverty as wealth.

Allah revealed to one of His prophets: "When you see poverty approaching, say: 'Welcome, the emblem of the righteous.' And when you see wealth approaching, say: 'A sin whose punishment has been hastened.'"

The content person is the one who counts Allah's blessings upon him in what he dislikes as greater and more numerous than His blessings upon him in what he loves. As one of the knowers ('arifin) said: "O son of Adam, Allah's blessing upon you in what you dislike is greater than His blessing upon you in what you love." And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216].

One of the knowers also said: "Be content with Allah in all that He does to you."

For He withholds from you only to give to you, tests you only to grant you well-being, makes you ill only to heal you, and causes you to die only to give you life.

So beware of departing from contentment with Him for the blink of an eye, lest you fall from His sight.

(Section)

Mutarrif ibn Abd Allah, or someone else, said: "The pleasures of this world in their entirety, compared to the pleasures of the Hereafter, are less than a speck compared to the mountains of this world."

Whoever fixes the eye of his insight upon this world and the Hereafter will know that the matter is so.

How, then, is it fitting for one of sound intellect and knowledge to be cut off by a hope in this worthless portion from a pleasure that does not cease or vanish? Still less should he be cut off from seeking Him, whose pleasure in knowing Him, loving Him, intimacy with Him, and joy in His nearness, compared to this lasting pleasure, is like the comparison of worldly pleasures to the pleasures of Paradise. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of Eden. And approval from Allah is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

So a little of His approval, which cannot be called little, is greater than the gardens and all that is in them.

In the hadith of the vision: "By Allah, Allah has not given them anything more beloved to them than looking at His Face." And in another hadith: "When they see Him, the Glorified, they will not turn to anything of the bliss they are in, until He is hidden from them."

So whoever is cut off from this by a hope has achieved deprivation, has been content for himself with the ultimate loss. And Allah is the One whose help is sought, upon Him is reliance, and what Allah wills comes to be.

His saying "and no wish hinders him": the wish (umniyyah) is what the servant desires of pleasures, and its plural is amani.

The difference between it and hope (amal) is that hope relates to what is expected to exist, whereas wish may relate to what is not expected to be attained, as the incapable person wishes for lofty ranks.

False wishes are the capital of the bankrupt. With them they pass their times and take pleasure in them, like the pleasure of one whose mind is removed by an intoxicant, or by false imaginings.

In the raised (marfu') hadith: "The clever one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death. And the incapable one is he who follows his soul's desires and wishes for things from Allah."

Only those of base and fallen souls are content with wishes instead of realities, as it has been said:

"Leave aside the wishes of the soul; do not think they satisfy it. Indeed, wishes are the capital of the bankrupt."

A man's wish indicates the height or lowness of his aspiration. In a divine report (athar ilahi): "I do not look at the words of the wise person, but I look at his aspiration." The common people say: "The worth of every person is what he does well." The knowers say: "The worth of every person is what he seeks."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 13, verse 28 (part 1 of 3)**

*Tuma'nina* (tranquility): the heart's settling upon a thing, and its freedom from agitation and anxiety.

From this is the well-known report: "Truthfulness is tuma'nina, and lying is riba," meaning that truthfulness brings the listener's heart to rest in it, and he finds calm in it, whereas lying causes agitation and doubt. From this too is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Righteousness is that which the heart is at rest with," meaning that it settles upon it, and its agitation and anxiety depart from it.

Regarding "the remembrance of Allah" (*dhikr Allah*) here, there are two opinions.

The first: it is the servant's remembrance of his Lord, for his heart is at rest with it and calm in it. When the heart is agitated and anxious, it has nothing to be at rest with except the remembrance of Allah.

Then the proponents of this view differed concerning it. Some said: this refers to oaths. When a believer swears an oath about something, the hearts of the believers come to rest in it and are reassured. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Others said: rather, it is the servant's remembrance of his Lord between himself and Him, by which his heart is calmed and at rest.

The second opinion: the remembrance of Allah here is the Qur'an, which is His remembrance that He sent down to His Messenger, and through which the hearts of the believers find tranquility. Indeed, the heart is not at rest except through faith and certainty, and there is no way to attain faith and certainty except through the Qur'an.

The calm and tranquility of the heart come from its certainty, and its agitation and anxiety come from its doubt. The Qur'an is what produces certainty and repels doubts, suspicions, and illusions. Therefore the hearts of the believers find rest only in it. This second opinion is the one preferred.

The same two opinions apply to the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion﴾ [43:36].

The sound view is that it is His remembrance that He sent down to His Messenger, which is His Book. Whoever turns away from it, Allah appoints for him a devil who misguides him and bars him from the path, while he thinks he is upon guidance.

The same two opinions apply to the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [20:124].

The sound view is that it is His remembrance that He sent down to His Messenger, which is His Book. For this reason, the one who turns away from it will say: ﴿My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was [once] seeing?﴾ He will say: ﴿Thus came to you Our verses, but you forgot them; and similarly, this Day, you are forgotten﴾ [20:125–126].

As for the interpretation of those who understood it as referring to oaths, it is extremely far from the intended meaning. The remembrance of Allah through oaths is uttered on the tongue of the truthful and the liar, the righteous and the wicked. The believers' hearts come to rest in the truthful person even if he does not swear, and their hearts do not come to rest in one they doubt even if he swears.

Allah placed tranquility in the hearts and souls of the believers, and He made envy (*ghibta*, admiration), praise, and the glad tidings of entering Paradise belong to the people of tranquility. So good tidings to them, and a good final return.

**(Benefit)**

The Exalted informed that the hearts of the believers are at rest through His remembrance, which is His Book by which He guided His servants. He said, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back [to Him]" (27). Those who believed, and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured" (28)﴾.

He, glorified be He, answered their request, which was to stop sending down signs of their suggestion, with two answers:

The first: such signs do not necessarily produce faith. Rather, it is Allah who guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, not the signs you have proposed.

The second: He drew their attention to the greatest of signs and the most powerful in necessitating faith, and that in necessitating faith it is more eloquent than the signs you propose. It is His Book, which is His remembrance, and what it contains of the truth in which hearts find rest and souls are calmed. Had it been falsehood, it would have increased the hearts only in doubt and suspicion, for lying is suspicion and truthfulness is tranquility. So if its words and expressions did not convey certainty through their meanings, hearts would not be at rest with it, for tranquility is the heart's calm toward a thing and its trust in it, and this does not occur except with certainty; indeed, it is certainty itself.

**(Section)**

Tranquility in Allah, glorified be He, is a reality that descends from Him upon the heart of His servant, gathering him unto Him and returning his wandering heart to Him, until it is as if he sits before Him; he hears by Him, sees by Him, moves by Him, and grasps by Him. That tranquility flows into his soul, heart, joints, and outward and inward powers, drawing his spirit to Allah, and his skin, heart, and joints become soft in His service and in drawing near to Him. True tranquility cannot be attained except through Allah and His remembrance, which is His speech that He sent down to His Messenger, as the Exalted said: ﴿Those who believed, and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured﴾.

The tranquility of the heart is its settling and stability, with the removal of anxiety and disturbance from it. This is not attainable by anything other than Allah, the Exalted, and His remembrance, absolutely. As for anything besides Him, tranquility in it is delusion, and trust in it is weakness. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has decreed an irrevocable decree that whoever finds tranquility in anything other than Him, anxiety, agitation, and turmoil will come to him from that very thing, whoever he may be. Indeed, if he finds tranquility in other than Him, He will target him with arrows of trial, so that His servants and His friends may know that the one who attaches himself to other than Him is cut off, and the one who finds tranquility in other than Him is barred and prevented from his interests and aims.

The true tranquility by which the soul becomes at rest is that you find tranquility, in the matter of knowing His names, attributes, and the descriptions of His perfection, in His report about Himself, and in what His messengers have reported about Him, so that you receive it with acceptance, submission, surrender, expansion of the chest toward it, and joy of heart in it.

For it is one of the means of knowing the Lord, glorified be He, that He makes known to His servant through the tongue of His Messenger. The heart will not cease to be in the greatest anxiety and agitation in this matter until faith in the names, attributes, and unity of the Lord, and His being exalted above His Throne, mixes with it, and His speech through revelation becomes the cheerfulness of its heart. It descends upon it like pure water upon a heart burning with thirst, and so it finds tranquility in it, is calmed by it, rejoices in it, and its heart and joints soften before it, until it is as if he witnessed the matter just as the messengers reported it. Indeed, that becomes for his heart like seeing the sun at midday, clear; so if all people from the east and west of the earth were to oppose him in this, he would not turn to their opposition.

He also said: When one feels estranged in his strangeness, the Greatest Companion (Abu Bakr) was at rest through faith alone, while all the people of the earth opposed him, and that did not diminish his tranquility in the slightest.

This is the first degree of tranquility. Then it continues to strengthen whenever one hears a verse containing an attribute of one's Lord. This matter has no end. This tranquility is the foundation of the foundations of faith upon which faith is built. Then one finds tranquility in His report about what follows death, the matters of the barzakh (intermediate realm), and what comes after that of the conditions of the Resurrection, until it is as if one witnesses all of that with one's own eyes. This is the reality of certainty (*yaqin*) by which the Exalted described the people of faith, when He said: ﴿And of the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [2:4]. Faith in the Hereafter is not achieved until the heart finds tranquility in what Allah, glorified be He, has reported about it, a tranquility toward matters about which one has no doubt and no suspicion.

This is the one who truly believes in the Last Day, as in the hadith of Harithah: "You have become a believer." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, for every truth there is a reality. So what is the reality of your faith?" He said: "I have turned my soul away from this world and its people, and it is as if I see the Throne of my Lord manifest, and the people of Paradise visiting one another therein, and the people of the Fire being tormented therein." He said: "You are a servant whose heart Allah has illuminated."

**[Section: Tranquility]**

Tranquility in the attributes of the Lord, the Exalted, and His attributes is of two kinds: tranquility in faith in them, affirming them, and believing in them; and tranquility in what they require and direct of the effects of worship (*ma'budiyya*).

An example: tranquility in qadar (divine decree), affirming it, and believing in it, requires tranquility in the places of decrees that the servant has not been commanded to repel and has no power to repel. So he submits to them, is content with them, and does not become angry, complain, or become agitated, and his faith is not disturbed. He does not despair over what has escaped him, nor rejoice over what has come to him, because the calamity was decreed in it before it reached him and before it was created, as the Exalted said: ﴿No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being. Indeed, that is easy for Allah. So that you will not despair over what has eluded you, nor exult over what He has given you﴾ [57:22–23].

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿No disaster strikes except by permission of Allah. And whoever believes in Allah – He will guide his heart﴾ [64:11].

Several of the early Muslims said: it is the servant who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, so he is content and submits. This is tranquility in the rulings of the attributes, their requirements, and their effects in the world. It is a degree beyond tranquility through mere knowledge of them and belief in them. Likewise all the other attributes and their effects and objects, such as hearing, sight, knowledge, contentment, anger, and love; this is tranquility of faith.

As for the tranquility of excellence (*ihsan*), it is tranquility in His command, through obedience, sincerity, and sincere counsel. One does not proceed toward His command with personal will, desire, or blind imitation. One does not dwell with a doubt that opposes His report, nor a desire that opposes His command. Rather, when such thoughts pass through him, he regards them as whisperings, and falling from the sky to the earth is more beloved to him than finding them. This, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, is the clear faith. The sign of this tranquility is that one finds calm, after the anxiety and agitation of sin, in the stillness of repentance, its sweetness, and its joy. This is made easy for him by knowing that pleasure, sweetness, and joy lie in attaining repentance. This is a matter known only to one who has tasted both states and whose heart has experienced their effects. Repentance is a tranquility that stands opposite the agitation and anxiety found in sin. If the sinner searched his heart, he would find it filled with fears, agitation, anxiety, and turmoil. What veils him from witnessing this is the intoxication of heedlessness and desire, for every desire has an intoxication greater than the intoxication of wine, and likewise anger has an intoxication greater than the intoxication of drink.

For this reason, you see the lover and the angry person do what the drinker of wine would not do.

Likewise, one passes from the anxiety of heedlessness and aversion to the calm of turning toward Allah, the sweetness of His remembrance, and the spirit's attachment to His love and knowledge. There is never tranquility for the spirit without this, ever. If the soul were just to itself, it would see that when it lacks this, it is in the utmost anxiety, agitation, and turmoil. But intoxication veils it, and when the covering is lifted, the reality of what it was in becomes clear to it.

Here is a subtle secret that must be pointed out, and the guidance to it and success in it are in the hand of Him in whose hand are the reins of success. It is that Allah, glorified be He, has given each limb of the human being a perfection, and if that perfection is not realized for it, it is in anxiety, agitation, and turmoil because of the loss of its perfection, which He made as an example. The perfection of the eye is sight, the perfection of the ear is hearing, and the perfection of the tongue is speech. When these limbs lose the powers by which they are perfected, pain and deficiency occur in proportion to the loss of that. He made the perfection of the heart, its bliss, joy, pleasure, and delight to lie in knowing Him, glorified be He, in His will and love, in turning to Him in repentance, in turning toward Him, in longing for Him, and in intimacy with Him.

When the heart lacks that, it becomes more severely tormented and agitated than the eye that has lost the light of sight, or the tongue that has lost the power of speech and taste. It has no way to tranquility in any manner, even if it obtains the world and its means.

Among the knowledge is that it is not attained except by Allah being alone His beloved, His god, His worshipped one, and the ultimate object of its seeking, and that He alone is its helper in attaining that. The reality of the matter is that there is no tranquility for it without realizing ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [1:5], and the statements of the commentators on tranquility come back to this.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "al-Mutma'inna" (the tranquil soul) is the one who affirms the truth. Qatada said: it is the believer whose soul is at rest with what Allah has promised. Al-Hasan said: the one who affirms what Allah, the Exalted, has said.

Mujahid said: it is the soul that has become certain that Allah is its Lord, submitting to a matter concerning what He will do with it. Mansur narrated from him, saying: the soul that became certain that He is its Lord, and that stood firm (*dhamma jash*) for His command and obedience. Ibn Najih narrated from him: the tranquil soul that is humble (*mukhbita*) toward Allah.

He also said: it is the one that became certain of meeting Allah. So the statements of the early Muslims regarding the tranquil soul revolve around these two foundations: tranquility of will and tranquility of action.

When one finds tranquility from doubt to certainty, from ignorance to knowledge, from heedlessness to remembrance, from betrayal to repentance, from showing off to sincerity, from lying to truthfulness, from weakness to intelligence, from the arrogance of self-admiration to the humility of submission, from wandering to humility, and from slackness to action, then he has truly touched the spirit of tranquility. The root of all this and its origin is wakefulness (*yaqza*), and it is the first key to goodness. The heedless one, who is unprepared for meeting his Lord and does not provision himself for his return, is like a sleeper, indeed in a worse state than him.

The sensible person knows the promise and warning of Allah, and what the commands, prohibitions, and rulings of the Lord, the Exalted, require of rights. But what veils him from the reality of perception and prevents him from correcting himself is the sleep of the heart, which is its heedlessness, in which it slept and its sleep lengthened, and it grew stagnant and settled toward the impulses of desires, so its settling and stagnation intensified. It immersed itself in the depths of desires, habits took hold over it, and it mixed with people of idleness, and it was content to imitate people who waste their time. So in its sleep it is with the sleepers, and in its intoxication with the intoxicated. Whenever the sleep of this heedlessness is lifted from his heart by a jolt from the admonishments of the Truth in his heart, it responds to the preacher of Allah in the heart of His believing servant, or to a resolve stirred upon it by the plow of reflection in the receptive place. So it strikes with the plow of its reflection and gives a takbir (proclamation of "Allahu akbar") by which the palaces of Paradise are illuminated for it, and it says:

*O soul, woe to you, help me, by your effort in the darkness of nights.*
*Perhaps on the Day of Resurrection you will succeed in the good life in those lofty heights.*

That reflection stirred up a light, by whose glow he saw what he was created for, what he will meet before his Lord from the moment of death until entry into the abode of permanence. He saw the swift passing of the world, and knew its treachery toward its children, its killing of its lovers, and the various punishments it inflicts upon them. So he rose in that light, on the leg of his determination, saying: "Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning Allah's side" (39:56). He then faced the remainder of his life, which has no value, seeking to make up what had passed, reviving with it what had died, facing the stumbles that had preceded him, seizing the opportunity of possibility which, if lost, would cause him to lose all goods.

Then, in the light of that wakefulness, he observes the blessings of his Lord upon him from the moment he settled in the womb until now, as he moves in them outwardly and inwardly, by night and day, in wakefulness and in sleep, secretly and openly. If he were to strive to count their kinds, he would not be able. It suffices that the least of them is the blessing of the self, and for Allah upon him, every day, are twenty-four thousand blessings. So what do you think of the others?

Then he sees, in the light of that illumination, that he is hopeless of enumerating and counting them, incapable of fulfilling their rights. And that if the Benefactor were to demand from him their rights, all of his deeds would be consumed by the right of a single blessing among them. Then he becomes certain that he has no hope of salvation except through the pardon, mercy, and grace of Allah.

Then he sees, in the light of that wakefulness, that even if he were to perform the deeds of both humans and jinn, of righteousness, he would belittle them in comparison to the magnificence of the Lord, the Exalted, and what He deserves by the majesty of His Face and the greatness of His authority.

That is if his deeds were from himself. How much more so when they are purely the grace, favor, and kindness of Allah, in that He facilitated them for him, helped him in them, prepared him for them, willed them from him, and brought them into being. Had He not done that, he would have had no path to them. Then he does not see his deeds as coming from himself, and that Allah, glorified be He, will never accept a deed that its doer sees as from himself, until he sees the very grace of Allah's success and favor upon him and His bounty, and that it is from Allah and not from himself, and that he has nothing from himself except evil and its causes. Whatever blessing he has is from Allah alone, a charity He bestowed upon him and a favor He brought to him without his deserving it by any cause or meriting it by any means. Thus he sees his Lord, his Protector, and his Worshipped One as worthy of every good, and sees himself as worthy of every evil. This is the foundation of all righteous deeds, outward and inward, and it is what raises them and places them in the register of the companions of the right hand.

Then, in the light of that wakefulness, there flashes upon him another flash, by whose glow he sees the defects of his self, the afflictions of his deeds, the transgressions and wrongdoings that preceded him, the violation of sacred things, and his shortcomings regarding many rights and obligations. When this is combined with witnessing the blessings of Allah upon him and His favors, he sees that the right of the one who has bestowed favor upon him, in his blessings and commands, has left him no single good deed by which he could raise his head. Thus his heart finds tranquility, his self is humbled, his limbs are submissive, and he proceeds toward Allah with his head bowed, between witnessing His blessings and contemplating his transgressions and the defects of his self and the afflictions of his deeds, saying: "I acknowledge Your blessing upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins except You." Thus he sees no good in himself and does not regard himself as worthy of any good, and this necessitates two great matters for him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 13, verse 28 (part 2 of 3):

One of them: considering abundant what Allah has bestowed upon him.
The second: considering little the obedience he has performed, whatever it may be. Then another flash shines upon him, in whose light he sees his honour and nobility, and that it is the capital of his happiness. So he is stingy with it, not wishing to waste it on what does not bring him closer to his Lord, for in wasting it lies loss, regret and remorse, while in guarding and cultivating it lies profit and happiness. So he is miserly with his breaths, not wishing to spend them on what will not benefit him on the Day of his return.

Then, in the light of that flash, he observes what his waking state requires of him, after the sleep of heedlessness: repentance, self-reckoning, watchfulness, and jealousy for his Lord, that he should not prefer another over Him, nor over his share of His good pleasure, nearness and honour, by selling them for a paltry price in a house of swift decline, nor by enslaving his soul to a beloved.
Or he reflects upon the ultimate end of His beauty, and sees its outcome with the eye of insight, so that he is not jealous of His love.

All of this is among the effects and requirements of wakefulness, and it is the first of the stations of the soul at peace (al-nafs al-mutma'innah), from which its journey to Allah and the Hereafter arises.

[Section: The Kinds of Hearts]

Indeed, the servant becomes strong enough to be present in prayer and occupied therein with his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, only when he subdues his desire and his passion. Otherwise, a heart that has been overpowered by desire and captured by passion, in which Satan has found a seat he has firmly established, how can it be freed from whisperings and thoughts?

The hearts are of three kinds:
A heart empty of faith and of all good: this is a dark heart, in which Satan has been relieved of casting whisperings into it, because he has taken it as a house and a homeland, and governs it as he wills, and has established himself in it to the utmost degree of establishment.

The second heart: a heart that has been illumined by the light of faith, and in which its lamp has been kindled, but upon which lie the darkness of desires and the storms of passions. For Satan there is advance and retreat, incursions and greed. So the war is one of alternating victories and defeats.
The conditions of this category vary in frequency and abundance: among them are those whose times of overcoming their enemy are more numerous, and among them are those whose times of their enemy overcoming them are more numerous.
And among them are those who are at one time and at another.

(The third heart) a heart filled with faith, illumined by the light of faith, from which the veils of desires have been lifted and those darknesses have dispersed. So its light in its breast shines, and upon that shining is a kindling: if the whisperer approaches it, he is burned by it. It is like the sky which was guarded with stars, so that if Satan approaches it, he is struck by a meteor and burned.

The sky is not greater in sanctity than the believer, and Allah's guarding of him is more complete than the guarding of the sky. The sky is the place of worship of the angels and the abode of revelation, and in it are the lights of acts of obedience; and the heart of the believer is the abode of monotheism, love, knowledge and faith, and in it are their lights. So he is worthy to be guarded and protected from the plotting of the enemy, so that he obtains nothing from it except that it is snatched away.

This has been illustrated with a fine example: three houses. A house belonging to the king, in which are his treasures, his stores and his jewels.
A house belonging to the servant, in which are the servant's treasures and stores, but not the king's jewels and stores.
And an empty house, bare, with nothing in it.

A thief came to steal from one of these houses. From which of them will he steal? If you say, from the empty house, that is impossible, because an empty house contains nothing to be stolen. For this reason it was said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The Jews claim that they do not have whisperings in their prayer." He said: "What does Satan do with a ruined heart?" And if you say he steals from the king's house, that is like the impossible and the unattainable, for upon it are guards and watchmen, and what the thief cannot approach. How could he, when its guard is the king himself? How can the thief approach it when around it are the guards and soldiers that surround it? So there remains for the thief only the third house, and it is the one upon which he launches his raids.

Let the discerning one reflect upon this example with true reflection, and apply it to the hearts, for they are upon its pattern.
So a heart emptied of all good, which is the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite: that is the house of Satan, which he has secured for himself, taken up residence in, and made a dwelling and a home. What then is there to steal from it, when in it are his treasures, his stores, his doubts, his imaginings and his whisperings?

And a heart filled with the majesty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with His greatness, His love, His watchfulness over it and modesty before Him: what Satan would dare to approach this heart? And if he wishes to steal something from it, what would he steal? At most he may win, at times, a snatching and a plundering, obtained upon a moment of unawareness from the servant and a heedlessness that is unavoidable, since he is human, and the rules of humanity apply to him: heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction and the dominance of nature.

It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "In some of the divine books: I do not dwell in houses, nor do they contain Me. And what can contain Me, when the heavens are a mere cushion within the Kursi?" "Rather, I am in the heart of the humble one who abandons everything other than Me." This is the meaning of the other report: "My heavens and My earth do not contain Me, but the heart of My believing servant contains Me."

And a heart in which is the monotheism of Allah, His knowledge, His love, faith in Him, and belief in His promise and His threat, and in which also are the desires of the soul, its traits, and the impulses of passion and nature.

And a heart between these two callers: at one time the caller of faith, knowledge and love of Allah, and the will for Him alone, inclines the heart; at another time the caller of Satan, passion and natural dispositions inclines it.
This heart is one in which Satan has hope, and between them are battles and encounters, and Allah gives victory to whom He wills: "And victory is only from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise" [Al-Anfal: 10]. Satan can gain power over this heart only through what he finds in it of his weapons. He enters it and finds his weapons present, takes them and fights with them. For his weapons are the desires, the doubts, the imaginings and the false hopes, and these are in the heart; so Satan enters, finds them ready, takes them and attacks the heart with them.

If the servant has ready an equipment of faith that opposes that equipment and exceeds it, he gains the upper hand over Satan; otherwise, the victory belongs to his enemy over him, and there is no power nor strength except with Allah.

So if the servant gives permission to his enemy, opens to him the door of his house, admits him, and empowers him with the weapons with which to fight him, then he is the one to be blamed.
"Blame yourself, not the mounts, and die of grief, for you have no excuse."

[Section: The Station of Tranquillity]

Among the stations of "You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help" [Al-Fatihah: 5] is the station of tranquillity (al-tuma'ninah).
Allah the Exalted says: "Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest" [Al-Ra'd: 28]. And Allah the Exalted says: "O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing. Enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise" [Al-Fajr: 27-30].

Tranquillity (al-tuma'ninah) is the heart's settling upon a thing, and its not being disturbed or restless. From it is the well-known report: "Truthfulness is tranquillity, and lying is doubt," meaning that truthfulness brings the listener's heart to rest in it, and he finds calm in it; while lying causes him disturbance and suspicion. And from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Righteousness is that with which the heart is at peace," meaning it settles upon it and its disturbance and restlessness depart from it.

Regarding the remembrance of Allah here, there are two views.
The first: it is the servant's remembrance of his Lord, for his heart finds rest in it and is calm. When the heart is disturbed and restless, there is nothing to bring it tranquillity except the remembrance of Allah.

Then the proponents of this view differed concerning it.
Some said: this refers to oaths. When a believer swears to something, the hearts of the believers settle and are at rest with it. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.
Others said: rather, it is the servant's remembrance of his Lord between himself and Him, by which his heart settles and is at rest.

The second view: the remembrance of Allah here is the Qur'an, which is His remembrance that He sent down to His Messenger. By it the hearts of the believers find tranquillity, for the heart does not find rest except through faith and certainty, and there is no way to attain faith and certainty except through the Qur'an. For the calm and tranquillity of the heart come from its certainty, and its disturbance and restlessness come from its doubt. The Qur'an is what brings about certainty and dispels doubts, suspicions and illusions, so the hearts of the believers find rest only in it. This view is the one preferred.

Likewise, these two views also apply to His saying: "And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion" [Al-Zukhruf: 36].
The correct view is that His remembrance, which He sent down to His Messenger, which is His Book: whoever turns away from it, He appoints for him a devil who misleads him and bars him from the way, while he thinks he is upon guidance.

Likewise, these two views also apply to His saying: "And whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a straitened life, and We shall raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection" [Ta-Ha: 124].
The correct view is that it is His remembrance which He sent down to His Messenger, which is His Book. That is why the one who turned away from it will say: "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was seeing?" He will say: "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten" [Ta-Ha: 125-126].

As for the interpretation of those who understood it as referring to oaths, it is far from the intended meaning. For the remembrance of Allah through oaths is uttered on the tongues of the truthful and the liar, the righteous and the wicked, and the believers' hearts find rest in the truthful even if he does not swear, and their hearts do not find rest in one they doubt even if he swears.

Allah the Glorified placed tranquillity in the hearts and souls of the believers, and He made envy (of their state), praise, and the good news of entry into Paradise for the people of tranquillity. "Good tidings for them, and a good return" [Al-Ra'd: 29].

In the saying of Allah the Exalted, "O soul at peace, return to your Lord" [Al-Fajr: 27], there is evidence that it does not return to Him except when it is at peace. Then it returns to Him, enters among His servants, and enters His Paradise.

It was among the supplications of some of the early righteous (salaf): "O Allah, grant me a soul at peace in You."

[Section: The Degrees of Tranquillity]

[The First Degree: The Tranquillity of the Heart through the Remembrance of Allah]

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: the tranquillity of the heart through the remembrance of Allah. It is the tranquillity of the one who fears to hope, of the one weary to the judgment, and of the afflicted to the reward.

It has already been stated that tranquillity through the remembrance of Allah is through His speech and His Book, and there is no doubt that what he mentioned in this degree is among the forms of tranquillity through His remembrance, and it is more important than that. He mentioned the tranquillity of the fearful in hope, for when fear lengthens upon the fearful and grows severe upon him, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic wishes to give him rest and bear it for him, He sends down upon him tranquillity, and his heart finds rest in hope and is calmed by it, and the blaze of his fear subsides.

As for the tranquillity of the weary in the judgment:
What is meant by it is that whoever is overtaken by weariness from the strength of the obligations, and the burdens and weights of the command, especially one who is appointed to convey the message from Allah, to struggle against the enemies of Allah, and against the brigands on the road to Him, then what he carries and bears is more than what people carry and bear. He is bound to be overtaken by weariness, and his patience weakens. When Allah wishes to give him rest and bear it for him, He sends down upon him His tranquillity, and he finds tranquillity in His religious judgment and in His predestined judgment. There is no tranquillity for him without witnessing both judgments, and his tranquillity is in proportion to his witnessing of them. For when he finds tranquillity in His religious judgment, he knows that His religion is the truth, that it is His straight path, and that He is the helper of it and of its people, their sufficiency and their protector.

And when he finds tranquillity in His cosmic judgment, he knows that nothing will befall him except what Allah has written for him, and that what He wills comes to be and what He does not will does not come to be. There is no reason for impatience and anxiety except weakness of certainty and faith, for what is feared, if it is not decreed, there is no way for it to occur, and if it is decreed, there is no way to avert it after its decree has been finalised. So there is no impatience then, neither at what has been decreed nor at what has not been decreed.

Yes, if there is a remedy for this calamity, he should not become impatient with it; and if there is no remedy for it, he should not become impatient with it either. This is the tranquillity of the weary in the judgment. And in this regard one said:
"What has been decreed, O soul, be patient with it, and you will have security from what was not decreed.
And know that what is decreed will certainly occur; it will befall you whether you were cautious or not."

As for the tranquillity of the afflicted in the reward:
There is no doubt that when the afflicted's witnessing of the reward is strong, his heart is calmed and finds tranquillity in witnessing the recompense. Affliction intensifies upon him only when the contemplation of the reward is absent from him. The contemplation of the recompense may grow so strong that he delights in the affliction and regards it as a blessing. Do not find this far-fetched, for many wise people, when they realise the benefit of a bitter medicine, almost take delight in it, and their contemplation of its benefit makes them forget its pain from its taste, or lightens it for them. The practice relied upon is only upon insight. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Second Degree: The Tranquillity of the Spirit in Intending Unveiling, and in Longing for the Promise, and in Separation Toward Union]

The tranquillity of the spirit is that it finds rest in its intention and does not turn to what lies beyond it.
By unveiling is meant the unveiling of reality, not partial, lower unveiling. It has three degrees.
An unveiling of the path that leads to the goal: this is the unveiling of the realities of faith and the laws of Islam.
And an unveiling of the goal intended by the journey: this is knowledge of the Names and Attributes, the two kinds of monotheism and their details, and observing these as they should be observed.
Beyond that there is nothing but pretensions, ecstatic utterances and delusion.

As for his saying: "and in longing for the promise."
He means that the spirit becomes manifest in its longing for what it has been promised and to which it has been made to yearn; its tranquillity in that promise calms the blaze of its longing. This is the condition of every yearner for a beloved who has been promised union with him; tranquillity comes to his spirit only by its resting upon the promise of meeting, and its knowledge that the promised thing will be attained.

As for his saying: "and in separation toward union"

That is, the soul, in its state of separation, finds rest in what it has become accustomed to of union, when its spirit meets it, so that it settles and is at peace with it, just as the very hungry person is at peace with the food he has. His heart is at rest with it. This only happens to one who has looked upon union from behind a thin veil and glimpsed its lightning. He is at peace by its attainment. As for one between whom and it are thick veils, he is not at peace with it.

[Section: The Third Rank: The Tranquillity of Witnessing the Presence in Gentleness]

He said: The third rank is the tranquillity of witnessing the Presence (al-hadrah) in gentleness, the tranquillity of union (al-jam') in remaining (al-baqa'), and the tranquillity of station (al-maqam) in the light of the pre-eternity (al-azal).

This third rank is connected with annihilation (al-fana') and subsistence (al-baqa'). The one who arrives at witnessing the Presence is at peace with the gentleness of Allah. By "the Presence of union" (hadrat al-jam') they mean the essential witnessing (al-shuhud al-dhati).

Their witnessing has levels according to what it is related to. The witnessing of actions is the first level of witnessing. Above it is the witnessing of the Names and Attributes. Above that is the witnessing of the Essence, which combines actions, Names and Attributes. Manifestation (al-tajalli) among the people of this path is according to these three witnessings.

The companions of the manifestation of actions have as their station the Oneness of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah). The companions of the manifestation of Names and Attributes have as their station the Oneness of Divinity (tawhid al-uluhiyyah). The companions of the manifestation of the Essence are so absorbed in Him that they are rendered oblivious to themselves.

Sometimes, according to the strength of what comes upon the heart and the weakness of the vessel, some of them become incapable of standing and moving. Thus they may neglect some of the obligations. For such a person the ruling is that of others like him among those who are incapable and remiss. The perfect ones among them may slacken, in that state, from arduous deeds, and restrict themselves to the obligatory acts together with their sunnahs and their rights. That witnessing and manifestation does not keep them from these, and they do not prefer over them any of the voluntary acts or movements which have not presented themselves to them at all. That, on their path, is a regression and a cutting-off.

The most complete of these is the one for whom that state accompanies his movements and voluntary acts, so that he neglects not an atom of his litanies. Allah, glorified is He, has made the differences between the powers of hearts far greater than the differences between the powers of bodies. In everything there is a sign. The possessor of this station is a sign from the signs of Allah for people of understanding and insight.

The purpose is this: were it not for his tranquillity in the gentleness of Allah, the witnessing of the Presence would annihilate him and efface him entirely. Moses fell down in a swoon when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, and the mountain was crushed and sank into the earth from His manifestation, glorified is He.

Let no one imagine that what the human being attains in this world is like that, or anywhere near it. What is attained is only knowledge (al-ma'arif) and the domination of the station of excellence (maqam al-ihsan) over the heart, and nothing more.

Beware of the trivialities of these people, their fancies and their follies. Even if they name you "veiled," say: "O Allah, increase me in this veil, beyond which there is nothing but fancies, trivialities and ecstatic utterances (al-shathahat)." The one who spoke with the Most Merciful alone, even with this, the Essence did not manifest to him. His Lord, exalted is He, showed him that he could not endure the manifestation of His Essence, when He made him witness the state of the mountain. Moses the interlocutor fell down in a swoon, unconscious, when he saw what he saw of the state of the mountain at the manifestation of his Lord to it. And that was not an absolute manifestation.

Al-Dahhak said: Allah made appear from the light of the veils the like of the nostril of a bull. 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Nothing of the greatness of Allah manifested to the mountain except like the eye of a needle, until it became dust.

Al-Suddi said: Only the measure of the little finger manifested.

In al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: 'Like this,' and he placed the thumb on the upper joint of the little finger, 'and the mountain sank.'" Its chain is according to the condition of Muslim. When Humayd narrated it from Thabit, some of his companions considered it grave and said: "You narrate this?" So he struck his chest with his hand and said: "Thabit narrates it from Anas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you deny it, and I should not narrate it?"

If those who have been deceived testify that you are veiled from their trivialities and fancies, then that testimony is for you a testimony to your uprightness.

So do not feel estranged from it. Success is from Allah, and He is the One sought for help.

(Fā'idah) [A benefit/point]

He argued for the preference of marriage over devoting oneself to voluntary acts of worship (nawāfil al-ʿibādah) by the fact that God, Exalted and Majestic, chose marriage for His prophets and messengers, saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and assigned for them wives and offspring﴾

And He said concerning Adam: ﴿And He created from it its mate that he might find tranquility in her﴾. He also set aside, from the time of His interlocutor (Kalīm, Moses), ten years of tending sheep as the bride-price (mahr) for the wife. The length of these ten years spent in voluntary acts of worship is known. He chose for His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ the best of things, and He did not desire for him to abandon marriage; rather He married him to nine or more women, and there is no guidance superior to his guidance.

And if there were nothing in it but the joy of the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Boasting over his community, and if there were nothing in it but that his deeds would not be cut off by his death (because a righteous child would remember him)...

And if there were nothing in it but that there would come forth from his loins one who bears witness to God's oneness and to His Messenger's prophethood...

And if there were nothing in it but lowering his gaze and guarding his chastity from turning to what God has forbidden...

And if there were nothing in it but the protection of a woman whom God keeps chaste through him, and his being rewarded for fulfilling his desire and hers, so that he continually increases in his pleasures and in the pages of his good deeds...

And if there were nothing in it but the reward he receives for his expenditure on his wife, her clothing and her dwelling, and for lifting the morsel to her mouth...

And if there were nothing in it but the multiplication of Islam and its people and the enraging of the enemies of Islam...

And if there were nothing in it but the acts of worship that follow from it, which are not attained by one who devotes himself exclusively to voluntary worship...

And if there were nothing in it but the moderation of his carnal power, which diverts him from attaching his heart to what is more beneficial to him in his religion and his worldly life. For the attachment of the heart to desire, or striving against it, prevents it from attaching itself to what is more beneficial to him, since the resolve, whenever it is directed toward one thing, turns away from another...

And if there were nothing in it but his being exposed to daughters, whom if he is patient with and treats well, they will be a screen for him from the Fire...

And if there were nothing in it but that if he has two children who do not reach puberty, God admits him to Paradise because of them...

And if there were nothing in it but that it draws the help of God to him, for in the raised (marfūʿ) hadith: "Three are a right upon God to help them: the one who marries seeking chastity, the one who makes a contract of manumission (mukātab) seeking to pay, and the one who fights in the way of God."

[Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 13, verse 43]

﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾ That is, whoever has knowledge of the Book bears witness for me, and his testimony is accepted because it is testimony based on knowledge. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you. He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And Allah is sufficient as a witness﴾ [al-Nisa: 166]. He also said: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah is witness between me and you"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. In these verses, He, glory be to Him, informs us of His testifying to His Messenger, and His testimony is sufficient as a confirmation of his truthfulness, and He is sufficient as a witness.

If it is asked: What is His testimony to His Messenger?

It is said: It is the signs and proofs He established confirming his truthfulness, which necessarily entail his truthfulness once they are known with certainty. Their indication of his truthfulness is greater than the indication of any evidence or witness for a right. Therefore His testimony to His Messenger is the most truthful and greatest testimony, and the most indicative of the establishment of what is testified to. This is one aspect.

Another aspect: He confirmed him by His word, and established decisive proofs of his truthfulness in what he reports from Him. So when He reports that He testified for him by saying (the testimony), it necessarily follows that the report is true, and the testimony for him by it is certainly valid. This is the meaning of the verse.

[Section: Seeking Testimony for the Message through Allah's Testimony to Him]

From this is His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "You are not a messenger." Say: "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]

So He sought testimony for His Messenger's message through Allah's testimony for him. This testimony must be known, and the proof must be established by it against those who deny him. Likewise is His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah is witness between me and you"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. Likewise is His saying: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you. He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And Allah is sufficient as a witness﴾ [al-Nisa: 166]. Likewise is His saying: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya Sin: 1-3], and His saying: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 252], and His saying: ﴿And Allah knows that you are His messenger﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], and His saying: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. All of this is testimony from Him to His Messenger. He has made it manifest and clarified it, and clarified its validity with the utmost clarity, such that He has cut off excuse between Him and His servants and established the proof against them. Thus His being a witness to His Messenger is known through all kinds of evidence: rational, transmitted, innate, self-evident, and reasoned.

Whoever reflects on this and contemplates it will know that Allah, glory be to Him, bore witness to His Messenger with the most truthful, most just and most manifest testimony, and confirmed him in all kinds of confirmation: by His word, which establishes the proofs of his truthfulness in it; by His deed and His approval; and by what He has instilled in His servants of acknowledging His perfection and His transcendence above defects and above whatever is unfitting for Him. At every time He brings forth signs indicating the truthfulness of His Messenger, by which He establishes the proof, removes the excuse, and decides in his favor and in favor of his followers what He has promised them of might, deliverance, victory and support, and decides against his enemies and deniers what He has threatened them with: disgrace, punishment and hastened penalties, which indicate the realization of the deferred penalties. ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion, and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [al-Fath: 28]. So He makes him prevail in two ways: prevailing by proof, clarification and indication, and prevailing by victory, triumph, dominance and support, until He makes him prevail over his opponents and he becomes victorious.

As for His saying: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you. He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness﴾ [al-Nisa: 166], what it contains of the report about Allah's knowledge, which no one else can produce, is among the greatest testimony that He is the One who sent it down. As He said in another verse: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful." And if they do not respond to you, then know that it was sent down with the knowledge of Allah, and that there is no deity except Him. Will you then be Muslims?﴾ [Hud: 13-14].

The intention is not merely the report that He sent it down, which is known to Him as He knows all other things, for everything is known to Him, whether true or false. Rather the meaning is that He sent it down containing His knowledge. So its descent containing His knowledge is the sign that it is from Him and that it is truth and sincerity. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Say: "He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Furqan: 6], which He mentioned as a denial and rejection of those who said: "He has invented it."
